https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmx2: At least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, according to Russian government statistics analysed by the BBC.

The leaked Rosstat data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia, and show the high cost paid in human life in a war that Vladimir Putin had assumed would last only days but is now almost five years old.
BBC Russian has had access to more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, after a hack by Belarusian group Cyber Partisans BY and Ukraine's Silent Crow.
Russia's statistics agency admitted to a cyber-attack, but denied any protected information had been leaked.

Together with independent Russian outlet Mediazona, BBC Russian has compared the Rosstat data with its own list of confirmed military deaths, pulled from open sources since the start of the invasion, and it has found matches for 90% of the records.

Military experts estimate that the BBC's list of 290,012 deaths, gleaned from official reports, social media, new memorials and graves, may account for 45-55% of the true death toll, which would range from 527,295 to 644,471.

The records show that 65% of 18 to 24 year-olds in Russia who lost their lives in 2025 died in the war. For those aged 25-34 the number was 59%. Only among 45 to 54 year-olds does cardiovascular disease claim more Russian lives than the conflict.
The data also reveal the extent of losses in specific areas of Ukraine. Some 20,000 Russian soldiers died fighting for control of 10 Ukrainian villages whose combined pre-war population was 12,000.
During the fight for one small village called Andriivka, south of the town of Bakhmut in Donetsk region, 1,122 Russians lost their lives. Before the war 74 people lived there.

Russia does not give public figures for losses sustained since the war began in February 2022. And two years ago Rosstat stopped publishing data of deaths from external causes, which was used to gauge the extent of military losses.

For example, only 70% of deaths we have established of soldiers from the occupied regions of Donetsk and Luhansk in eastern Ukraine who fought in the Russian army were accounted for in the Rosstat files.
Overall, the Rosstat dataset confirms the trends that we have observed with our own count.
Ukrainian losses were last put at about 50,000 by President Volodymyr Zelensky in July 2026, but another list based on open sources by the anonymous UA Losses website puts the figure at 115,952.
The Rosstat dataset contains no names but does include ages, places of residence, places of death and also circumstances of death.
We have filtered the records first by location, leaving only Ukraine as well as Russian border regions that saw incursions by the Ukrainian army.
Next, we identified 425,174 entries explicitly indicating a military-related cause of death, such as explosions or shrapnel during combat operations.

As this count could include civilians, we filtered out women as well as men outside the 18-65 age group. And if someone lived and died in the four Ukrainian regions occupied by Russia, we excluded them as a possible civilian – unless he had a record of military service attached to his entry.

Another 14,093 entries were identified by looking at employment, and 51,067 were recorded in the database as deceased on the basis of a court ruling. This often happens when a soldier goes missing in a combat zone for more than six months and their body has not been recovered.
Again, we filtered out civilians by only counting deaths in the war zones in Ukraine and Russia.

According to BBC Russian's analysis of the leaked files, in the first year of the war the average age of those killed was 34. By 2025, as prisoners and contract soldiers entered the ranks, it had risen to 40 (38 according to our own list).
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crpd: US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether the AI chipmaker was under federal investigation.
Blanche said he had no information about newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang's security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's comeback.
Huang was given his job back less than two weeks after being forced to resign over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
Asked several times on Tuesday if the justice department or FBI had investigated Huang, Blanche responded: "I don't know what you're talking about."

Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where he will be questioned about national security concerns over his relationship with an alleged China spy who led Megaspeed, a Singapore-based corporate customer of Nvidia.
Trump has said he would consider pardoning Huang for any potential criminal activity, though he does not think it will come to that.
"It's always an option, I guess, but I don't think it'll be necessary," Trump told the New York Post in an interview published on Tuesday.
With Huang rescue, Trump riskily ties his political fortunes to Nvidia
The US commerce department has also announced it was preparing to blacklist the tech company Megaspeed, which has been suspected of helping to divert advanced chips to China.
In a joint statement last week, the commerce and justice departments said they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations" .
But speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Blanche said the latter department has "hundreds, if not more" export investigations occurring at any one time.
"So when you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don't know what you're talking about," he said.

Asked if he was satisfied Nvidia had been co-operative with any efforts to get to the bottom of whether the company or Huang potentially knew about any chips being diverted to China, Blanche said: "I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.

"Obviously, if Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that the president is saying to the American people.
While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the announcement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.
The company's share price closed down nearly 6% - still well above where it ended last week. On Monday, Nvidia stock rocketed more than 31% following news of Huang's return.
Huang reportedly apologised to Nvidia employees on Tuesday, the day after returning to the company as chief executive, saying he made "terrible mistakes" and is now in therapy for 90 minutes per day.

The company's board reinstated Huang on Monday in a shock U-turn. Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said Huang's return was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".
The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.
On Monday, Trump said he spoke to the company's directors and convinced them to bring back Huang .
Republican congressman Don Bacon said Nvidia should have "ignored the Administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang".
Republican Senator Pete Ricketts said Huang's behaviour "doesn't absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips".
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmy4: Defence lawyer Brian Heberlig makes closing arguments at the Huawei Technologies trial at Brooklyn federal court on November 17.
Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark case in the US.
In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage.
Huawei's defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm's success was due to its own innovation.
Huawei said , external the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis", adding that it would "take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests".
Jurors in a Brooklyn court found Huawei guilty of 10 out of 12 counts, which included conspiracy to violate US sanctions.
However, the jury declined to convict Huawei of the racketeering conspiracy charge, which required members to find the firm acted like a criminal enterprise.
Federal prosecutors first announced the charges against Huawei in 2019, after the dramatic arrest in late 2018 of senior executive Meng Wanzhou in Canada.
Meng, also known as Cathy Meng, was held for three years in Canada before she was released to return to China through a deal with US prosecutors.

During closing arguments last week, assistant US attorney Meredith Arfa told jurors Huawei spent 20 years doing whatever it took to expand its business, including lying to banks about its business dealings in Iran and stealing technology secrets from rival firms to ensure it had a competitive edge.
"For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft," US Attorney General Todd Blanche said in statement , external .
"Thanks to the work of the FBI and our federal prosecutors, those who engaged in these criminal activities will be held accountable."
However, defence attorney Brian Heberlig said it was by dint of hard work that Huawei's business had expanded with operations in 170 countries and more than 200,000 staff.
Following the verdict, Heberlig told the BBC that Huawei was gratified that the jury had rejected the racketeering charge.

"The RICO [Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act] count that alleged that Huawei was a corrupt organisation, with a corporate culture and policy of committing crime. That was, in our view, a significant overreach, and the jury soundly rejected it," he said.
"Of course, we have mixed emotions about the rest of the verdict ... [we] thought that Huawei was deserving of acquittals across the board."
Sentencing is planned for September 2027. Heberlig said there will be "significant advocacy" to achieve the lowest sentence possible. Following that, he said he fully expects Huawei to appeal.
"If I know Huawei, that fight will continue, and the company's not going to rest until it's pursued every last argument it can through appeal, and hopefully, ultimately toward vindication," he said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw8d: The Hera spacecraft will study the 150m-wide (490ft) asteroid called Dimorphos
A spacecraft has arrived at an asteroid to investigate the damage caused by an unprecedented cosmic crash.
It what may sound like the plot of a disaster movie, Nasa's Dart spacecraft deliberately smashed into the space rock in 2022 to knock it off course.

The Nasa craft was obliterated on impact. Four years on, a European Space Agency (ESA) mission, called Hera, is scouring the scene to fully assess the aftermath of the collision - with the first images set to be released later on Wednesday.
The asteroid poses no threat, instead this was the first ever test of our planetary defences to see what action we could take if a space rock was heading for our planet.
"Hera is a sort of Inspector Columbo going back to the crash scene to investigate what is the outcome of this impact," said Patrick Michel, principal investigator of ESA's Hera mission.
This was the last image from Dart before it crashed into Dimorphos in 2022
The crash test focussed on a pair of asteroids: a larger one called Didymos - about 730m (2,400ft) wide - which is orbited by a smaller rock called Dimorphos, about 150m (490ft) wide.

The Dart spacecraft targeted Dimorphos, hurtling into the rock at 22,000km per hour (14,000mph). Images beamed back showed the asteroid's rocky surface coming ever closer until the feed cut out on impact.
It was such a big smash-up that the trail of debris, measuring about 10,000km long (6,200 miles), was spotted by telescopes on Earth and in space.
The crash showed it was possible to change the path of the smaller asteroid.
Before the collision it took Dimorphos 11 hours and 55 minutes to orbit around Didymos. After the Dart crash, the duration of its orbit had shrunk by about 33 minutes.
But the arrival of the second spacecraft, Hera, will help scientists to answer many more questions.
"Dart exploded in the asteroid, and therefore we don't have the information of what is its final state," explained Michel.
"The impact could have left a crater - and if it is the case, we need to understand the size and the depth. Or [the impact] may have entirely reshaped the asteroid."
A 10,000km-long (6,200 miles) debris trail was spotted by the Hubble Space Telescope
The Hera mission will spend the next year studying Dimorphos, and take a look at Didymos too.
The spacecraft is packed with instruments, and it also has two small shoe-boxed sized satellites onboard, which can study the impact site up close, and then later land on the asteroid.
A key task is to measure the mass of Dimorphos, to work out how effective the spacecraft's shove was.
This information would be vital if we ever spotted a space rock that was on a collision course with Earth.
"It would help us to predict what would happen if we had to hit another asteroid," said Prof Simon Green, a planetary scientist who is on Hera's science team.
"We [could] measure its properties and say: 'Well, we need this mass of spacecraft, travelling at this speed, this early, in order to deflect it enough so that it misses the Earth'."
Hera has already sent back an image of Didymos with Dimorphos in the background
The biggest, which measure more than a kilometre across, could cause global devastation. But medium-sized asteroids around the same dimensions as Dimorphos could wipe out a city.

"We all know what happened to the dinosaurs, right? And we don't want that to happen to us," said Carolyn Ernst, Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, who works on both the Dart and Hera missions.
"The good news for us is that there are far fewer potential threats out there in the Solar System than there were millions of years ago. But there are objects out there."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmy0: As food inflation rises, vegetables are becoming an increasingly expensive part of the household budget
India's inflation is rising again. And the biggest worry is what's happening to food prices.
The latest government data , external shows retail inflation climbed to 6.09% in October, up from 5.54% in September.
But look more closely at food inflation. It has surged to 8.94%.
The squeeze was sharper in rural India, where food inflation was 9.09%, compared with 8.68% in urban areas.
In other words, food prices are rising considerably faster than the overall rate of inflation.
Food inflation this year has been driven by a combination of weather disruptions, supply shortages and rising input costs, say economists.

With nearly 60% of its farmland dependent on rainfall , external , India remains acutely vulnerable to the vagaries of the monsoon. This year, the southwest monsoon was 13% below normal and unevenly distributed, while intensifying El Niño conditions have heightened risks to farm production.
Onion prices have surged, adding to the pressure on household food budgets
A survey by polling agency LocalCircles found that six in 10 consumers say household essentials cost them over 20% more each month than a year ago, prompting calls for government intervention.
Rising prices are also forcing cutbacks: 74% are curbing discretionary spending on eating out, shopping and entertainment, while half are buying smaller quantities of essentials.
Food accounts for a smaller share of Indian household spending than it once did, but remains the biggest driver of inflation, with significant economic, social and political consequences.
In India's latest consumer price index, food and beverages account for 36.75% of the basket of goods and services used to measure inflation.
That is down sharply from 45.86% under the previous series, reflecting changing consumption patterns as Indians spend more on services, transport, healthcare, education and other non-food items.
Yet a sharp increase in food prices can move the overall inflation rate significantly, while disproportionately affecting people whose incomes leave little room for adjustment.

"Adjustability for a poor country like India is significantly lower," says Rajeswari Sengupta, an associate professor of economics at Mumbai-based Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, pointing to the fact that a substantial proportion of household income is still spent on food.
According to calculations by Dharmakirti Joshi, chief economist at analytics firm Crisil, the bottom 20% of rural households faced inflation of 6.9% in October, against 6.5% for the richest 20%.

Crisil's Roti Rice Rate analysis , external found that the cost of a home-cooked vegetarian thali - a meal platter - rose 12% year-on-year in October, driven by higher prices of onions, tomatoes, vegetables, edible oil, rice and cooking gas. A non-vegetarian thali became 9% more expensive.

Rice prices were up about 10% year-on-year, pulses 8%, edible oil 13% and LPG 10%, according to Pushan Sharma, director of intelligence at Crisil. "It's no longer a few commodities that are driving this increase, it's becoming a little more broad-based," he says.
When onion prices spike, households can cut back on their consumption to some extent. But substituting rice, pulses and cooking oil is considerably harder.

And food inflation is not just about what farmers produce. It is also about how efficiently that food is stored, processed and moved to the market. Weaknesses at each stage can turn seasonal shortages into sharp price spikes - and gluts into waste.
Onions, for instance, are particularly susceptible to seasonal price swings.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crwy: Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex has been charged by a federal grand jury in Los Angeles with possessing child sex abuse images.

Markle, who remains in custody in Florida, allegedly possessed materials that include at least one image involving a prepubescent minor and a minor under 12 years old, court documents filed in California show.
The 82-year-old has denied possessing images of child sex abuse.
Last week, a judge in Florida declared Prince Harry's father-in-law mentally competent to stand trial.
The FBI arrested Markle on 6 November at an elderly care home in Florida on a single federal charge of possessing child sexual abuse material. He now faces two counts.
US attorney Bill Essayli said Markle faces a maximum of 20 years in prison on each count if convicted.
His arrest came after a search of a storage unit he had allegedly rented in Los Angeles for almost two decades uncovered the abuse material.
Markle was initially released on conditional bail but was then ordered to stay in jail pending trial after allegedly removing a location monitoring device.
Watch: Thomas Markle's charges over child sexual abuse material

In the indictment, filed by the US Attorney's Office in the Central District of California, Markle is accused of knowingly possessing 35mm film negatives on 30 October and 4 November that contained child sexual abuse materials.
The US Attorney's Office said that during both instances Markle allegedly knew the images contained such materials.
Inside the storage units, federal agents found two images that depict an adult man - whom a witness identified as Markle - with an underage child, the US attorney's office said.

They also alleged that a third image appears to depict a child in a room believed to be part of a motel chain in the Philippines. Markle moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and he lived in Cebu until May.
"The affidavit also describes additional photographs that appear to show Markle with children in various stages of undress," prosecutors said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c680: Kilmar Ábrego García, whose deportation last year to El Salvador sparked a bitter deportation battle, has left the US for Spain.

After the government admitted it had wrongfully sent Ábrego García to his home country, he was returned to the US to face human trafficking charges, which were later dropped. The administration then continued its attempts to send him to other countries, including Uganda and Ghana.
His deportation and return became a flashpoint in the debate over President Donald Trump's immigration agenda.
Ábrego García, who is married to a US citizen and lived in Maryland, came to the US illegally from El Salvador as a teenager.
Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, visited Ábrego García while he was in the notorious Cecot prison in El Salvador in 2025 and advocated for his release.

"A year and a half ago, the Trump Administration wanted to leave Kilmar Ábrego García to rot in a Salvadoran gulag," Van Hollen said in a statement on Tuesday. "Today, Kilmar is travelling to a country of his choice, a free man - unharmed and with dignity."
In a statement, Ábrego García's lawyer said his departure was "temporary" as he had "many options to return to the United States".

"We don't expect that to happen under this administration, which we know will never give him a fair shake, but we expect that the next administration will prioritize reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland," the statement said.
"Where he goes from here, where he chooses to settle for the next two years while he waits out the end of this administration, will be his choice, not the administration's choice."
The BBC has contacted the US Department of Homeland Security for comment.

Ábrego García was arrested in 2019 alongside three other men and detained by federal immigration authorities. A judge granted him protection from deportation to El Salvador at the time, citing the risk of persecution by a gang there.

In March 2025, the Trump administration deported him to El Salvador, where he was held in Cecot, a prison known for its harsh conditions. The US Supreme Court then ordered the government to facilitate his return.

The administration admitted that he was deported in error and brought him back to the US where he was set to face human trafficking charges. A federal judge dismissed the case, saying Ábrego García had been charged for political reasons.
For months, he was locked in a battle over deportation with the government.
Ábrego García had repeatedly said he would be willing to be deported to Costa Rica, and the Costa Rican government had agreed to accept him as a refugee and provide him with legal status.
After reports emerged that the administration was considering sending him to Uganda, a judge barred the government from deporting Ábrego García to a third country.
At one point the Trump administration requested that the judge lift the order so that Ábrego García could be deported to Liberia, CBS reported.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqgk: Kim Jong Un's communist regime is accused of brutal crackdowns on religious freedom in a new report
Living in North Korea, Kim Bo-bin got used to praying with her eyes open.

She found ingenious ways to keep her Christian faith a secret in the Communist dictatorship, which tightly controls how and where its citizens worship. Unauthorised displays of faith could land people in prison, she tells the BBC.

So Kim would silently mouth hymns and clap with just two of her fingers. "In North Korea, if there are three people in a room, you are being spied on. So I would only close my eyes [and pray] when I lay on the floor."
Now 44, Kim lives just outside the South Korean capital Seoul, where she fled 15 years ago.

Her testimony - of how she prayed in secret for years, and was jailed and beaten for her faith - is part of a new report documenting the experiences of 570 North Korean escapees, most of whom say they experienced or witnessed anti-Christian persecution.

Spanning five years and featuring interviews with defectors from across the country, the report by British human rights group Korea Future accuses Kim Jong Un's regime of repeatedly violating religious freedom through a system of surveillance, fear and violence. It suggests little has changed after sustained international pressure, with multiple incidents of suspected Christians being beaten and tortured as recently as last year.

North Korea maintains that it allows religious freedom in spite of years of evidence heard by rights groups and the United Nations. While churches exist in Pyongyang, they are controlled by the state and widely seen as projecting an illusion of religious liberty.

"The North Korean leader's authority is god-like," says Kang Dong-wan, professor at Dong-a University. "So they cannot allow gods whose authority is above him." Pyongyang fears that religious freedom may threaten the regime itself, he adds.

First established in Korea in the late 1700s, Christianity exploded across the north after Protestant missionaries arrived in the 1880s. North Korea provides no figures on its Christian population but the UN has referred to estimates of 200,000 to 400,000 of them practising secretly, some of whom are detained in camps.
Surveillance and control over religion, like many other aspects of North Korean life, intensified under Kim Jong Un, who succeeded his father in 2011.

Three South Korean missionaries operating in the Chinese border region were arrested between 2013-2014 and sentenced to life in prison on charges of espionage and plotting a coup. It's not clear if they are still alive, as Seoul says Pyongyang has refused to share any information about the detainees.

Pyongyang has also been cracking down on smuggled memory sticks containing South Korean-made videos of Christian sermons. In 2020, it passed a law - on Rejecting Reactionary Ideology and Culture - to block so-called "foreign influence". Owning Bibles and hosting services can now result in imprisonment, while distributing religious books or videos is punishable by death.

Lessons against religion begin as early as kindergarten for most North Koreans. Children must attend "self-criticism" sessions at school in which they are warned against "superstitions", widely understood to refer to Christianity and other faiths.
An image from 2010 showing the inside of a state-sanctioned church in Pyongyang

This is what Kim Bo-bin recalls being taught. The faiths Koreans have long practised - Christianity since the 18th Century and shamanism, a millennia-old practice rooted in ancestral spirit worship - were dismissed as superstitions.
Her teachers never mentioned that Kim Il Sung himself was born into a fervently Christian family, or that Pyongyang had once been dubbed the "Jerusalem of the East."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6d9: Bellarmine Chatunga is the youngest son of Robert Mugabe and his second wife, Grace Mugabe
A Zimbabwean court has issued an arrest warrant for Bellarmine Chatunga Mugabe, the youngest son of the country's late former president Robert Mugabe, after he failed to appear in court.
Mugabe was arrested earlier this month alongside four others over assault allegations on a police officer during an investigation into the suspected smuggling of luxury vehicles.
The group subsequently faced charges of robbery and malicious damage to property. They have yet to enter pleas.

They were granted bail on 6 November and were due back in court on Tuesday. However, Mugabe failed to attend. His co-accused, an aide and three security guards appeared and were remanded until 10 December.
Prosecutors allege that Mugabe and the others assaulted an investigating officer using their hands and broomsticks.
The officer's phone was allegedly taken and smashed on the ground, while one of the accused is said to have seized the officer's loaded pistol.
Bellarmine Chatunga is the youngest son of Robert Mugabe and his second wife, Grace Mugabe.
Robert Mugabe ruled Zimbabwe for 37 years before being forced from power in 2017, aged 93, following a military intervention. He died in 2019.
His son has attracted public attention in recent years over a series of legal troubles and his high-profile lifestyle.
Last month, he admitted to drug-related charges involving the possession of cannabis.

In April, he was deported from neighbouring South Africa after pleading guilty to pointing a firearm and being in the country illegally. He had been arrested following the shooting of a 23-year-old man at his home.
In 2023, he was arrested in Harare, Zimbabwe's capital, over allegations that he damaged property and spat at a police officer during a party.
He was later freed after reaching an out-of-court settlement with the complainant, who was a friend.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cv70: Taiwan's ruling party is being repeatedly targeted with AI videos spreading false claims about its leader and other key members ahead of crucial local elections, BBC Verify has found.

A China-linked network has pumped out more than 500 fake videos about the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) in the past year, which experts suggest is part of a long-running campaign to influence the outcome of the elections.

The videos appear to try to smear President Lai Ching-te by claiming he holds a US green card - and would abandon Taiwan if war broke out with China - which Taiwan's presidential office says is completely false. Deepfakes also appear to show Puma Shen, who is running to be the mayor of capital Taipei, using drugs, which he denies. Others seek to undermine or ridicule the politicians by showing them in children's clothing or as popular film characters.

The Taipei mayoralty has traditionally served as a springboard to the presidency. Experts say this has made Shen, who has been openly critical of Beijing, an obvious target for disinformation campaigns. The current mayor, Chiang Wan-an, is part of Taiwan's Kuomintang (KMT) party, which favours closer ties with China.

Taiwan is a self-governing island that China claims as part of its territory. Beijing and Taipei have long observed an uneasy status quo under which Taiwan, backed by the US, neither formally declares independence nor unites with China.

But tensions have risen since the DPP came to power in 2016. Beijing has repeatedly accused the party of pursuing independence while China's leader Xi Jinping, who has said "reunification" with Taiwan is a key goal, has stepped up pressure against the party with increased military activity around the island.
Experts believe the current disinformation activity is part of a broader campaign against Taiwan designed to undermine trust in its democratic process.
The campaign has targeted Taiwan's President Lai (top) and his predecessor Tsai (bottom)

"The account operators are trying to make people distrust the DPP politicians so that they will not believe whatever they say," Austin Horng-En Wang, an expert in cognitive warfare at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, told BBC Verify. "If you don't trust that candidate then you will not listen to what they say," he added.

The videos, many of which were shared from an account called "noxparable" or carried a watermark with the same name, have been viewed tens of millions of times across several social media platforms since May 2025.

More than half of those views were tracked in the past four months as the activity has ramped up ahead of the elections. Many of the accounts involved in spreading disinformation listed their locations on social media as mainland China and Hong Kong, while a number of the clips carried labels showing they were generated with AI. Many people who engaged with the videos were often seen repeating the false claims or attacking DPP figures in the comments, while others appeared to treat the clips as entertainment.

One of the most widely shared videos targeted Shen by superimposing his face onto a man who is seen holding a lighter and exhaling smoke alongside claims he is smoking drugs. The video appears to build on accusations from Taiwan's opposition party that he supports drugs decriminalisation, which Shen denies, and was debunked by a local news network.

Shen has taken legal action against people sharing deepfakes, local media reported, while his campaign office said AI videos showing the candidate appeared to be part of a "classic tactic China uses to smear specific targets". BBC Verify contacted the Chinese embassy in London for comment.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6rr: A funeral was held earlier in southern Gaza for three Palestinians killed in an Israeli strike
At least seven Palestinians, including a senior Hamas security official, have been killed in Israeli air strikes in the Gaza Strip, health officials and first responders say.

Naeem Abu Nahel, the head of Hamas's internal security service, was targeted in western Gaza City, Gaza's Hamas-run interior ministry said. The 50-year-old had only been in the position since September, when his predecessor was captured in a raid by Israeli special forces .
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz announced that Abu Nahel was "eliminated" by the Israeli military.
The six other people were killed in two earlier air strikes elsewhere in Gaza.

Three people, including a teenage boy, were killed in the Wadi Gaza area, south of Gaza City, according to the health officials and first responders. The other three were killed at a police station in the al-Mawasi area, west of Khan Younis, they added.

Gaza's police force, which operates under the interior ministry, said two of its officers were among those who died in the second attack. It also accused Israel of "an ongoing campaign targeting the police apparatus aimed at sowing chaos" in the territory.
The Israeli military said it struck "military operatives" in both areas.
Witnesses said an Israeli drone targeted Naeem Abu Nahel as he was walking on a side street near a tent camp for displaced people in Gaza City.
Several other people were reportedly seriously injured in the strike.

The Israeli military said Abu Nahel had "possessed extensive institutional knowledge" about Hamas's internal security service - which is responsible for enforcing discipline, protecting infrastructure and rooting out informants - and that his death constituted "a blow to the apparatus's management capabilities".
It also alleged that he had advanced attacks on Israeli troops and civilians during the war and that it killed him "to remove the threat he posed".

Gaza's interior ministry said Abu Nahel's killing followed what it described as the internal security service's "important achievements in combating gangs collaborating with the occupation [Israel] and operating in areas under the control of its military".
Gaza's health ministry warned that there was a rapid rise in cases of meningitis in October

Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under Hamas's control, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.
At least 1,679 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza during the same period.
The humanitarian situation also remains dire, with heavy rainfall earlier this month causing flooding and damage to thousands of shelters for displaced families.

The UN and its partners have called on Israel - which controls Gaza's crossings - to allow in more supplies to help Palestinians prepare for the winter, including tents, heaters and water pumps, as well as vaccines and medicines to combat infectious diseases.
On Tuesday, the health ministry warned that there had been a rapid rise in cases of meningitis, with 272 reported in October - about eight times the usual monthly average.
Fifteen deaths had been attributed to the infection so far this year, including five reported between August and October, it said.

Israeli military body Cogat said on Monday it was "working to provide a dedicated humanitarian response" and that a newly approved package of pumps, generators, water tankers and medical equipment had been presented at a meeting with UN agencies.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm5y: Watch: India's government is 'scared', cockroach movement leader says after travel ban
One of the leaders of India's "cockroach" movement has said the Delhi government has "completely lost the plot" after he was stopped from leaving the country for the UK.
Saurav Das said he was meant to board a flight on Tuesday morning but was told by immigration officers his passport had been "flagged" because of discrepancies involving his date of birth.

In an interview with the BBC, Das said there were no discrepancies in his documents, accusing the Indian government of using cheap tactics to stop activists from travelling and speaking on issues that matter to young people.
The BBC has reached out to the federal home ministry, Delhi police and airport officials for comment.
Saurav told the BBC World Service's Newshour programme the incident showed the government was "scared".

"They are scared of the cockroach movement. They're scared of young people asking them questions because they have never had to deal with a generation that wants to ask questions so head on. So that jitters them."
By not allowing him to travel, he said the government had lowered India's stature in the world.
"It's international news that I am unable to travel to the UK," he said. "And this shows Prime Minister Modi in such poor light.
"It's a way to harass, to target activists, young voices in India by the Modi government."
Das said he had been invited by the Oxford Union, as well as universities including Cambridge and Edinburgh, to speak about the movement.

Ratna Singh, another leader of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), wrote: "The manner in which Saurav was not allowed to board today raises deeply troubling questions about the state of freedom of expression and the space being allowed for young voices in this country."

On Tuesday, the London School of Economics Student Union's Amnesty International Unit, a student-led charity group, shared a post on Instagram saying that an event featuring Das had been "indefinitely postponed".
Saurav Das (L) speaking following the resignation of India's education minister in July
Das, a former journalist, became one of the faces of the CJP - a Gen Z-led movement that began as satire but has since emerged as a youth-led pressure group.
In July, protests spearheaded by the CJP over exam paper leaks led to the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan .

In October, CJP leaders including Das were among thousands detained by the police for trying to hold protests demanding the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls. Kumar and the Election Commission have denied wrongdoing.
The same month, Das and Ashutosh Ranka, another CJP leader, were jailed for seven days after being arrested for trespassing at a banned protest site in Delhi.
Das insisted the CJP would continue protesting, but it did not want to be a political party "as of today".

"It's a long haul. We are not here for a short time. We are looking at India in the next 10 to 20 years. How do we develop India into a better country? That is the vision that we want to carry forward."

Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of CJP, wrote on X that if Das "had looted a bank or committed financial fraud", he may have been allowed to fly to London, referring to billionaire bank-loan defaulters who have left India.
There have been other instances in recent years of people being prevented from boarding flights.
In September 2025, Bhanu Tatak, an environmental and anti-dam activist from India's north-eastern Arunachal Pradesh state, was stopped from boarding a flight to Dublin.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c893: Syrians coming back after the war are falling victim to mines and other explosives
Eleven-year-old Alaa was tending her family's goats with her siblings in a field behind their home in Umm Khuzaym, north-west Syria, on Sunday when there was a flash and a deafening bang.
"Then we heard people screaming," Alaa's father, Walid Mohammed Al-Ghafar, told the BBC.
Walid ran outside to find his daughter lying face down, killed, and her 10-year-old brother, Mahmoud, seriously injured.

The incident and others this week bring to nearly 1,000 the number of children killed or injured by explosive ordnance in Syria since the fall of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, according to the UN Mine Action Service (Unmas).
The village is one of many where families have returned to homes and farmland that were once on the front lines of Syria's 13-year civil war.
Alaa's father said demining teams had visited several times to clear the fields. He and other residents believed it was safe for farmers and children to move around.
But mines and other explosives can lie far beyond former battle lines, making it difficult to establish which areas are safe.

"Remnants of war from today's conflicts are often very widely and broadly scattered, often without patterns, which makes it extremely difficult to do clearance," Katrin Atkins, research lead at Landmine Monitor, a global mine monitoring initiative, told the BBC.
The dangers are reflected in a sharp rise in casualties across Syria.

A total of 1,602 people were killed or injured by landmines and explosive remnants of war in 2025 alone, an increase of more than 50% on the previous year, according to the Landmine Monitor report, published by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines on Tuesday.
The report attributes the rise in Syria partly to the large-scale return of refugees and internally displaced people following Assad's overthrow.

"When you look at population movement, a couple of months later you see an increase of incidents in these areas, because that's exactly where people go and start to use the fields again," Atkins said.

More than 60% of casualties recorded by the world's largest landmine clearance charity, the Halo Trust, involve farming, agriculture or shepherding, according to its Syria programme manager, Simon Jackson.
"They're not going to wait for the government or for organisations like us to come and tell them that everything is safe and clear," he told the BBC. "People are taking risks out of desperation."
Since Assad's fall on 8 December 2024, Unmas has recorded at least 1,556 incidents in Syria involving explosive ordnance.
They have caused 2,701 casualties: 935 people killed and 1,766 injured. Children account for 995 of those victims, or about 37%.
But the toll is likely to be higher, with experts estimating that overall casualties could be under-reported by 25-50%.
Both government forces and rebels laid land mines during the civil war
For many of those who survive, the consequences are devastating and permanent.

Majid Abdul Rahman, 27, was travelling in a car in the Ghouta region on the outskirts of Damascus in March 2025 when it struck an explosive device. The vehicle filled with smoke and he felt a pain in his leg.
More than a year later, Majid has difficulty walking and has been unable to return to work, leaving him struggling to provide for his family.
The danger has continued into this month, with at least 20 people killed and more than 40 injured by explosive ordnance in November.

In one of the worst recorded incidents, an explosion in a school courtyard in Hasakah on 4 November killed a 12-year-old and injured 19 others. And on Monday, a 13-year-old boy was killed when an unexploded cluster munition detonated in southern Daraa province.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmgl: Umar Farouk Umar has been on the throne since 2007, succeeding his brother, who reigned for 41 years
One of Nigeria's best-known monarchs, the Emir of Daura, has been suspended from all official engagements and travel following allegations of sexual assault by a Polish tourist.
The visitor said Umar Farouk Umar, 92, had grabbed her chest during a tourism encounter and that she felt disgusted by the experience.
The allegation sparked widespread discussion across social media platforms, with many calling for the suspension of the emir and an investigation - calls the Katsina state government has now heeded.

He is one of several emirs - a traditional role dating back to pre-colonial times - who still wield great cultural and religious influence in northern Nigeria, although they have lost their political power.

Daura, where Umar serves as emir, holds an extremely important position for the Hausa people who dominate northern Nigeria. It is widely regarded as their spiritual homeland and the origin of the Hausa royal lineage, serving as the core of Hausa origin mythology and the legitimate foundation of traditional authority.
Politicians routinely visit his palace for royal prayers and to gain his support.
On her Instagram page, the tourist said she had spent 30 days travelling around Nigeria before visiting the Emir's palace on 14 November.
She posted a video, which has since been deleted, in which a man who appears to be the emir is holding her hands in his lap.
After some moments she was heard saying: "Stop, stop" as the hands reached for her chest.
According to a statement, Katsina Governor Dikko Umaru Radda directed the immediate constitution of a committee to investigate the allegations.
The statement said the state government was taking the allegations seriously and would rely on the committee's findings to determine the appropriate course of action.
It said the committee's findings and recommendations would be fully implemented, stressing that justice would be served.
However, it did not disclose the membership of the investigative committee, its terms of reference or the timeline for submitting its report.
The emir has been on the throne since 2007, succeeding his brother Bashar dan Umaru, who reigned for 41 years.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c65y: Nicolas Sarkozy and his wife Carla Bruni-Sarkozy are to face trial next year over charges stemming from the former French president's conviction for conspiring to fund his election campaign with money from late Libyan dictator Muammar Gaddafi.
The charges centre on the retraction of the testimony of a key witness who had initially said he had evidence that could incriminate Sarkozy.

Sarkozy was given a five-year sentence in the case last September and became the first French ex-president to go to jail, even though he only spent 20 days behind bars. He has always denied doing anything wrong in the case and the appeals verdict is expected next Monday.
Since losing his re-election bid in 2012, Sarkozy has faced several criminal investigations.
In 2024, he was handed a one-year sentence – of which six months were suspended – over the illegal financing of his 2012 re-election campaign.

In 2021, he was found guilty of trying to bribe a judge and sentenced to three years in jail – two of them suspended – and thus became the first former French president to get a custodial sentence. He was allowed to serve his time at home wearing a tag instead of going to jail.

The new case centres on a Libyan businessman, Ziad Takieddine, who had said he had written proof that Sarkozy's 2007 campaign bid was "abundantly" financed by Tripoli, and that the €50m (£43m) in payments continued after he became president.
Takieddine, who died last year, withdrew his accusations in an interview in 2020.

At the time, Sarkozy was said to have stated: the "truth is finally coming out", but officials found the retraction to be "insincere" and a new investigation was launched into the "Save Sarko" file – the nickname the alleged perpetrators had used for the operation, according to French media.

So the former head of state and his wife, an Italian-born former supermodel and singer, will now face charges of "criminal conspiracy with intent to commit fraud" and benefiting from witness tampering. They deny any wrongdoing.

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/environment_c: Link: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/environment_climate/2768377%2Fcop31-format-needs-re-think-former-nz-climate-ambassadors-say
The world's annual climate summit may need a re-think after talks at this year's conference broke down with no final agreement , two former New Zealand climate ambassadors say.
However, the lack of consensus did not mean multilateral action on climate change was failing, one stressed.
COP31 ended in Antalya, Türkiye, early on Monday (NZT) after more than two weeks of fraught discussion between countries that were unable to produce a 'cover decision'.

The European Union, Panama, and some Pacific countries formally objected to the final draft decision because, among other things, it failed to mention fossil fuels - the main driver of global warming.
New Zealand caretaker climate minister Simon Watts said New Zealand would have supported the decision if there was "consensus in the room".
However, Green MP Francisco Hernandez, who attended most of the conference, said the EU and others were right to walk away .
Jo Tyndall, who was New Zealand's climate ambassador for nearly a decade and co-chaired negotiations to develop the Paris Agreement 'rule book', said the lack of consensus was "disappointing".
"I think it was, in some ways, important and no bad thing not to accept a very watered-down, weakened kind of outcome."
However, attendees "will be leaving feeling very deflated", Tyndall said.

"The negotiators who are there at the end will not have slept for one, possibly two nights, nor have they had showers often - which makes it slightly, you know, less than pleasant to be in a crowded hall."

She believed the talks had struggled to build on a 2023 commitment from all members to transition away from fossil fuels, because of "post-purchase regret" from some of the petro-states that had agreed to it.
"They really felt they'd given away too much and they've dug their heels in increasingly with each COP since then."
During her time as ambassador, some crucial decisions had been reached at COPs, including the "elation" of 2015 when the Paris Agreement was adopted.
With that agreement and the rules underpinning it now in place, though, there were increasingly questions around the purpose of the annual talks.
"There is a bit of a feeling that, to some extent, it's been a case of negotiating for its own sake," she said.
"Everybody wants an outcome [each year] and it creates a lot of pressure, but how necessary is it? And if it's not necessary in the way it has been in the past what should we do instead?"
The processes underlying the Paris Agreement had "their own rhythm and momentum that should continue", she said.
"We must keep remembering that when there are claims that this is a blow to all that, that multilateralism is suffering and not working, we do have the bones of the architecture well in place."

The growing trade fair that occurred alongside the main negotiations each year was useful for "peer learning and exchange" around climate action, but had seen attendees balloon to 90,000 people this year.
"All of that has just become bigger and bigger and bigger and … they don't sit that easily together, I don't think."
Tyndall's predecessor Adrian Macey, who served as climate ambassador between 2006 and 2010 and went on to chair the Kyoto Protocol negotiations, said the format of COP had to change.
The Paris Agreement was a huge achievement but the conference was producing "diminishing returns" every year.

"It gives people this false impression that the barometer of global progress on climate change is words coming out of the COP, and that's absolute nonsense - the barometer is actually what transitions are happening in what countries."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm20: Energy bills will soar by 26% for millions of households in January after a surge in gas prices sparked by the Iran war.

Regulator Ofgem said typical bills will increase by about £37 a month in the first three months of the new year, although individual households costs will depend on how much they use at the coldest time of year.

For a household using a typical amount of energy in England, Scotland and Wales and paying by direct debit for gas and electricity, the increase would push annual bills from £1,723 to £2,166 if it was sustained for a year.
The government will pay millions of households £100 from 4 January to help cover winter costs on top of an existing VAT cut on electricity.
Charities and suppliers expect debt to rise and a wave of people to need emergency support.
Ofgem said the rise in the cap, which is set every three month, had been driven entirely by higher wholesale costs faced by suppliers owing, primarily, to the Iran war.
The warm home discount will also take £150 off bills for six million households on benefits this winter. There have been calls for this support, funded through everyone's bill, to be extended.
"We are staring down the barrel of a brutal winter," said Dame Clare Moriarty, chief executive of Citizens Advice.

Neil Kenward, Ofgem's director general for markets, said: "Conflict in the Middle East continues to drive energy costs higher, and we know this price increase will be a worry for many households as winter approaches."

He said Ofgem had written to energy suppliers "reminding them of their responsibilities" to customers this winter. They have been told to identify people who need help early, make support easy to access and ensure repayment plans are affordable and sustainable.
Suppliers said their own profits are also capped, and everyone was feeling the "impact of our exposure to volatile fossil fuel markets".
Energy UK, which represents suppliers, said the UK needed to develop more domestic clean power and accelerate the electrification of our homes and transport.
The increase is the largest seen since Russia's invasion of Ukraine drove up prices significantly. It comes at a tough time of year, when the weather is at its coldest and use is peaking.
Individual usage differs, so for every £100 spent on energy now, the new cost will be about £126.
People on prepayment meters will be hit as spending comes when energy is needed, rather than spreading the cost over the year.
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said people will be "deeply concerned" by another rise in energy bills.
"For too long, British families have been paying the price for conflicts overseas and volatile fossil fuel markets," she said.

Andrew Bowie, shadow energy secretary, said: "It is an outrage that, as bills soar, Labour are not only piling green levies and taxes onto bills but signing us up to an EU scheme that risks pushing them even higher.
"Labour are utterly out of touch and could fix this tomorrow if they had the backbone."

Stacey, 40, a single mother from Bristol, said dealing with rising energy costs has felt like a "battle" recently and she's worried about 2027.

The office worker, whose daughters are 10 and 12, is on a fixed-term tracker tariff with E.On Next, which charges rates set below the quarterly Ofgem price cap. She expects to pay £1,800 for energy this year, £400 more than last year.
Stacey, who is part of the Changing Realities project at Glasgow University, which documents life for people on low incomes, has tried a number of things to control her energy costs.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cdd2: Energy bills are to soar in January, as prices governed by regulator Ofgem's cap rise at the coldest time of the year.
The cap affects millions of people in England, Scotland and Wales, and reflects higher wholesale gas costs which have been pushed up by the US-Israel war with Iran.
It means people on variable tariffs should give an accurate meter reading, ensure they are receiving all the support to which they are entitled, and take care over energy use.
The energy cap fixes the maximum amount which customers on standard variable tariffs can be charged for each unit of gas and electricity used.
It covers more than 20 million households in England, Wales and Scotland and is set by the regulator Ofgem every three months , external .
It affects those paying by direct debit, by standard credit (they pay when they get a bill), or prepayment meters in slightly different ways.
Most of the increase in the energy price cap has, and will be, driven by higher gas prices.
The government's decision to temporarily remove VAT from domestic electricity bills has cut about £45 a year from a typical bill.
Meanwhile, millions of households will receive a £100 automatic payment to help cover winter costs.
The typical annual usage figure applies to the first category: dual-fuel households on a standard variable tariff which pay by direct debit.
But customers' actual bills depend on the amount of energy used and how they pay for it.
The roughly 11 million households on fixed tariffs do not see their prices change until the end of their fixed term.
Ofgem regulates the energy market in England, Scotland and Wales. Northern Ireland has a separate system.
Although the price cap sets the unit prices for gas and electricity, your household's actual bill depends on the overall amount of energy you use, and how you pay for it.
Where you live, the type of property you have, how energy efficient it is, how many people live there, and the weather all make a difference.
The Ofgem cap is illustrated using "typical" household energy use in a year with a single bill for gas and electricity settled by direct debit.
The vast majority of people pay their bill this way to help spread payments across the year.
In July, Ofgem reduced what it believes to be a "typical" level of energy use, because many homes have cut back due to high prices in recent years while energy efficiency has improved.
Its new estimate is 9,500 kWh of gas and 2,500 kWh of electricity a year.
Submitting a meter reading when the cap changes means you are not charged for estimated usage at the wrong rate.
Customers with working smart meters do not need to submit a reading as their bill is calculated automatically.

Ofgem also controls standing charges, which are a fixed daily fee to cover the costs of connecting households to gas and electricity supplies. These vary slightly by region , external and payment method.
Between 1 October and 31 December 2026, average standing charges for direct debit customers will be 54.83p a day for electricity and 29.68p a day for gas.
The electricity charge is lower than the amount charged in the previous three-month period, while the gas charge is largely unchanged.

Campaigners have long argued that standing charges are unfair because they make up a bigger proportion of the bill for low-energy households. Others say it just shifts the cost from one part of the bill to another rather than cutting it.
The government has announced plans to remove gas standing charges, although no details have been published on how that will happen
Fixed deals provide certainty for a set period – often a year, or longer – but if energy prices drop while you are on the deal, you could be stuck at a higher price.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckj0: Trump boosts Nvidia boss return but are US politicians on board?
After the AI chipmaker Nvidia announced it was bringing back embattled former head Jensen Huang and the company's stock shot up like a bullet, President Donald Trump took a very public victory lap.
"I made the deal," he said during a lengthy phone interview with cable business news channel CNBC.

Trump followed that with an AI-generated image posted to his social media platform that riffed on the famous photograph taken moments after the 2024 attempt on his life in Pennsylvania. But instead of Trump in the image, Huang was the one surrounded by Secret Service guards. It depicted him in front of an Nvidia banner - with a raised fist clenching a red bra.
The post was classic Trump – potentially offensive, yet still a bit opaque.

Was Trump suggesting Huang survived a scandal – one that includes allegations of recklessly jeopardising US national security by consorting with a suspected Chinese spy – the way he had survived an assassin's bullet?

Was the bra a celebration Huang's reported extramarital affairs? By replacing the US flag with an Nvidia standard, was he claiming that America and one of its largest, most powerful companies are one and the same?
At the very least, the image underscores how inextricably linked Huang and Trump now are, with the fate of the former hinging on the successes and failures of the latter.
And with that comes significant risks for the American president and for Republicans, including Vice-President JD Vance, who played a key part in his efforts to rescue Huang.

While Trump has said that a "very thorough investigation" by federal officials "exonerated" Huang and his reinstatement poses no national security threat, that is far from the final word on the matter.
"Every time you have a Chinese woman that's good looking or beautiful, they say she's a spy," Trump told CNBC, adding that "with Jensen, I don't believe that's true".
Democrats and some concerned Republicans in Congress have a different view.

They are promising to launch their own oversight of Huang and Nvidia, with subpoenas and compelled witness testimony, in order to assess whether they violated laws by allowing China to access sophisticated microchip technology.
State governments could also launch their own investigations.
Any new revelations could further damage the company's standing – and, by association, Trump himself.
"I have warned the administration from the start about Communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through both smuggling and remote access," Republican Senator Tom Cotton posted on X.
US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation
While Huang has a long record of success at Nvidia, there is no guarantee that he can recapture past glory now that his star his dimmed.
Even if he is free from any criminal liability, the tech mogul is about to be in a much harsher spotlight than he has ever experienced.
Trump also appears to be on the wrong side of public opinion when it comes to AI writ large.

In the recent US midterm elections, candidates on both the left and right campaigned on imposing new restrictions on data centre construction, with many calling for new legal guardrails to prevent AI-fuelled economic and social disruption.

"Rather than addressing the American people's growing concerns about AI, this administration remains asleep at the wheel or willfully ignorant as our most advanced technologies fall into the hands of our greatest competitors," congresswoman Sydney Kamlager-Dove, a California Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, told the BBC.

The president's own political base is also suspicious of the new technology, with rural conservatives often rebelling at the demands that big tech companies have placed on their local resources and civic infrastructure.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c820: Domestic energy prices are set to soar in January under the regulator Ofgem's new price cap, pushing up bills for millions of households across England, Scotland and Wales.
With household budgets already under pressure, finding ways to reduce gas and electricity costs has become increasingly important. But how much difference can simple changes really make?
The BBC spoke to three people about what they're doing to keep their energy costs down.
Kelly Anne Harvey uses electric blankets and portable oil radiators in some rooms to save on the central heating
Like many people, Kelly Anne Harvey, a building surveyor from Cleveleys near Blackpool, is worried about her energy bill going up next year.
The 44-year-old, who is married with a five-year-old son, has a combined household income of £60,000.
She currently pays about £154 a month for gas and electricity on a standard variable rate with Octopus, but is looking for a fixed-rate deal to offset the rise.
The family fell into arrears on their energy bills a few years ago and Kelly says she won't let it happen again.
To control her costs she pays by direct debit, which spreads her payments and is typically £138 cheaper a year than paying on receipt of a bill .
The family uses electric blankets and portable oil radiators in some rooms so they don't have to turn the central heating on as often.
They also take part in Octopus's energy saving scheme, which rewards customers who use less electricity at peak times, such as early evenings, with a free hour of energy at the weekend.
"On Sunday we'll turn on the dishwasher, tumble drier, washing machine and maybe even charge our electric cars," says Kelly.
Stacey says she keeps the curtains closed "to keep the heat in" and her daughters wear thermal clothing
Stacey, 40, a single mother from Bristol, says dealing with rising energy costs has felt like a "battle" recently and she's worried about 2027.

The office worker, whose daughters are aged 10 and 12, is on a fixed-term tracker tariff with E.On Next, which charges rates set below the quarterly Ofgem price cap. She expects to pay £1,800 for energy this year, up £400 on last year.
Stacey, who is part of the Changing Realities project at Glasgow University, which documents life for people on low incomes, has tried a number of things to control her energy costs.
She's turned her central heating down from 22C to 19.5C, bought electric blankets and pays her bills by direct debit.
She also leaves her curtains shut to "keep the heat in", while her daughters wear thermal clothing if it gets chilly in the house. The family is also using less hot water.
"I've got girls and they're growing up and they want to spend loads of time in the shower [but] it's just not possible."
Around 1.5 million households in the UK rely on heating oil for heating and hot water, and their costs have already soared in the past year due to disruption in global oil markets.

"When I first moved here two years ago you could get a litre of heating oil for 50-60p," says Bradley Knowles, 32, who lives in a barn conversion with his husband, mother and sister in rural Lincolnshire.
"At the height of the Iran war it went up to £1.20 or £1.30 and now it's stabilised at around £1."

To cut costs, the finance worker orders oil in bulk, buying 1,000-1,500 litres, preferably in the summer months when prices are lower. He also tries to order a few weeks in advance to avoid expensive next-day deliveries.
Bradley uses comparison sites to see which local suppliers offer the cheapest oil and puts money aside each month so he can always afford his orders.
Oil-powered boilers may take time to heat up, but Bradley advises against leaving them on all day as that can be very expensive.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmwy: Selena Buse, 16, reverses her Citroën Ami out of a parking space and heads off past the school playground. Heads turn. The Ami looks pretty remarkable. Futurist or like-a-toaster depending on your point of view. But it's changed her life.
"I got it because I really needed it to get to school. And I use it to visit friends on the weekends. It's indispensable in rural areas like where I live," she says.
In France, you can drive a car like this from the age of 14 with a road safety certificate and eight hours training. In Italy too.
In Germany and Spain it's 15, in the UK 16. Because they are classed as motorised quadri-cycles. Four-wheel mopeds in other words.
Registrations have risen from about 13,000 in 2019 to around 25,000 last year in France.

In Europe, sales have gone from 30,000 to 60,000 in the past five years. And the Ami, launched in 2020, has really changed the image, with teenagers who now account for a quarter of all mini-car sales.
In Selena's very small Citroën, we are soon rolling along at the top speed of 45km/h (28mph). For other road users, no-licence cars like this can seem like mobile traffic calming.
"When I'm on faster roads and there's a lot of traffic the cars behind me sometimes honk their horns but I can't go any quicker!" Selena says.
Daniel Laprès says the Aixam car was "the exact solution to our problem"
Another local Daniel Laprès, who drives a micro-car made by French firm and market-leader Aixam, tells me he actually pulls over to let the cars behind pass.

He and his wife moved from Paris to this country village two years ago. Of Canadian nationality, he didn't swap his foreign licence for a French one in time and lost the right to drive. That didn't matter much when he was in Paris. Like many Parisians he didn't need a car. He used public transport. But that's not possible here.

"We tried living off of taxis and it was in the end a disaster. Then we heard about how you could drive without having to have a licence, and it was the exact solution to our problem. Cheap, inexpensive to operate, basically no administrative formalities, you get insurance."
However, Laprès feels less safe in his small car. "They're little more than tin cans on wheels, right? I mean, you're not going to be driving fast, but someone else could be."
These cars are forbidden on motorways. But even on medium-fast roads, being considerably slower than the average vehicle can be a problem.

"You go on national highways at your risk and peril. I did it once and I will never, ever do it again. On those roads (speed limit 110km/h), everybody is passing you, including the biggest trucks. And they come at you very fast from the rear, so it's scary," Laprès says.
Daniel is 77 so fits in with the long-established market for these cars: older people living in the countryside.

Traditionally the market also included quite a few people who'd lost their licences, often because of drink-driving offenses. But the launch of the electric Citroën Ami in 2020 changed the customer profile and the product.

"The launch of the Ami was the beginning of the transformation of the sector, with more and more electric models coming on to the market. In 2026, more than 67% of new licence-free cars are electric," says Marie-Laure Nivot, market analyst at AAA Data.
The launch of the Citroën Ami in 2020 "transformed the sector" analysts say
This tendency was encouraged by stricter EU regulations on motorised two-wheelers that had been the vehicles of choice for European teenagers until then.

"It proved too costly for manufacturers to apply the new EU rules, so mopeds and small scooters have almost disappeared from the market since 2020 and licence-free cars have taken their place," Marie-Laure Nivot says.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c689: As the market bell rang out at the Nasdaq today, the Nvidia super-bounce faded.
Its shares slid and are down almost 30% over the past six months, well before the scandal involving Jensen Huang emerged earlier this month.
The legitimate fears about the staying power of the tech boom pre-dated Huang's exit. They have not gone away with his return.

Investors are jittery. Already Anthropic is now trading notably lower than last week's stock market flotation. The firm is the first purely AI company to be publicly listed, and is being seen as a big test for continued investor appetite for the technology.

President Trump's extraordinary phone call to CNBC taking credit for telling the board to reinstate Huang showed the extent of the operation - of some in Silicon Valley and within the US administration - to get him back at the helm.
Among the truly astonishing reflections from President Trump was a suggestion that a two-day investigation of allegations was done and had cleared Huang of national security concerns.
The President said his remarkable move to intervene was because Huang is a "national treasure" who has the next generation of AI chips "in his head". Trump says this is why he needed to act.

In markets, those sceptical about the AI boom say they have never seen an operation to prop up a stock market boom like this. The bond vigilantes and short sellers are now up against Silicon Valley and the White House.
Investors are trading not revenue numbers but levels of political support at a time when US voters have just delivered a backlash against AI data centres.
Against this backdrop, the recovery of the central cash-generating foundation of the tech boom - Nvidia and its $400bn (£304bn) annual sales of advanced chips - looks politically fragile.
This worsens other uncertainties and risks, such as Nvidia's central role in the web of financing, borrowing and cross-ownership to support every corner of the build out of data centres.
The brief interim Nvidia chief executive Colette Kress had already signalled a rowing back from elements of this strategy last week. Where is that now?
The fall back in Anthropic's share price also raises questions about OpenAI's planned listing on the stock exchange. Ultimately these two companies might be the most critical part of all this.

They remain valuable companies with phenomenal technology relied on by the world's biggest companies. The real question is whether that reliance eases, as corporations eschew expensive frontier models for cheaper generic models offered by China.
In turn, all this could be affected by the political backlash, to which the Nvidia psychodrama now contributes.
It is simply not normal to have trillion dollar swings in the value of individual companies.
The extraordinary volatility shows the fragile mood of investors.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c35y: Up to 20 million households in England will get a £100 payment to help with their energy bills this winter, Chancellor John Healey has announced in his Budget.
For many people, the £100 on offer is a lot of money, but it's worth considering the context.
A typical energy bill is forecast to jump by £443 a year from January , according to consultants Cornwall Insight.
Therefore many people will still feel worse off despite the payment.
Those living in properties which are in council tax bands A to D in England will get the payment, the government has said.
As such, it's worth checking which council tax band your home is in , external . If you live in England, you can use the search function by typing your postcode into the box.
If you get a paper council tax bill, your band will also be printed on there.
The chancellor said the policy was for England but that funding would be given to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland to make the payment as well.
The Scottish and Welsh governments have confirmed they will use the funding to introduce equivalent or similar payment schemes.
The Northern Irish government does not have the legal authority to make the £100 payments unless it agrees its budget, which it has failed to do since the start of this financial year.
Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you
If you pay your council tax by direct debit, the money will be paid directly into your bank account.
Those who don't pay by direct debit will be contacted by their council and given the choice to receive the £100 directly into their bank account or as credit on their council tax bill.
The government will ask councils to make payments from 4 January, and the scheme will be open until the end of May.
Students living in halls will not get the payment because student halls are not in council tax bands A to D.
However, if you're a student living in a property that is in council tax bands A to D, as in a private home or flat let out by a landlord, then you will get the payment.
Students do not pay council tax so the local authority will be responsible for finding a way to give them the payments.
This is also the case for those who do not pay council tax because of another kind of exemption, or if you do pay council tax but you do it by cash or some other way.
The government said it would give councils guidance on how local authorities should do this in due course.
The government has said the support is to help households with the cost of energy.
But the money will appear directly in people's bank accounts so you could choose to spend it on something else, while some people may choose to receive the £100 as a credit on their council tax bill.
The chancellor said the money for the £100 cash payments is coming from a tax rise on banks.
The surcharge on banks' corporation tax will rise from 3% to 6% for 15 months from 1 January 2027 to 31 March 2028.
