https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq5y: A comeback for the ages: Trump's influence on Huang's return to Nvidia

Jensen Huang has been reinstated as the boss of Nvidia less than two weeks after he was forced to resign following the revelations of extra marital affairs, one of which was with a suspected Chinese spy.
The AI chipmaker handed its co-founder his job back, despite rejecting his initial offer to return, after pressure from US President Donald Trump.
Trump said he "made the deal" with the tech giant's board to get Huang his job back, but both the president and Nvidia are facing backlash from lawmakers.
But his comeback added almost $1 trillion to Nvidia's market value as its share price jumped 31%, ending ended a streak of losses on the US stock market.
Nvidia's gains helped boost shares in other tech companies and financial markets in Asia while European markets were flat.
However, despite Huang's return, Nvidia's share price remains down over the past month amid investor concerns about the wider AI industry and future development.
But it is a dramatic return for the man dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech" to the company at the centre of the AI spending boom.

Attention will soon turn to Huang's appearance before Congress next week, where the Nvidia boss will be questioned over his relationship with Alice Huang, alleged to be a spy for China, due to national security concerns.

On Monday, the US Commerce Department announced it was preparing to blacklist Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer where Alice Huang (no relation) was chief executive. China has denied the spying allegations.
Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said Huang's reinstatement after originally resigning on 12 November was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".
The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.
Last Tuesday, the board explicitly said it did not intend to reinstate him following calls to do so and Huang himself stating he would be open to returning.
Asia markets jump as Nvidia boss Jensen Huang reinstated after spy scandal
The U-turn suggests Nvidia's board believe Huang is irreplaceable.
The 63-year-old, who co-founded the company in 1993, transformed it from a chipmaker for video and computer games to the semiconductor powerhouse it is today, making the chips used in AI systems.

It is now one the most valuable firms in the world. Some believed Huang's departure risked not only the future of Nvidia, but the wider AI industry given the position the company, under Huang, has in the financing of other tech firms.
In a interview with CNBC on Monday, Trump said he had spoken to Nvidia's board of directors and convinced them to bring back Huang.
"They did ask for assurance on the national security threat," Trump said. "And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot."
"People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it's a threat to lose him," the president added.
The president was asked whether Nvidia stock losses after Huang resigned last week had influenced his decision to personally intervene.
Since returning last year to the White House, the president has amassed a significant level of investment in Nvidia.
Recent financial disclosures show he purchased $265,000 in its stock and sold as much as $15,000 worth of shares in September.

A BBC review of his government financial disclosures for the last two years shows he purchased shares of Nvidia shares worth between $23m and $86m (£18m and £66m). And he has bought Nvidia stock 85 separate times through a number of investment accounts.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6n9: The shake-up facing renters as a new kind of landlord emerges

On Christmas Eve 2021, there was a knock on the door of Lexi Levens' rented flat. It was a letter sent by special delivery from the NHS nurse's landlord saying she, her husband, and four children had two months to move out.
"The kids all thought it was a present arriving," she recalls.
Lexi's landlord had used something known then as a Section 21 notice to evict her family without needing to give a reason.

Lexi, along with the housing charity Shelter, went on to lobby the government to improve rights for renters. The Renters' Rights Act, which came into force in May this year, banned Section 21 evictions and also made it illegal to refuse to rent to people based on their status as a family with children.
The landlords Lexi had been renting from at that time were typical of the English housing market - individuals who owned one or a handful of properties.
Lexi Levens received a letter on Christmas Eve 2021 telling her that her family had to move out

Many of these small landlords say the Renters' Rights Act has left them feeling squeezed. They also say rising interest rates, new regulations and tax changes (including some in the most recent Budget) are making things harder. Some say they are selling up.

Meanwhile, according to Savills estate agents, 2026 is likely to be another record year for investment from large institutions in what is known in the property industry as build to rent (BTR). This is when big developers build blocks of flats or family housing to rent out, something that is commonplace in parts of Europe and the US. It means that rather than dealing with an individual landlord or letting agent, tenants are instead renting from larger, typically corporate, entities.

So does the shift, as some believe, represent a welcome professionalisation of the UK rental sector? Or will renters increasingly miss the positive elements of the personal touch that small landlords can provide?
According to the latest government survey of private landlords in England, 83% of English landlords own four properties or fewer, representing 51% of tenancies.

And according to 2024 research by real estate agency Savills, around 40% rental homes in the US and Germany are owned by large institutions - be they private firms, listed companies, pension funds, or co-operatives. For the UK, Savills calculated that figure was just 3%.

But the rental market is changing. The trend is most visible in England, where BTR has boomed in large cities and where regulations like the Renters' Rights Act apply, but there are BTR developments in Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland too and the devolved nations are also seeing increased regulation on landlords, such as with Scotland's rent controls.
Lexi is pleased with the idea of a sector with stricter rules for landlords and more professional institutions getting involved.

"Anything that takes away from landlords having personal preferences [around choosing who they are or not prepared to rent to]… is a good thing," she says, adding that she believes large, corporate landlords would be less likely to act that way.

Clint Stevenson, a 44-year-old magician for weddings and events, has been renting his one-bedroom flat in Ramsgate for £550 a month for two years. He says he has "the most amazing landlady" - an older woman who he regularly chats to. He sometimes walks her dog and does her shopping as well.

He says he had considered renting from a BTR development, but found the accommodation to be "very industrial and very unpersonal". He also found what was on offer to be expensive compared to what he is used to paying.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8d3: BBC secret filming shows dog breeder selling sick puppies for £2k each
When Katie Thornton paid £2,000 for a nine-week-old puppy for her son, she knew it was a premium price - but was happy to be doing business with a "legit", council-approved breeder.
But Ozzy the Dobermann pup started coughing in the car on the way home, and within 48 hours he was in a veterinary hospital receiving urgent treatment for pneumonia.
Since then, his ongoing health problems mean Katie has racked up more than £5,000 in vet bills.
A BBC investigation has found the breeder had been stripped of his five-star rating two months before selling several sick puppies, but continued to advertise as five-star.
We have also found at least 15 other breeders in England advertising puppies alongside claims their star rating is higher than it really is.

An expert reviewing our findings - including undercover footage we recorded at the breeder's home - said the investigation exposes a nationwide "wild west" of dog licensing, making it "easy for consumers to be scammed".
Katie Thornton has spent more than £5,000 on vet bills since buying Ozzy earlier this year
When Katie visited the premises of Mikjulora Dobermanns in Whitby, North Yorkshire, she said the puppies' mother "didn't look very well" and was "skinny" and "shaking".
But she felt the breeder, Michael Estill, was "pushing me to buy Ozzy" so she paid for him and took him home on the spot.
Katie defended her decision because she had done extensive research to check the business was "legit".
The mother-of-one, from Harrogate, said she had checked his licence number and read through his website and online adverts, which said he had decades of experience and a "five-star" breeding licence.
In England, local councils grant breeders in their area a licence and star rating dependent on welfare standards.
Vet reports for North Yorkshire Council from August and December 2025, seen by the BBC, cited dozens of concerns with Estill's business, including:
"Poor" living conditions "akin to a prison", with dogs kept in cages, stacked on top of each other, that were too small for them to turn around in
Puppies for sale not matching descriptions - "in other words it is a scam"
Prospective buyers "very vulnerable to unsuspectingly purchasing unhealthy puppies"
The business was "more or less a puppy farm masquerading as an honest and conscientious breeder. This must stop"
Estill "bullied" a local vet to perform an "unnecessary" Caesarean section on one of his dogs, to reduce the time he would have to spend monitoring her
His "demanding" behaviour led the practice to give him several doses of a powerful stimulant which he gave to one of his dogs at home - which the vet considered to be "negligent"
He had a three-year-old dog euthanised because he suspected her to have a neurological condition, despite the vet encouraging him to get diagnostic tests and specialist treatment first.

Following the reports, which concluded that the business was "functioning outside the law", the council renewed Estill's licence in January but downgraded his rating from five-star (the highest standards) to one-star (minor failings).
Dr Caroline Allen, founder of Pet Lighthouse and former RSPCA chief veterinary officer, said she was "surprised and shocked" that the business kept its licence.
A North Yorkshire Council spokesperson said the threshold for revoking a licence "was not considered to have been met on the evidence available".
They added: "We take animal welfare very seriously and investigate concerns brought to our attention.

"Following the veterinary inspection reports, we have continued to work with the licence holder to address the identified concerns and are satisfied that standards have significantly improved, resulting in a higher level of animal welfare at the premises."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq62: A comeback for the ages: Trump's influence on Huang's return to Nvidia
Nvidia's market value rose by nearly $1 trillion as its share price skyrocketed after the tech firm reinstated Jensen Huang as its chief executive with immediate effect.

His shock reinstatement comes less than two weeks after Huang resigned after admitting an affair with a woman who was alleged to be a Chinese spy, a period in which shares in the chipmaker have also fallen significantly.
Nvidia shares rose by more than 31% which also lifted stock markets, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq climbing by 6.5% and the S&P 500 also rose 4.75%.
Tech stocks more broadly have also rallied following large falls on Friday , with much of the rally starting in pre-market trading before Huang's return was announced.
Other chipmakers experienced large increases following Monday's announcement from the Nvidia board. Shares in Micron Technology jumped 19%, while AMD shares rose nearly 7%.
Tesla shares also lept up by nearly 11.5%, while other tech gains were more muted by comparison: Amazon shares were up nearly 3.5%, and Apple and Microsoft rose by less than 2%.
While the surge in Nvidia shares was large and drove its market value back towards $4tn, the firm's share price remains about 21% down from a month ago.
A sharp drop occurred on 4 November, after the Democrat's midterm election victory sparked fears of tougher AI regulation to come led to a broad tech stock sell-off.

On Friday alone, Nvidia shares fell by 13.7% as tech stocks more broadly fell, and as Reuters reported - unconfirmed by the BBC - that the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) over its accounting practices.
Nvidia is a key firm at the core of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, with the chips it makes central to the industry.

Nvidia's board of directors voted unanimously to reinstate the firm's co-founder following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him, the company said - but US President Donald Trump has claimed he "convinced" the board to reinstate Huang.
Kathleen Brooks, research director at brokerage firm XTB, said Huang's return showed Huang was the "godfather" of AI, and "has a talismanic influence over the sector".
"Barely two weeks ago this man was ousted from the company that he founded due to serious misconduct and potential national security issues," she said.
"Even though Huang did not hold special voting shares on the board, Nvidia's directors cannot see a future for the company without him."
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said Huang's reinstatement was an astonishing about-turn for Nvidia, particularly given reports of an as-yet unconfirmed SEC investigation.

"This is the biggest corporate U-turn in living memory. To go from being embroiled in a spy scandal to being reinstated as the head of one of the world's most valuable companies in less than a fortnight is nothing short of remarkable," he said.
"Today's stock market rebound represents a massive sigh of relief by investors. However, one cannot rule out a more conservative approach by Huang going forward.
"His every move will be scrutinised by the market, and he may wish to tread more carefully to protect his integrity and ensure that Nvidia is being run responsibly."

Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said Huang's reinstatement "reportedly at the encouragement of Trump Administration officials and without any apparent accounting or response to the risks to our national security, demands an explanation."
She added: "What is abundantly clear is that the AI industry requires guardrails and oversight."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9gk: I've just spent a week using Muse, Meta's AI agent that rolls out in the UK today.
Agents are systems that don't just respond to questions but can carry out tasks for you. With Muse, Meta gives the examples of "searching for a cheaper energy deal" or "sorting the school calendar."
And it's true that it has helped me run my life - but it also challenged my personal privacy boundaries, and made me endure some cringeworthy interactions.
It has made a truly enormous bet on AI - of the $145bn (£111bn) it will spend this year much of it will be on building out the tech.

For that to pay off we all need to start using it much more, and Meta hopes Muse will do for AI agents what WhatsApp did for messaging - that is, become the AI agent of choice for billions of people, putting Meta at the forefront of the AI revolution.
But it's not just about what consumers think. Regulators are keeping a careful eye on these emerging tools too.
"Agentic AI has significant potential to benefit people and businesses", the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) noted as Muse launched in the UK.

But its chief executive, Paul Arnold, added it had been "clear with Meta about its responsibilities under data protection law prior to launch, particularly the requirement to ensure that users and the wider public can meaningfully understand and control how their personal data is used in the Muse product".
Muse bills itself as a personal AI agent available to anyone aged 18 and over.
"It doesn't just answer questions, it actually goes out and does work for you," said David Singleton, Meta's VP of engineering on AI products.
"So it helps people stay on top of things," he added. "[It] helps you take tasks and projects off your plate, and also helps you turn your long-term goals into action plans."

What this means is you can set it up to do something for you, like find some specific holiday options, and it will work away on that even as you move off the app and get on with your day, reporting back once it has finished.
It won't book the holiday without your permission - but it can then make the purchase, if you let it.
And the permission requests keep on coming. Every time Muse wants to do something, send something or post something, you have to allow it.

It is reassuring to know that an AI agent isn't running amok in your name, even if it also gets a bit annoying, though you can give it more autonomy (and so get fewer messages) if you adjust the settings.
Muse can't access many apps at the moment but the fundamental ones are the most personal.
I found myself wincing as I hooked it up to one of my personal email accounts, my personal calendar and my personal phone messages. I did not allow it any access to my BBC accounts.
It can't access WhatsApp except to set up a separate chat between it and the user, and while it found me some train tickets, it could not book them via the app which I use, and which is cheaper.

Amazon has blocked it from its marketplace, citing data security concerns but my agent didn't seem to know that, and spent a fruitless hour repeatedly telling me it was still waiting for the page to load in order to find me some shelves.
A number of big UK firms are working with Meta though, including Marks & Spencer, Debenhams Group, Currys, Sainsbury's and Ocado.
The ICO is urging consumers to be cautious with AI agents though: "consider the pros and cons," it said in a blog post to coincide with Muse's launch. , external
"Agents can make mistakes. Mistakes can be magnified if the agent is acting autonomously," it noted.
Meta is keen to emphasise how its agents can be personalised: "No two Muses are alike," , external it says in its press release.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cv98: The US has said it intends to ban a Singaporean artificial intelligence (AI) company allegedly tied to the Nvidia scandal from doing business in America.
The Department of Commerce announced it planned to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are blacklisted from buying or selling goods in the US.

The company is mainly a developer of data centres, but in recent weeks a former executive of Megaspeed was accused of working as a spy for China while having a romantic relationship with Nvidia head Jensen Huang.
The relationship led to additional scrutiny by US officials and heightened concern that Megaspeed was funnelling Nvidia's advanced AI computer chips to China.

When exactly the ban against Megaspeed will go into effect was not specified in the commerce department announcement. The BBC has asked the agency for comment, along with the White House and Megaspeed.
Megaspeed was not well known within the US until last month when media reports emerged that a former Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang, had an affair with Jensen Huang.
Alice Huang (no relation) was thought by US intelligence to be working as an asset for Beijing, creating national security concerns within the US.
China has denied that she is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.
On 12 November, Jensen Huang resigned after allegations he had had another affair, this one with a Nvidia employee.
On Monday, Nvidia's board reinstated him after US President Donald Trump said he had "convinced" the company and "made the deal".
The commerce department has said it had been investigating Megaspeed for almost two years.
The department said it had suspected the company was violating US export controls by helping to get Nvidia's chips into the hands of companies within China.
China has been blocked from buying such technology since 2022.
Although based in Singapore, Megaspeed has significant business dealings in China.
Alibaba, for instance, the major Chinese online retailer, has been reported to be one if its largest customers.
Megaspeed was a known buyer of billions of dollars of Nvidia computer chips, including through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, which has also been added to the Commerce blacklist.
Nvidia's computer chips, originally designed for use in gaming consols, in recent years have become crucial to the continued growth of the AI industry.

Without enough supply or access to computer chips that are capable of processing the huge amount of data needed to make things like AI chatbots and models run, AI companies will not be able to meet or grow demand from people using AI tools.
That has driven up the value of Nvidia on the stock market, as well as its influence in the AI industry and the White House.
Although tech stocks have in recent months been volatile and trending lower, when Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia because of his affairs, the company's stock fell by more than 30%.
Anxiety about the company's influence and ability to operate within the AI ecosystem without its famed executive appeared to take down shares of other tech companies, too.
Huang was reinstated on Monday to his position as head of Nvidia, a move that US President Donald Trump said he told the company's board to take .
The company's stock rallied on his reinstatement, as did several other tech stocks, but shares of Nvidia did not climb to where the company had been before being immersed in scandal.
In the weeks ahead, Huang and the company he now runs again are facing multiple government agency investigations.
Huang and the chief legal officer of Nvidia are set to appear next for a closed-door briefing with the House Foreign Affairs Committee.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c687: Nvidia and its co-founder Jensen Huang have been at the centre of the artificial intelligence (AI) spending boom.

No company or chief executive has arguably been more consequential to the development of AI in recent years, with the US microchip manufacturer under Huang positioning itself as a critical cog in the development of the world-changing technology.
That central position prompted questions, in the aftermath of Huang's departure over revelations of extramarital affairs, over how important he was to the wider AI industry and US economy.
The fact he has been handed his job back after just 11 days in a U-turn by Nvidia's board implies the top brass believe Huang is irreplaceable.
Shares in the company have surged on the news of Huang's shock return, following a period of sharp declines.
While Nvidia is not as much of a household name as other Big Tech players such as Apple, Amazon and Microsoft, the company has been just as integral to the booming US stock market of recent years.
The billions of dollars being funnelled into AI and the construction of data centres has bolstered the American economy, with Nvidia being one of the biggest spenders.
Originally focusing on chips which process graphics for computer games, it pivoted to making the chips used in AI systems and now dominates the market.
It is now one the most valuable firms in the world and its rapid growth is poised to continue as the firm's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier.
Huang played a major role in the company, leading its shift towards AI, and maintained a firm grip on it, with up to 200 people directly reporting to him.
Some suggested his departure, which was sparked by the emergence that Huang had an affair with a woman alleged to have been a spy for China, posed a risk to the wider AI industry.

That was because it was unclear whether Nvidia would change strategy and potentially rein in spending - a move could have had wider implications for the US economy, but which looks unlikely now Huang has returned.

The fears were sparked due to Nvidia being a key source of finance for many firms, as well as being a microchip supplier. On its journey to the top of the AI industry, it has, through Huang, created a spider's web of deals through what is known as "circular financing".

Not only does it sell microchips to its customers, which include the likes of Meta, SpaceX and OpenAI, it has also provided funds for them and other firms in the supply chain by either handing out loans or investing in them directly.

The practice has prompted concerns among some investors, who worry what might happen if Nvidia were to turn off the spending taps. If investment dried up, would other firms in the supply chain cut spending or jobs themselves? Would that spread to the wider US economy?
That risk was perhaps why tech bosses including Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, the CEO of Fortnite maker Epic Games, had called for Huang's reinstatement.
Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation, and backed a campaign, along with shareholders and supporters, to "Bring Jensen Back".
Following the announcement of Huang's return, Musk posted: "The mistake has been corrected."
Kathleen Brooks, research director at investment platform XTB, said Huang's return suggested he was "the godfather" of AI and has the status to shift "the dial for corporate finance".

"Is Jensen Huang the most valuable man on the planet? His return suggests more of the same when it comes to circular financing and the rapid AI infrastructure build out, and the market loves it," she added.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmze: For a long time it seemed that Jensen Huang, the leather jacket-clad founder of Nvidia, dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech", could do no wrong.
Then came allegations of two affairs - one with a businesswoman suspected of being a Chinese spy - that rocked the world of tech and the global stock market. Huang resigned.
Now, just 11 days later, he's been reinstated by the board, who says it believes he is the right person to lead the company.
So what do we know about the man who is once again at the head of Nvidia, a linchpin in the US's race for technology leadership with China?
Huang may not be a household name on the same level as Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg.

But his role in the tech industry, especially in relation to the explosion of artificial intelligence in the last three years, may prove more consequential. Nvidia dominates the market for the microchips that are used to power the new technology.
The company is at the centre of the AI race between the US and China, the world's tech and economic powerhouses.
Huang enjoyed access to the seats of political power on an unrivalled scale, being courted by both US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping.

His remarkable rise to the top of his profession saw him amass an estimated fortune of close to $200bn earlier this year, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, though that has since dropped to around $105bn.

Despite always donning his trademark all-black outfits and taking a playful approach to investor presentations, Huang has worked for years to present himself as a family man, someone who exemplified the American Dream.

Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang and his family moved to the west coast of the US when he was nine years old. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a Master's degree in the same field from Stanford University.
It was at college where he met his wife, Lori Mills. The pair were lab partners and married in 1985, eight years before Huang founded Nvidia.
They have two children, Madison and Spencer, who now both work in senior roles at Nvidia.

The company became a key provider of the computer chips and circuits used for gaming before it expanded in a new direction. It now creates the key processing chips used to power the growing AI technology.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns after tech giant rocked by second affair allegation

Huang has hailed AI as a "new industrial revolution" that is on a par with the advent of electricity. Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company and its customers include the biggest firms on the planet, Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Tesla, OpenAI and Anthropic, all spending big on its products.

So it is no surprise that at a recent AI summit at the White House, Huang was picked out from a group of 42 to flank the president, alongside Elon Musk, both men with whom Trump has famously close relationships.

"Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on Jensen Huang, told the BBC, referring to the late boss of Apple. He added that Huang was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today.
He described him as a "demanding" boss, who "really pushes his people to the limit".
But while Huang is "very brilliant" and a "world-class computer scientist", there's also "a level of arrogance" and "a level of self-deception as well", he said.
Huang had gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, he added, something that was "very important to him".

First reports emerged on 29 October in the New York Times that Huang had conducted a relationship with Alice Huang, no relation. US officials allege the businesswoman associated with Singapore-based firm Megaspeed is a Chinese intelligence asset.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqpv: During the trial, the prosecution described Kurtaj as a "leading light" in the teen gang Lapsus$
A cyber criminal who hacked the maker of Grand Theft Auto has been released on licence on the same day as being sentenced to 7 years in prison.
Multiple offender Arion Kurtaj, from Oxford, was released from custody with the judge warning him: "Don't let this happen again."
The now 21-year-old hacked several companies and individuals, including GTA 6-maker Rockstar Games, whom he tried to extort after stealing clips of the unfinished game in 2022.
Kurtaj had pleaded guilty last Monday at Woolwich Crown Court to the Rockstar hack and a handful of others which he carried out when he was 16 and 17 years old with the hacking gang Lapsus$.
Kurtaj was originally sentenced to an indefinite stay in a secure hospital due to the severity of his autism.
But, in an unusual move, he was subsequently deemed fit to stand trial and released to a normal prison in January.
Now, he has been sentenced and released on the same day as the judge considered his hospital stay and remand in prison long enough.
He has been given a Serious Crime Prevention Order which will last five years. It restricts his activity online including barring him from using Telegram and Discord.
City of London Police said the case "highlights the dangers that young people can end up being drawn to online".
He hacked Rockstar games, Revolut and Uber while on bail and under police protection in a Travelodge in Bicester.
He was there for protection from rival hackers who had threatened to attack him for his stolen stashes of Bitcoin.
With his computer confiscated, Kurtaj hacked Rockstar using an Amazon Fire Stick plugged into his hotel room television along with a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse.
He stole internal company data including 90 clips showing nearly 60 minutes of gameplay from the unfinished GTA 6, which had been shrouded in secrecy until its release last week.
He then broke into the company's internal Slack messaging system to declare: "If Rockstar does not contact me on Telegram within 24 hours I will start releasing the source code."
The company refused to co-operate so he posted the clips and source code on a forum under the username TeaPotUberHacker.
Rockstar Games said it cost the firm $5m (£3.8m) to recover from the hack, plus thousands of hours of staff time.
The company also said the breach revealed for the first time that one of the playable characters in the game was a woman - a secret it was guarding closely for marketing purposes.
He had short hair and an unkempt beard and wore a suit and buttoned-up white shirt without a tie.
The Judge Mr Justice Turner told him "you are a very talented young man," and warned him: "Don't let this happen again."
Kurtaj's defence team said he found the online world a more comfortable way of interacting with other people.

"The restricted and repetitive patterns of behaviour and interests that are a core feature of ASD [autism spectrum disorder] led him to become preoccupied with the online world where he felt better able to function and exist," they said.
They said he was exposed to people who showed him how to cheat at games and then to "people who were involved in hacking".
During the pandemic, he was "very isolated" and his "connection to Lapsus$ provided him with a sense of community and self-worth that had been absent in his life previously," they added.
Kurtaj's Snapchat posts were the first sign for reporters that he had been released from a secure hospital

Kurtaj and the gang's other hacks on BT/EE, Revolut and Uber used social engineering techniques - tricking people into clicking malicious links or giving up sensitive information - to gain access to internal systems.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqe9: Lauren Goldboss is busy. The owner of a small San Francisco dog-walking company, she has been hiring staff and buying vans.
Fuelling the growth is her new office dog-walking service Paw Perk, popular with some local AI start-ups.
Her business is an example of how the AI boom in San Francisco is benefiting other sectors.
The city saw an exodus of residents during the pandemic and its downtown was weakened by remote work, but it's now enjoying a rejuvenation, with AI being the major driver.

Leading AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic – which have been hiring top engineering talent, often on eye-popping salaries – are based here. Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, last week listed on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.
Thousands of other AI start-ups have also sprung up , external in San Francisco.
Signs of the boom are evident in soaring rents and house prices, falling office vacancies, and buses and billboards plastered with cryptic AI adverts.

But what if there is a significant downward correction in AI share prices and a resulting big fall in investment in the industry? The International Monetary Fund last month became the latest organization to warn , external that this was a possibility.

Concerns have since continued due to the scandal surrounding Jensen Huang, the former boss of AI firm Nvidia, based south of San Francisco, causing some wider AI stock falls. However, Nvidia remains highly profitable, and Wednesday of this week it reported that its latest quarterly profits had doubled from a year earlier to $65bn (£49bn).
Simon Jack: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?
The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal
What are the thoughts of AI workers in the city, and should San Francisco – no stranger to tech's boom-and-bust cycles – be preparing for a possible crash?

One AI worker employed in the city is convinced that a crash is coming. "I am certain that the house of cards will come down… and I'm sure it will affect me," says the man who asked that we didn't use his name.
He questions whether leading US AI companies can generate enough revenues to justify their enormous spending commitments as cheaper, increasingly capable AI models emerge, especially from China.
But he isn't losing sleep over it. "Why worry about things I can't control?"
Another San Francisco-based AI worker, who also asked to remain anonymous, says that a significant market correction is "totally possible".

Yet he adds that most people don't think of it as the core risk. Instead, he says that the bigger concern in his circles, and the one he shares, is the existential risk that AI could pose to humanity.
"In some weird way, a market correction being the worst-case outcome feels great."
If there is an AI crash, San Francisco could be hit far more than Silicon Valley which lies 40 miles to its south.
That's because the AI boom is very much centred on the city itself rather than the wider San Francisco Bay Area, which includes Silicon Valley.

One study , external found that 60% of all venture capital invested in US AI firms from 2023 to 2025 went to the companies located in San Francisco, dwarfing the significantly smaller percentage given to companies in Silicon Valley.
But some factors suggest that the impact of a crash in San Francisco may be softer than some fear.
For all the investment they have attracted, AI companies are employing relatively few workers in the city compared to previous tech booms. So there may not be that many jobs to lose in a downturn.

"Hiring isn't necessarily on the scale as we would have thought with the amount of venture capital and new company formation," says Jeff Bellisario, executive director of the Bay Area Council Economic Institute, a business-affiliated think tank.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw8d: Whether it's scrolling through endless choice, spotting fake reviews, or working out if a "deal" is a deal at all, Black Friday sums up a lot of online woes.
Retailers promise bargains - but the sheer number of offers can leave us feeling no closer to finding the best deal.
It's an area where generative AI products, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, have promised to help.
But are they any good at finding Black Friday deals? We had a go ourselves a week ahead of the big day.
Figures suggest relatively few UK shoppers currently go to AI tools for help.
A recent YouGov survey of 19 countries found the UK ranked second-last in the proportion of people who said they had used AI to help them shop.
Crucially, 36% of respondents who said they would be shopping around Black Friday didn't plan to use an AI tool at all.
But the survey suggested a growing number of people were considering it - and tech firms have released features to capitalise on this.
Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping for UK users in November and OpenAI launched a Shopping Research tool on ChatGPT days before last year's Black Friday.
In the US, Google recently launched Universal Cart, with AI-powered features such as price tracking and identification of relevant promo codes.
But there has been criticism that fact-checking AI ends up taking more time, while some brands are working to try to make sure their products show up in chatbot answers.
We asked four models to find a 55-inch TV deal, using the free versions of many of the most popular tools.
While this was not a rigorous scientific test, the experience we had produced mixed results.
Its top pick was a Hisense TV on Chinese retailer Joybuy's website, on sale for £499 down from £649.
The next recommendation was a 55-inch TCL-branded TV, but a sidebar showed prices for the 50-inch version, from £379 to £814.
Option three was the same Hisense TV as before, but for full price at £649 from John Lewis and Richer Sounds.
This was the "best safer purchase" according to ChatGPT, as the sites offered longer guarantee periods.
But clicking on the links did not go well. Both retailers said the TV was no longer listed online.
The fourth option was equally fruitless - another TCL TV, at full price, £150 over our budget and not available online.
At the bottom, ChatGPT served one last offer - "one OLED option to compare" - for a £1,100 LG TV that was marked as "Ad" .
Claude produced the shortest answer of all the models we tested, and unlike the others, it did not give much detail on the specifications of each model.
Instead, it seemed to base its results on a small number of reviews published online.
But when we clicked on the links, they sent us to two dead pages on the Richer Sounds website.
Some other links led to year-old round-ups of Black Friday 2025 deals.
Claude was not very enthusiastic about its other two recommendations due to a lack of independent reviews - calling one "a decent option" but saying it "wouldn't pick" the other.
It also listed two Samsung TVs, but it told us not to buy them, with one "over budget and not clearly better than the TCLs".
We were left wondering why it even mentioned them in the first place.
Different AI model, same TV manufacturers - albeit different Hisense and TCL models to the previous chatbots' recommendations.
Gemini generated a table comparing four different models, but offered no links to the stores it named, so we searched for them ourselves.
The prices for one TCL TV were correct at £649, but it was sold out at one of the named retailers.
It said the other TCL model was available from Argos and Currys for £539 - correct for Argos, but when we checked Currys, it was £60 more expensive.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6pq: An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.

Levent Alpöge said , external on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut , that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.
If found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. Alpöge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".
The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months announced scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.
As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.
It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.
Named after the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.
Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.
Alpöge said that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery.
"The precise timing is horrible," Alpöge said, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier."
"I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added.
The complete textual proof that Alpöge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 pages long.

Terence Tao, a prominent mathematician, said on Friday , external that digestion of the proof - the process of understanding the reasoning behind it and how it connects to other mathematical ideas - is still some way off.
"I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao said.
No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI.

OpenAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.
More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.

The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.
Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths , external and physics , external .
A group of maths scholars said , external AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics".
"We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter.
A month later, OpenAI released , external what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.
It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/art: Bellingham has scored seven goals this season but this will be one to remember

Manager Jose Mourinho described Jude Bellingham as "without any doubt, the best midfielder in the world" following a wonder goal which inspired a brilliant second-half performance for Real Madrid in a 5-1 win against PSV .

Mourinho opted to leave the England midfielder out of the starting line-up for Tuesday's Champions League game at the Bernabeu - an understandable decision given the demands of Madrid's fixture schedule and the strength in depth at his disposal.
But after watching his side trail 1-0 at half-time against the Dutch side, Mourinho knew changes were needed.

"He is an amazing player that has everything," the Portuguese manager said. "He has physicality, he understands the game, he has absolutely everything. Today, he has changed how the game was evolving."
Captain Fede Valverde equalised in the 50th minute and 10 minutes later Bellingham produced his moment of magic.

Receiving the ball just outside the penalty area, he took two touches to lift it into position before unleashing a magnificent volley with the outside of his right foot, leaving PSV keeper Matej Kovar with no chance.
It was a sensational finish, executed with extraordinary precision.

"I was a bit surprised, honestly," Bellingham said about the goal. "I knew that I could control the ball well and get it into my grasp. But normally from there, I'm looking to see who's on as an option to play through.
"It popped up nicely and I thought I'm just going to hit it. So yeah, it was a nice goal and important for the team, being the second goal, and gave us control."
The 23-year-old celebrated in trademark fashion, standing with his arms outstretched in front of the home supporters as thousands serenaded him with chants of 'Hey Jude'.
It was his fourth goal in his past five appearances for Real.
Asked whether he should be compared to Real and France legend Zinedine Zidane, who won the Ballon d'Or and World Cup in 1998, Bellingham maintained his humility.
"I think Zidane is much better than me. He's much more elegant and he's my idol," he said.
'I'm just going to hit it!' - Bellingham reacts to stunning goal
Kylian Mbappe scored two more goals and Vinicius Junior put away the fifth to complete a super turnaround from a team that had looked short of ideas in the first half.
At the suggestion that he is currently in the form of his life, Bellingham said: "I think you're only as good as your next one [game]. Your last one doesn't really matter.
"But my focus has to change now to preparing for the next game. Thinking about my best form or being the best player in the world doesn't mean anything to me."
For Bellingham, the ability to respond when things are not going according to plan is what separates the best teams from the rest.
"We're managing to show that mentality that good teams do, that even if you're not playing well, you can raise the level at any point," he said.
His adaptation to life in Spain has also been an important part of that journey.
Asked about his increasingly impressive Spanish, Bellingham admitted he still gets nervous when speaking the language in public.
"It's getting a little bit better. I get a little bit nervous speaking to you guys. It's much easier in the changing room," he joked to journalists.

"I'm loving living in Spain. I'm loving the club. I think for English players it's such an important thing to go and move abroad and learn new things and I've obviously benefited massively from that."
And while his performances have inevitably brought renewed attention to individual awards, Bellingham said that personal recognition is not what motivates him.
Rayan Cherki (left) rescued a late draw for Manchester City against Napoli
Manchester City's slick footballing machine is starting to grind to a halt.
The quick passing patterns and edge-of-the-seat action that was evident for so long under former manager Pep Guardiola was supposed to be taken forward by incumbent Enzo Maresca.
It started flawlessly under the Italian with the side winning their first eight games, but that smooth operation is beginning to turn into a turgid and pedestrian showing.
Similar to Saturday's 1-1 draw against Fulham, moans and groans filled a rather flat Etihad Stadium as the home faithful watched their side labour to a 2-2 Champions League draw against Napoli.
City's recent defensive issues also continued, now conceding in 10 successive games and letting in the first goal in seven of those matches.

Maresca said: "We are always looking for three points but when you are not able to win it is important you that don't lose. We take the point, five games [played],10 points and overall I think it is a good result in the end.

"Today, off the ball, once again we didn't concede a lot, the problem is that in this moment they are clinical when we concede a chance, almost every time it is finishing with a goal. We created many chances but in this moment it is like this and move on.

"The first 10 games we always scored first and then in this moment it is exactly in the opposite way, we just need to find a way to avoid that, but I don't think it affects the players in terms of their confidence. We fought until the end."
City were strong favourites for this game and should have had few issues in collecting all three points against a Napoli side that are languishing in eighth place in Serie A.
Their injury issues mean they were able to name only seven substitutes, two of those being goalkeepers, while they had suffered defeat in their past three meetings with City.
They threatened a shock result after twice going ahead through well-taken goals from Rasmus Hojlund and Noa Lang, but Rayan Cherki managed to salvage a late draw for the hosts.
Maresca's side had 62.7% possession and attempted 665 passes, which largely lacked incisiveness, and of that figure 303 were in the final third compared to Napoli's 77.
The latest disappointing result means City's perfect start is quickly unravelling, now having won only one of their past seven games in all competitions inside 90 minutes.
"It was really surprising to see Manchester City so dull in the first half and so predictable," former Scotland winger Pat Nevin said on BBC Radio 5 Live.
"If you play a team that takes their time, you get yourself set. It is 100% easier to defend.
"You sit and watch City pass, pass, pass, slow, slow. You can get a cigar out."
Star striker Erling Haaland has been in prolific form again this season, scoring 20 goals for club and country, but the 26-year-old has drawn a blank in his past two games.
The Norwegian had chances but failed to score against Fulham on Saturday and though he was handed the captain's armband against Napoli, Haaland was on the periphery for much of the game.
The frontman managed only 14 touches of the ball against the Serie A side on Tuesday, the lowest figure of any player that started the match.
It raises the question whether he is receiving the service to try and find the back of the net.
"I feel I am getting more than enough chances to score," Haaland told TNT Sports. "We tried to push at the end for a goal but we couldn't. Not good enough and we let them in too easy.
"Football is easy and difficult; when you win it's easy and you know what to do, when you don't you start questioning everything. The perfect thing would be to not think but it's not so easy."
Mauricio Pochettino has taken over a Manchester United team in the Premier League relegation zone
Last season, Tottenham - a member of the so-called 'big six' - escaped relegation from the Premier League on the final day.
Now, with Manchester United making their worst start to a league season since 1972, it raises the question: are United this season's Spurs?

While Tottenham finished 17th with just 41 points last term, they actually started the season better than United have this season. After 11 games in 2025-26, Spurs were riding high in fifth with 18 points - 10 more than United have now.
But one of the biggest myths in football is 'the table never lies' and it was certainly lying about Tottenham at this stage last season.

While the table prompted talk of a possible Champions League place, expected goals (xG) had already recognised a relegation battle lay ahead for Tottenham, even predicting the position they'd finish in.
United's expected goal difference is almost identical to Tottenham's at this stage last season, but this time the table is more honest, even if United are perhaps not as bad as it makes out.
But there's no denying United's statistics are those of a team in a relegation battle, with many of them in the bottom six of Premier League teams this season.
While United have performed poorly defensively, their attack is actually not bad.
Remarkably, United have taken the most shots in the Premier League so far this season, and their expected goals scored figure is in the top five.

But what new head coach Mauricio Pochettino has to implement quickly is some quality control when it comes to shots at both ends of the pitch. United are converting just 7% of their chances and conceding 16% of their opponents' - a poor combination for any team.

And it is not simply down to finishing or shot-stopping, though they should have scored a few more. Based on xG per shot, United are currently taking the second-worst chances to score and giving up the easiest ones at the back.

As a result, Opta give United just over a one-in-four chance of being relegated at the end of the season (27.5%), making them the fifth-most likely side to go down after Crystal Palace, Sunderland, Ipswich and Coventry.
By analysing historical and team performances as well as the strength of opponents, Opta predict the percentage chance of each club finishing in each position.

While the above means it is more likely United will survive, it is worth noting the one position Opta predicts United are most likely to finish is 18th, with a 10.1% chance. That would mean the 13-time Premier League winners are relegated.

There is a 90% chance they finish anywhere else, but the next most likely are the three places just above the relegation zone, including a 9.9% chance of them finishing where Tottenham did last season.
History also suggests a relegation battle lies ahead for United given their poor start.
Of the 26 previous sides that had exactly eight points after 11 games, 13 survived and 13 were relegated. Among those that stayed up, only four finished more than six points above the danger zone.
A top-half finish looks unlikely. Since the competition became a 20-team league in 1995-96, no side has finished in the top half after taking eight points or fewer from their first 11 games.
Two teams did finish there more than 30 years ago but they had four more games to climb the table as teams played 42 games a season in those days.
Having said that, both were in the top half at the 38-game mark so United finishing there would not be entirely unprecedented.
It is a big ask, though, as the club have already taken 19 points fewer from the fixtures they have played than they did last season.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/: Fin Smith makes a break in last weekend's 37-12 win over New Zealand
With a grin and an expletive, Fin Smith describes Ben Earl as "greedy".
"It takes some doing to get just one carry when he's on the pitch," jokes Smith to BBC Sport. "He hogs them all."

Earl's performance in Saturday's win over New Zealand certainly caught the eye. The number eight carried a phenomenal 32 times in the 37-12 victory, more than twice as much as anyone else on the pitch.
But, further down the standings, Smith also stood out. He carried the ball 11 times against the All Blacks, the third-highest total of any England player.
That stat comes with context. The fly-half racked up his total in just 55 minutes on the pitch before cramp forced him to the bench.
For Smith, 5ft 10in tall and less than 14 stone, such physicality is not unusual.
A fortnight before beating New Zealand, against Australia, he carried nine times, his team's fourth-highest total.
According to stats from Oval Insights, he has carried more than any other fly-half in a Six Nations side this year.

If you include Rugby Championship teams in the mix, only three fly-halves - New Zealand's Richie Mo'unga, South Africa's Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu and Argentina's Tomas Albornoz - have backed themselves more with the ball.
Smith admits he does not haven't the athletic ability of some of those rivals.
But the Northampton man says his attempts to play through the defence, rather than in front of them, helps him lead the team to a more effective attack.
"I do like the physical side," he adds. "It gets me into games, but also I think it is just my character.
"I would hate to be someone that is asking everyone else to go and be physical and put their body on the line, if I wasn't particularly willing to do it. I think that's how I've been brought up."
With George Furbank, Henry Slade and Seb Atkinson all able to step in at first receiver, Smith being buried at the bottom of the breakdown is a price England are able to pay for a phase or two.
"The way we're playing at Northampton and England, and the way I feel like teams attack best when I'm in them, is when there are almost no numbers on backs.
"You play as quickly as possible and whoever ends up in the slots just does that job. You've got to be interchangeable.
"If the right thing to do is carry or the right thing to do is hit the breakdown then so be it, and then someone else can drop in as the first playmaker.

"I think that just makes us a harder team to play against. Our scrum-halves are running a lot more than they have and all of a sudden defences have got to think about do they tighten up to defend the nine and then if the 10s are running the ball a bit more they have to think about me.
"Then spaces open up and you've become so much less predictable."
After a miserable Six Nations, England have found a new attacking edge in the Nations Championship. They have scored 44 tries across their six games in the tournament, 10 more than any other side.
On Saturday, they are hunting a sixth-straight win as they face a rematch against New Zealand in the final's weekend's third-place play-off.

Smith says England's current streak, after the five straight defeats that preceded it, has coincided with the team becoming more introspective, both on and off the pitch.
"The big thing that's changed would be we've been a lot more inwardly focused," Smith said.
"We're confident that if we're at our best, it should hopefully take care of whatever the opposition brings to the table.
"I think that was a big learning we got from the South Africa game [July's 45-21 defeat] is actually 'let's just do what we want to do and do it really well'.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/art: Viktor Gyokeres has scored three goals in all competitions this season for Arsenal.
It might be emerging more as a theme than as a major problem, but in recent weeks Arsenal cannot seem to finish off matches when they are on top.
In their past nine outings across all competitions, just once have the Gunners won a game by more than a single goal.

The latest frustration came in Tuesday's 1-1 draw with Borussia Dortmund , though perspective is needed. Arsenal might consider it as two points dropped having gone into half-time ahead, but they remain unbeaten in the current Champions League league phase and have not lost at this stage of the competition for more than two years.
But of late, despite dominating large parts of matches, Arsenal have had periods where they have dropped off and allowed opponents back into the game.

Against Slavia Prague away in the Champions League, after scoring twice in the first half, Arsenal 's standards dropped. The same happened against Newcastle in the Premier League last weekend where they found themselves 2-1 behind in the second half having led at the break, before recovering to eventually draw 2-2.
They are producing periods of high-level football, but the struggles to consistently turn that into more goals can lead to nervy finishes.
In the draw with Bundesliga leaders Dortmund, Arsenal had 30 shots but just four of those attempts were on target.
Boss Mikel Arteta mentioned the failure to capitalise post match, though was keen to praise his side's "brilliant performance".

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/: Wales wing Louis Rees-Zammit has impressed since returning to rugby union from a stint in American Football
Australia wing Harry Potter had Louis Rees-Zammit exactly where he wanted him.
As Wales attacked in Cardiff on Saturday, Potter showed Rees-Zammit the outside – a four-metre channel between him and the touchline.
The touchline is a defender's best friend. An extra defender. The edge of the cliff. It would take something extraordinary to beat Potter without running out of ground.

A shake of the hips and a change of direction later, Potter was diving like a cricketer in the outfield, grasping at thin air. Rees-Zammit was on his way to setting up a wonderful try for Blair Murray.
Rees-Zammit has been turning heads for years. On the pitch with his pace, off it with his pristine teeth and pop star looks.
Alex Cuthbert knows a thing or two about running. A former national-level 400m runner and British and Irish Lions wing, he spent much of his rugby career working on his technique.
What fascinates him about Rees-Zammit now is not his speed but how he generates it.
"His leg drive and strength from his knee to his hip has got so much stronger," said Cuthbert, who scored 17 tries in 57 Tests for Wales.
The difference is most apparent not over 100 metres but over four or five, changing direction and accelerating before a defender can adjust his feet.
"If you do that shimmy and you stand any sort of player up, you can't recover. Literally can't recover," Cuthbert said.
Cuthbert attributes much of that development to Rees-Zammit's 18 months in American football with the Kansas City Chiefs and Jacksonville Jaguars.
"I thought last season he was a little bit heavy. He looked like a running back last year, whereas this year he is more of a wide receiver," Cuthbert said.
A running back, says Cuthbert, powers through traffic, a wide receiver thrives in open space. He now sees elements of both in Rees-Zammit.
Rees-Zammit's coach at Bristol Bears, Pat Lam, estimates he returned from America eight or nine kilograms heavier.
"What was very clear was his pace was still there, if not quicker, but he was a bigger man and he needed to adjust," said Lam.
Lam is arguably one of rugby's most system-driven coaches. Understanding your role is fundamental at Bristol, where only a select few are afforded the freedom to deviate from the script.
Having established himself as a wing before his American adventure, Rees-Zammit was keen to experiment on his return to rugby.
"He spoke to me about a desire to play full-back and give full-back a go," said Lam.
Lam sees the modern full-back as an auxiliary centre in attack, responsible for creating opportunities for others.
"But we had to go through that process for him to actually say to me, 'Pat, I'm a world-class winger and I'm a world-class finisher'. And I said, 'I agree'," Lam said.
According to Lam, Rees-Zammit now considers himself a wing who can cover full-back, rather than a full-back who can play on the wing.
Louis Rees-Zammit's time in the NFL included stints with the Kansas City Chiefs and Jacksonville Jaguars
Another moment from Saturday offered a reminder of Rees-Zammit's extraordinary pace when Joseph-Aukuso Sua'ali'i intercepted a Welsh pass and set off downfield.
The Australian, a formidable athlete in his own right, had a head start of at least five metres.
The speed has always been there. The numbers reveal how much more there is to his game now.
Rees-Zammit scored five tries in 10 Premiership appearances for Bristol last season. This season he has matched that tally in five games, beating 28 defenders and making 12 clean breaks.

His perfectly weighted assist for Gassama showed the touch of a player full of confidence and playing at the peak of his powers.

India's 15-year-old batting sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi hit the most sixes ever recorded in a senior men's innings in blazing 204 from 53 balls for India A against the United Arab Emirates.

While almost halving the record for the fastest double-century in List A cricket, Sooryavanshi hit 28 sixes and seven fours in the Asia Cup Rising Stars competition - easily breaking Chad Bowes' previous record of 103 balls from 2024 .
The teenage opener also broke the record for the fastest century and 150, the latter of which he already held, before being caught at long-off with his side five runs from victory.
India A ultimately passed their target of 250, played against a UAE side that featured a number of internationals but was not their current first-choice side, in 14.2 overs in Doha.
Sooryavanshi now holds the following records in List A cricket, the categorisation given to senior one-day matches:
Fastest fifty: 11 balls v Sri Lanka A , 21 June (previously Kaushalya Weeraratne, 12 balls, 1 November 2005)
Fastest hundred: 28 balls, today (previously Jake Fraser-McGurk , 29 balls, 8 October 2023)
Fastest 150: 40 balls, today (previously himself , 59 balls, 24 December 2025)
Fastest 200: 52 balls, today (previously Chad Bowes, 103 balls, 22 October 2024)

The previous record for the most sixes in senior matches was 26, struck by Tanmay Agarwal in an innings of 366 for Hyderabad against Arunachal Pradesh in India's first-class Ranji Trophy competition in January 2024.
The record in List A cricket was 23 sixes, struck by D'Arcy Short for Queensland in his 257 against Tasmania on 28 September 2018.
Sooryavanshi also holds the records of being the youngest century-maker in both List A and T20 cricket and the youngest captain in T20s .
"The first thing that's required in this format is being fearless, he's got plenty of that," former India batter Deep Dasgupta told BBC Radio 5 Live.
"Technically he's quite unique. There is a tendency of being over-coached in this generation, there's so many coaches and when you start playing franchise cricket.
"The best part is he has been fast-tracked so he hasn't had a lot of coaches, he's kind of untouched. What you see of him is predominantly what his natural game is.
"That bat swing, the hand speed, which is very, very natural and one of the quickest you'll come across. Technically he's very gifted, he's very special and he's definitely the real deal."
Sooryavanshi has rapidly become a sensation in T20 cricket since making his debut in the Indian Premier League in 2025 at the age of 14.
He has hit two hundreds and six fifties in his first two seasons in the competition and has earned 10 caps for India in the shortest format since making his debut against England in July.
The left-hander, who was batting in only his 16th List A innings in Doha and made his second century in the format, is yet to play for India in 50-over cricket.
He put on partnerships of 68 with opening partner Abhishek Sharma, who scored 12, 40 with Prabhsimran Singh, who added just three, and 137 with Rinku Singh, who scored an unbeaten 27.

The India A side, which featured a number of internationals, restricted the UAE to 249-8 in 50 overs , external after their opposition had chosen to bat and swiftly reached 254-3 to win by seven wickets and guarantee their place in the semi-finals.
The Rising Stars competition features A sides from India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Afghanistan alongside squads from the UAE, Nepal and Hong Kong.
India A, who now top Group B, beat Nepal and lost to Pakistan A in their previous two matches in the competition, with Sooryavanshi making scores of 26 and 11.

"A big reason why I wanted to come to Auckland and play in this team is because I thought I'd fit in well.

"We need to put the ball on the net to solve this and not suffer goals easily, it's very important.

Moreira often references the "fight" of his team as they battle to improve this season. An actual skirmish broke out against Victory and the coach saw it as two teams showing how much a result matters.

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/sport/2771437: One of the reasons for Jordie Barrett's recent nomination for World Rugby's player of the year award is his directness on the field, and the midfielder took a similar approach when addressing the media about the All Blacks' recent failings.

Barrett's defensive commitment alone sets him apart in a team beset by issues in this area, but, not surprisingly, any pleasure he received from being nominated along such luminaries as French wing Louis Bielle-Biarrey (the likely favourite) and South African front rowers Malcolm Marx and Ox Nche for the top award has been tarnished by the events in Cardiff and London.

All Blacks loose forward Peter Lakai scores the try against the Wallabies which earned him a World Rugby award nomination.

"It's nice to be recognised as an individual but to be honest there's a bit of a knot in my gut about how we're performing as a team," Barrett said. "I've put that aside pretty quickly and I just want to win as an All Black.

Barrett confirmed he had confidence in the All Blacks' game plan and direction from the coaches.

Barrett makes a break during the All Blacks' win against Scotland in Edinburgh.

"Competitive" and "committed" are some of the words teammates of former Silver Ferns captain Julie Carter are using to describe her, as news of her death reaches the far corners of the netball community.
Netball New Zealand on Monday said it was deeply saddened to share the news that Carter had died, aged 60.
"Jules", or "JC" as she was often referred by her teammates, played 50 Tests for New Zealand between 1986 and 1993.
The crafty goal attack, who could also slot in at wing attack, became the Silver Ferns' 16th captain in 1992.

Carter was known as one of the great thinkers of the game, and someone who set high standards for herself and those around her - qualities that served her well as the game entered the semi-professional era.
Julie Coney was the 14th captain of the Silver Ferns and was in the later stages of her career when Carter started making a mark.
"She was selected in 1986 and played in the series against Jamaica, but then Jules just missed out making the team to travel to Glasgow in 1987 for the World Championships," Coney said.
"She was re-selected for the World Games in 1989 and we travelled to Germany for the World Games where we won gold."
Carter also played in the 1990 Commonwealth Games demonstration match when Coney was captain.
"We were all pretty proud to pave the way to Comm Games inclusion, even though we were beaten so badly on that particular day by Australia."
For Coney, what stood out about Carter was that she was "very, very committed".
Julie Coney (right) commentating in 1995 at a Test between between the Silver Ferns and England.
"Julie was such a great person within the team. She was a down to earth, no nonsense sort of girl and very committed and very very fit and gritty, just gave everything to the game on court.
"The words that come to mind for me are competitive, driven, tough and clever. She was the sort of person that you wanted on your side.
"She was also good fun off the court. She loved a good laugh with her teammates."
At a domestic level, Coney represented Auckland and often had to mark Carter, when she played for Wellington.
"I was a goal defence and she was one of the most difficult goal attacks I've ever played against.

"We had some real tussles over the years, and she was just the type of player that really got under your skin and you had to use all your smarts and skills. You had to pull your best moves, put it that way."
The majority of Carter's Silver Ferns career was played alongside goal shooter Tracy Eyrl-Shortland. The pair seemed to have an invisible connection in the shooting end.
The 1991 Silver Ferns team that contested the World Championships in Sydney.
Both stood at just 5 ft 9 in, which would almost be unheard of in today's game, where most international shooters are over six foot.
"They were an incredible partnership, they sort of came to the forefront after Glasgow, the late 80s through the 90s, Julie and Tracy were the shooters," Coney said.
The Silver Ferns won silver at the 1991 World Championships in Sydney after a heartbreaking one goal loss to Australia.
When Carter was appointed Silver Ferns captain in 1992 she was leading a rebuild after a number of retirements.
Carter grew up in Hamilton and played for Melville High School, where the great Lyn Parker was a selector and PE teacher.
Parker would go on to coach the Silver Ferns during Carter's national career.
Carter started playing her domestic netball for Waikato, where she's remembered by former Silver Fern Tracey Fear as "versatile, tough and athletic!"

"The recruitment is bloody difficult but we've had a couple of wins and we've got some good young guys and a good balance of experienced guys as well.

"It's really challenging to attract players down to Dunedin. If I go back a few years ago the team was predominantly made up of Southland boys and the Otago guys… now the majority of our team, including the coaches, are coming from outside the region. While we love [the region], it is hard to entice guys to come down south.

Moyin Odeniran said he was "in shock" after being crowned the winner of the 17th series of The Great British Bake Off.
The 22-year-old from Loughton, Essex, described it as a "very busy time" as he juggled competing in the Channel 4 baking competition with completing his university studies .
Despite his dissertation being due a month after filming wrapped, Odeniran achieved a first in his political economy degree at King's College London.
He beat fellow finalists Tom Whittaker, from West Yorkshire, and Birmingham student Mo Mahir to the title in Tuesday night's episode.
"I don't know how that happened, I don't know how I got here. I can't believe it – I am in shock," the talented baker said.
"I have made friends for life and I have just loved every single second of it, and I don't think I could have asked for anything more."
Judge Paul Hollywood described Odeniran's efforts as "pure magic" after watching his jubilant celebrations with family and friends.
"He has done an amazing job because out of all the bakers he struggled at the beginning, and he actually got better and better," Hollywood said.
Fellow judge Nigella Lawson praised Odeniran as a "worthy winner", but also said the other finalists were "sensational".
The high-stakes final saw the three contestants tasked with making a citrus celebration cake, creme brulee donuts and a "spectacular tribute to iconic British landscapes".
Reflecting on his performance in the final, Odeniran said: "I didn't want to put too much pressure on myself, but I knew I had put my best foot forward.
"I couldn't have done anything better than I did and I had a great time doing it."
He said he got "quite exhausted" while filming the series and praised his mother, sister and close friends for their support.
"Earlier on, some of the challenges were quite difficult for me and I was shocked that I kept going through," Odeniran said.
"Before you get there you think you know how to bake, and by week two you question whether you know anything about baking."
He shared his gratitude at being able to learn from Lawson and Hollywood.
"I will never forget my time there and the friendships made which will always continue," the winner added.
Prior to the final, Odeniran told BBC Essex he planned to view it at a huge "watch party" at his local church .

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqwy: Veteran Nigerian actor Pete Edochie, one of Africa's most celebrated film stars, has died at the age of 79, his family has announced.

Known for his deep voice, commanding screen presence and memorable use of African proverbs, Edochie became a household name across Africa, often portraying powerful traditional rulers, wealthy businessmen and family patriarchs.
In a statement, his family said Edochie died in the early hours of Wednesday in the south-eastern Nigerian city of Enugu following a prolonged battle with prostate cancer.
Tributes are pouring in from fans and fellow actors, remembering him as a Nollywood legend who helped shape Nigeria's film industry.

Edochie began his career as a broadcaster in 1967 before turning to acting. He rose to prominence in 1987 after starring in a television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart.

His portrayal of Okonkwo, the proud but troubled Igbo warrior in Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart, earned him international recognition helping establish him as one of Nigeria's most respected actors.
He went on to become one of the most recognisable faces of Nollywood, Nigeria's film industry, which has since grown into one of the world's largest film industries.
Over a career spanning several decades, he appeared in numerous films, including Igodo, Rituals, Billionaire's Club and the 2018 romantic comedy Lionheart.
His contribution to the arts was recognised in 2003 when he received one of Nigeria's national honours, the Member of the Order of the Niger (MON).
In recent years, his distinctive facial expressions, witty remarks and memorable scenes from his films found a new generation of admirers through viral social media memes.

"As we mourn this painful loss, we pray that Almighty God grants his gentle soul eternal rest and gives the entire family the fortitude to bear this irreparable loss," a statement shared on Instagram by his son Leo said.
Edochie had spoken publicly about his deteriorating health during a visit to Ghana in October, saying he was struggling to walk and experiencing swelling in parts of his body.
He is survived by his wife, Josephine, and their six children, including fellow Nollywood actors Yul and Linc Edochie.
