https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqrm: The substance was released near the end of US rapper Don Toliver's gig at Co-op Live on Sunday
An "unknown substance" that prompted a mass evacuation at a rap concert may be linked to robberies and stolen jewellery at the venue, police have said.
More than 12,000 people were evacuated from Manchester's Co-op Live during a performance by US rapper Don Toliver on Sunday.
One person was taken to hospital and 88 others were treated at the scene after concertgoers reported a "horrible smell" and some people "coughing up blood".
Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said officers received nine reports of jewellery being stolen during the concert but no arrests had been made and the substance had not yet been identified.
Assistant Chief Constable Tom Harding said there was "no wider ongoing risk" to the public.

"We are aware similar robberies have been reported at two European concerts for the same artist and will be linking in with our European counterparts to better understand the wider picture of this suspected offending," he said.
In a statement on Tuesday evening, Co-op Live said it was conducting a "full review" into the incident.
"The safety and security of our guests, artists and staff remain our highest priority, and we take that responsibility extremely seriously."
The venue, which opened in 2024, apologised to fans for what should have been an "enjoyable evening" and said it expects no disruption to future events.
The substance was released at around 22:00 GMT, near the end of Toliver's show as part of his Nitrous – Octane world tour.
Afterwards, 88 people underwent dry decontamination at the scene and were accommodated at the neighbouring Etihad Stadium while the incident was managed.
Friends Poppy Rutter and Sophie Billing say they felt "unsafe" as they left the arena
Poppy Rutter and Sophie Billing, both 19, who had travelled from Cambridge to see the concert, said it was not immediately clear what had happened.
Sophie said: "I thought something had gone wrong with smoke coming off stage.
"We started to suffer, coughing and spluttering and feeling tight-chested. A member of staff said it was tear gas.
"Security rushed in and went straight to the pit. We only left as we were starting to feel unsafe and not 100 per cent well."
She said there was "no communication", adding: "You would think Manchester would be extra vigilant, given what's happened in the past."

Posting on Instagram on Monday, Toliver said: "I just wanna make sure everyone is safe and the next show goes on properly. My heart and prayers are with everyone that was injured last night at Co-op Live.
"The only thing I love more than creating music is performing for my fans."
He also asked that people stop bringing substances into his shows.
GMP urged anyone who feels unwell or develops symptoms following the concert to seek medical advice.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cky9: The museum's Our Time space will host events among 13 large installations and flocks of sheep benches

Ten years ago the Museum of London announced it would be leaving its former home to move to the abandoned halls of Smithfield Market. Now rebranded London Museum, it is set to open its doors to the public on Saturday after a £437m project. So what's it like inside?
Leaning back on a leather sofa, museum director Sharon Ament looks across a vast brick-lined space that once bustled with market traders but is now filling with its newest visitors.
"I really love this space, it just makes me smile every time I come in - it's actually joyful," she says.
The vast room, now known as Our Time, is dotted with installations reflecting living memory.

In one corner a life-size mechanical giraffe flicks its ears in front of a lit-up NHS sign representing lockdown. Another wall has remnants of London's former greyhound tracks. Near it is the old switchboard from Buckingham Palace.
And beneath the magnificent domed ceiling roam several flocks of large plastic sheep which Ament encourages people to "pull up and take a seat" on.
"There are grins on people's faces, so I think we've pulled something rather incredible off," she says.
Sharon Ament says she wants the museum to be a shared space for everyone
The museum reflects London's more recent history such as its greyhound-racing tracks - the fireplaces of the market traders' former offices can be seen behind
A visit to the new museum starts before this point as people enter through a large covered street known as Real Time.
Here, data-filled digital displays tell of London in the moment, beside a Banksy-graffitied sentry box and the last bell to be cast at the historic Whitechapel Bell Foundry .
Next they enter the former General Market with its sheep, giraffe and signage.

This is the space where events like late-night house parties and dinner clubs will be held beside shops and eateries, including former Victorian cocoa rooms that will be open 24 hours a day at weekends.
Such hints of the building's past are everywhere. Halfway up the walls are the restored fireplaces of the traders' former offices, along with twisting metal staircases that once led up to them.
"Whenever we've found historic fabric, we've restored it or kept it, and we want to show the layers of history," explains Alec Shaw, who has led the entire project.
"We wanted a museum that worked like the market, that allowed you to come in any corner and just walk across, walk through the building on your way to work, or, hopefully, stay a bit longer."
Smithfield's General Market opened in the 1880s and was in use until the 1990s
The Our Time space seen in early 2024 when water was still splashing into the building
Shaw previously showed me around the site nearly three years ago , when scaffolding and supports were holding up the walls and there were constant splashes of water dripping on to the floor.

Restoring a Victorian relic that was abandoned in the 1990s "really tested all of us", he admits, and that was before the logistics involved in designing a new museum from the venue's seven-million object collection.
Five thousand of these are now on site and another 300,000 are due to arrive for when the former Poultry Market becomes a museum space in 2028.
"We think you could take at least eight hours to see every object downstairs, and that means you're going to keep coming back.
"The best museums are those that you go, 'Right I'll do that one today. I'll do this gallery next time,'" he says.
Our Past is based in the building's basement and tells a weaving story of London through five different chapters
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqpv: Hunter Schafer first came across Blade Runner when the 2017 sequel was released
"What does it mean to be human?" is a question that's always been at the heart of Blade Runner.
The first film in the series, released in 1982, depicted a technologically advanced yet dystopian version of Los Angeles in the then-distant future of 2019.
While the movie's flying cars haven't - quite - materialised yet in the real world, Blade Runner's themes of technological progress and the threats it poses feel just as relevant.
At least that's what the cast and crew of Blade Runner 2099, a new TV series set in the same universe, are hoping.

BBC Newsbeat spoke to stars Hunter Schafer, Lewis Gribben and Dimitri Abold, plus showrunner Silka Luisa, to ask why they think themes of artificial consciousness and existential threats still resonate.
The original Blade Runner, directed by Sir Ridley Scott, is considered a sci-fi classic that had a long-lasting influence on the genre.
It told the story of Detective Deckard, played by Harrison Ford, who hunted down synthetic humans known as replicants.
Schafer says her first exposure to the series was actually marketing for Blade Runner 2049 - the film sequel starring Ford and Ryan Gosling in 2017.
"I never thought I'd have the opportunity to make an addition to the world," she says.
"And so when that opportunity came along, I was quite thrilled."
Blade Runner 2099 is set 80 years after the original film, and portrays a Los Angeles where replicants have taken over.
Schafer plays Cora, a fugitive human forced to team up with replicant Olwen (played by Michelle Yeoh), as she tries to track down an artefact that could save humanity.
Schafer stars alongside Oscar winner Michelle Yeoh in the new TV adaptation
The series lands at a time when there are disagreements about the nature of the threat AI could pose to humans .
"I think it's particularly relevant right now, especially for the youth and young people who are inheriting a world that's asking a lot of the same questions that the show asks," says Schafer.
"I think that's timely and hopefully helpful to some degree."
But Blade Runner 2099 isn't "necessarily about just AI", says showrunner Luisa.
"It's this bigger question of what is the world going to be in 15 years and how can you plan for it?" she says.
The first Blade Runner also touched on themes of corporate greed and environmental damage, which are evident in the new series.
Luisa hopes the theme of a future that "is not going to be what you were promised" resonates with viewers today.
"The idea that you were born into a world and you thought you were expecting certain aspects of your life just to roll out," she says.
"That system is collapsing. And so what will be your place in whatever comes next?"
Blade Runner 2049 won awards and scored well with reviewers, but reports suggested it didn't hit box office targets.
This was partly blamed on marketing for the film trying to appeal more to existing fans than new ones - so what would the cast say to get younger viewers on board?
"It's just a very rich world," says Gribben, who plays Cora's younger brother Elias.
Gribben also points out that Blade Runner 2099, which employed "hundreds of artists and craftspeople" according to its makers, is a celebration of traditional film-making despite its themes.
"And I think studios will rely more on technology to make better-looking movies, but they won't have that soul."
Abold, who plays Cora's human ally Bebeto, says one of the show's key messages is about "the connections that you make".
"And the connections that you make are the foundation of humanity," he says.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9zr: Hey Duggee is among the shows which will be part of the CBeebies hub on Netflix
The BBC and Netflix are to launch a trial hub on the streaming service next month, featuring 24 CBeebies shows.
Programmes including Hey Duggee, Numberblocks and Teletubbies can be seen on a branded CBeebies hub on Netflix from 2 December.
The trial's aim is to test new ways for the flagship pre-school channel to reach audiences. The BBC is the UK's largest commissioner of children's content.

BBC iPlayer will remain the home for all CBeebies content. Some CBeebies shows such as Shaun the Sheep are already available on Netflix, but this is the first time they will have a home hub on the subscription streamer.

CBeebies shows will also be made available to Netflix members outside the UK in a distribution deal managed by BBC Studios, with the aim of driving investment into children's content in the UK. The deal does not include China.
Netflix will also commit to funding a small number of new CBeebies commissions, the BBC said.
BBC's chief content officer Kate Phillips said the corporation is "always looking at how we can help more audiences discover" its content and brands.
"This limited trial will make a curated selection of CBeebies programmes available on Netflix, while BBC iPlayer remains the home of the full CBeebies experience," she added.
Anne Mensah, vice president of Netflix's UK content said the "unique partnership allows us to work hand in hand with the BBC to support our brilliant British kids' programme makers".
She added: "We want to build a fun and safe space parents can feel good about, with content their kids will love."
The news comes against the backdrop of big changes at the BBC.
The corporation announced plans earlier this year to cut about 1,800 roles and close some programmes and services, but it has further savings to make to reach a £500m savings target.
The BBC's finances have declined in recent years as a result of falling licence fee income and rising production costs.
The corporation also faces growing competition for audiences from streaming services, gaming, social media and YouTube.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c65y: The first ever Children's Booker Prize has announced the eight books in the running for the new £50,000 award.
Five novels, two graphic novels and an illustrated collection of short stories are on the shortlist, which is aimed at children aged eight to 12.
The authors in contention include former Children's Laureate of Ireland Eoin Colfer, who is best known for his Artemis Fowl series, and teacher and children's author Catherine Bruton.
Four children have also been announced as new judges after a UK-wide competition. Twelve-year-old Ibrahim from Hampshire was one of those picked from more than 4,000 entrants.
He told me he was called back into school for a phone call with chair of judges Frank Cottrell-Boyce, who broke the news. Ibrahim said he couldn't be happier.
"First Children's Booker Prize judge! On my CV - that's going to take me a long way… I'm too overwhelmed to even be excited."

Cottrell-Boyce told the BBC "it's really, really important that this is a prize for children's books. Having judges who are children will be proof of that… If the children don't love a book, it won't win."

Ibrahim, his fellow child judges and Cottrell-Boyce will be joined on the judging panel by Ghosts and Horrible Histories actor Lolly Adefope and Sanchita Basu De Sarkar, who owns an award-winning children's book shop in north London.
Ibrahim said he loves reading "because it's just a way to unwind yourself from the outside world. If you get stuck in a book, you're not getting your face out of there until you finish it".

He's far too professional to share which books on the list he likes best, but he told me when he was reading one of them recently: "I had to tell my mum to confiscate it because I couldn't stop reading it and I was getting a headache."
Cottrell-Boyce said he isn't concerned over whether the adult judges might dominate the decision-making.
"If - like me - you've been visiting schools as a children's writer for 20 years, it's a rare thing to meet a child who is too over-awed to express an opinion. They're usually very forthright".
Ibrahim proves that point. He told me "the adults are not going to control that meeting… 100% not!"

He's looking for "something that has different perspectives, you can see it in a different way. New characters, not just the same old sloppy characters that authors make all the time. They just make these books that just have the same plot line".
The shortlisted books are by authors and illustrators from the UK, Ireland, Australia and Italy. Cottrell-Boyce described the list as "full of surprises." Here it is:
The Worst Thing That Could Possibly Happen by Guy Bass, illustrated by David Roberts. Readers on Goodreads describe it as "super creepy" and "how horror for kids should be written."

War by Eoin Colfer and Andrew Donkin, illustrated by Giovanni Rigano. It's the third book in their graphic novel series and tells the story of 14-year old Kat, living under siege in an unnamed European city.

The Night I Borrowed Time by Iqbal Hussain - the British-Pakistani author and former journalist's debut Children's book weaves a story through the eyes of Zubair, a seventh son who has inherited the power of time travel and tries to fix the lives of his family.

The Rambler's Curse by Mikey Please - the fantasy-comedy by the Aardman animator, who has also illustrated the book, has been described by The Guardian as a "laugh-out-loud, shaggy-dog spiral of purposes mistook".

The Teller of Tall Tales by Liz Hyder, illustrated by Tom de Freston, was a critic's choice in The Daily Telegraph. It's about a grandmother living in a remote cabin who weaves mysterious stories for her estranged grandchild.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3qj: King Charles and Elton John have paid tribute to Australian music industry legend Molly Meldrum, who died aged 83 after a long illness.
Meldrum's family said he "passed away peacefully" at a hospital in Melbourne in the early hours of Monday morning.
The music promoter and broadcaster, born Ian Alexander Meldrum, helped define the nation's music tastes for decades, championing local artists like INXS and Kylie Minogue and global acts like Abba.
Known for his chaotic demeanour and trademark Stetson hat, he interviewed an array of stars, with the king on Monday calling him "a true giant of the music industry".

Born in Victoria in 1943, Meldrum displayed a love of music from an early age and went on to host the Australian Broadcasting Corporation's music television programme Countdown, and later a segment on variety show Hey Hey, It's Saturday.
Meldrum in 2014 became the first person who was not a recording artist to be inducted into the Australian Recording Industry Association (Aria) Hall of Fame.
Meldrum lived with an acquired brain injury after falling from a ladder in 2011.
"Affectionately dubbed 'the Guru', Molly was the heartbeat, the champion and the spirit of Australian music," a statement from Meldrum's family said.
Among his most famous interviews was a 1977 sit-down with King Charles, in which Meldrum could not calm his jitters.
He stumbled over his lines, declaring: "Your Royal Highness... Oh, oh, I'm sweating like a pig".

King Charles reflected on the infamous interview for Countdown's 40th anniversary special , saying: "There is an old showbusiness saying which warns never to work with animals or children. But nobody prepared me for Molly Meldrum".
On Monday, an aide to the King said he had been "deeply saddened" to hear of Meldrum's death.

"His Majesty's interview with Molly is a moment he and many others will never forget - he hopes that interview will once again raise a few smiles as Australians honour Molly's legacy as a true giant of the music industry."
Elton John - a friend and regular interviewee - paid tribute to him as "an Australian legend and an institution", while pop star Kylie Minogue said she would be turning up the music in his honour.
"As a kid, I watched Molly Meldrum on Countdown every single weekend, in awe of the show and the magic it brought to our little TV in the lounge room."
"He championed so many Aussie artists and welcomed international artists to Australia in his own wonderful and inimitable way. I'm so grateful for his unwavering love and support."

Australia's Arts Minister Tony Burke said the country had lost an icon: "One of his greatest legacies will be the generations of Australians who grew up with his unmistakable enthusiasm and love of music."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckr5: Recording of the well-loved radio soap could leave Birmingham for the first time in 75 years
Audiences attending the final performances of The Archers' 75th anniversary roadshows are being urged to back a campaign to keep the long-running soap in Birmingham.

The BBC has shelved plans to build a drama studio at its new base in the city - which entertainment union Equity said threatened to "undermine everything that makes The Archers so special to millions of people."
Cast members will be chatting to fans outside The Archers: Live at 75 roadshows in Coventry and Wolverhampton to ask them to lobby the BBC and their MPs.
The broadcaster said it was having "constructive discussions with programme makers and local stakeholders," and remains committed to finding a long-term solution.

The BBC Radio 4 drama, which celebrated its 75th anniversary earlier this year, is set in the fictional West Midlands village of Ambridge. It is believed to have been inspired by the village of Inkberrow in Worcestershire, with The Old Bull Inn being closely associated with the show's pub The Bull.

The corporation had initially pledged to build the show a new studio in the Tea Factory, its new hub in Digbeth, Birmingham. However while the series production team will move there as planned, it was decided that the recording studio would no longer be built there .
A spokesperson for Equity said the cast was "unanimous in wanting to remain in the West Midlands".
Ben Norris, Equity representative for The Archers cast, said:
"All of the rich tapestry of Ambridge life has been recorded in Birmingham since it was launched 75 years ago and we want it to remain there.
"If the BBC pulls us apart it threatens to undermine everything that makes The Archers so special to millions of people. This is not a done deal and we're urging them to think again."
The Archers was launched 75 years ago and has always been recorded in Birmingham
Paul W Fleming, Equity general secretary, said the union feared programme makers were under pressure from the BBC to find "unrealistic and unworkable solutions".
He said: "The BBC is central to the cultural and economic life of our towns and cities, yet it plans to rip the heart out of the nation's best-loved radio drama."
A BBC spokesperson said: "We fully understand the strength of feeling about The Archers' legacy and connection to the West Midlands.
"Whilst financial pressures on the BBC mean we are unable to build a new studio in The Tea Factory, we are having constructive discussions with programme makers and local stakeholders.
"Together, we are exploring alternative options in the area, but we have time on our side, as there will be no change until 2028 and we remain committed to finding a long-term solution."
The live tour concludes in the West Midlands with events in Coventry on Wednesday and Wolverhampton on Thursday.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c65y: Sabrina Bahsoon now has more than 900,000 followers across social media
Sabrina Bahsoon became known globally as Tube Girl after self-shot videos of her dancing and lip-syncing on the London Underground blew up online.
The 26-year-old content creator had the world at her feet when she went viral in 2023 , going on to build a social media following of more than 900,000 people.
She signed major brand endorsement deals and was pursuing a music career.
But then her "whole life turned upside down" when she had what appeared to be a psychotic episode.
Her symptoms made her violent and erratic, leading to her being sectioned in a mental health hospital - where doctors treated her with anti-psychotic medication.
But Bahsoon's family, helped by her father's neurologist friend, pushed for further tests.
And two months into her hospital treatment, doctors got to the truth.
Sabrina Bahsoon shot to fame for her viral Tube videos but in March 2026 her life turned upside down overnight.
She actually had a rare, but treatable, autoimmune disease which is known to sometimes present as psychiatric symptoms, as well as seizures, confusion and memory loss.
In her first interview since the experience, she tells BBC News she wants hospitals to offer a series of tests as standard practice if patients have these symptoms.
"In a way I do feel let down by the care I received. I feel like the urgency to discover what was actually wrong with me wasn't there," she says.
"And I also feel as a woman being written off completely as a psychotic patient without further investigation was a mistake."
A spokesperson for the hospital she attended has apologised for Bahsoon's experience and says an investigation has been launched into her care.
The content creator was in hospital for about four months earlier this year
Bahsoon first had "psychotic symptoms" in March this year after filming a video on the Tube with girl group Flo.
She says that evening she began to scream, cry and her conversations became "very erratic".
The next day she broke up with her boyfriend, which prompted her sisters to check on her, as it was so unexpected.
Bahsoon says her condition got worse, becoming violent towards herself and posting videos which didn't make sense, before her sisters called 999 for an ambulance.

"I'm normally a very relaxed person, maybe anxious at times, but the way I was speaking about harming myself and the way I was screaming and being violent was super out of character for me," she says.
A&E doctors initially thought her symptoms could have been provoked by stress and a lack of sleep, discharging her with sleeping tablets.
She then began destroying things at home and spoke about having hallucinations, which led to police bringing her to hospital in handcuffs.
Bahsoon was sectioned and moved to a psychiatric ward where she was treated with antipsychotic medication, which she says made her "docile".
"I went from being a total firecracker to being completely catatonic," she says.
Bahsoon has "very faint memories" of this period, she says, but her family has since shown her clips of her having breakdowns which she finds "heartbreaking".
Sabrina Bahsoon was pursuing a music career at the height of her fame
After two months on the psychiatric ward, Bahsoon was diagnosed with an autoimmune disease called anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.
It was caused by tumours in her ovaries, known as teratomas, producing antibodies which attacked her body.
She had surgery to remove the tumours in June, which she says brought on a "drastic" change in her behaviour from "freaking out" to having more understanding of what was happening around her.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck3r: US rapper Don Toliver has postponed two shows in London this week, after his concert in Manchester on Sunday was evacuated when an "unknown substance" was released into the crowd.
Toliver was due to play The O2 on Monday and Wembley Arena on Tuesday, but Live Nation said his "stage and production equipment remains in Manchester and cannot be moved in time".
One person was taken to hospital and 89 people showed "symptoms believed to be linked to the exposure" after Sunday's Co-op Live arena show, police said.
Fans described "distressing scenes" with people "choking", "screaming" and "coughing up blood" because of the effects of a substance, which police initially believed to be tear gas.
Watch: Coughs, confusion and boos as Co-op Live concert cancelled
The Wembley show has been rescheduled to 14 December, while Monday night's O2 gig has been moved to 15 December.
"I'm very sad to sit here and say I have to reschedule The O2 London show to December 15th due to (the) unfortunate incident last night," Don Toliver wrote on Instagram.
Greater Manchester Police (GMP) declared a major incident on Sunday and said 12,000 people were evacuated from the arena.
One woman was taken to Manchester Royal Infirmary for further assessment and treatment after the incident, which happened at about 22:00 GMT, the force said.
A further 88 people "underwent dry decontamination at the scene and were subsequently accommodated within the Etihad Stadium while the incident was managed", according to GMP.
Leon Douzi said he was right next to where the substance was released, and described someone holding a can and "this gas coming out".
"It just hit me in the throat," he said, adding that it felt like "burning".
There was "a bit of panic", Douzi said: "Everybody was having the same feeling and trying to get out."
Some fans reported eye and respiratory symptoms, according to the North West Ambulance Service.
Hannah Baxter, who went to the concert with her partner, said the first thing she noticed was a burning feeling in her throat.
"[We] were just coughing and coughing... there was a guy next to us who had vomited. There were people with red eyes and... tears everywhere," she told the BBC.
Joey Howe, a football journalist at the gig, told BBC Radio Manchester there was a "horrible smell" and added: "People were coming through in wheelchairs choking – it was really distressing."
Police launched an investigation and are continuing to carry out tests on items at the venue to try to identify the substance. No arrests have been made.

Assistant Chief Constable Tom Harding said: "Enquiries remain ongoing to establish the nature of the substance, where it came from and any associated risk. Testing will take place throughout the day as the investigation into the cause of this incident progresses.
"We are trying to establish whether any criminality has occurred in relation to this incident."
Some fans complained about security and a lack of searches as people went into the Manchester concert.
Jessica Moult-Boffey, of Wigan, said people were "crying and screaming in pain" as they left the venue, adding she felt "confused on how something like that got into a venue of that size".
Malachi Clarke also claimed security was "not good at all", adding: "They weren't checking bags, to the point where I had to ask them if they needed to check mine."
Co-op Live said on its website there were a range of security measures, and while "some of these are visible, others you won't be able to see".
It said the arena used a "frictionless security screening that detects prohibited items without you needing to empty your pockets".

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq1j: Parastoo Ahmadi's performance was livestreamed on her YouTube channel in December 2024
A prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab and four members of her band and production team have been flogged by Iranian authorities, lawyers say.
Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were each given 74 lashes in the city of Qom, a member of their defence team told the BBC.
Ahmadi, 29, wore a sleeveless dress during a concert that was livestreamed in December 2024. Iran's laws ban public performances by women and require them to wear headscarves and modest clothing.
This June, a criminal court in Qom convicted Ahmadi and eight others of "offending public decency" through the publication of "obscene and indecent material", which they had denied.
In addition to being sentenced to 74 lashes, they were banned from audiovisual activities and from leaving the country for two years.
At the end of September, an appeals court in Qom rejected the defendants' appeal and confirmed the sentence, her lawyers said.

There was widespread condemnation of the sentences from other Iranian artists and human rights activists, who warned that flogging constituted cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment, and violated the international prohibition on torture.
On Monday, one of the defendants' lawyers told the BBC that Ahmadi and four of her male co-defendants had been flogged at the third branch of the Criminal Sentence Enforcement Office in Qom.
"We did everything in our power to have the verdict overturned, or at least to secure a reduction in the sentence or a suspension, but it didn't work out," he said.
"The other lawyers and I even tried to get the enforcement of the sentence postponed, but the enforcement branch insisted on carrying it out immediately."
Pro-reform daily Etemad cited another defence lawyer, Mostafa Nili, as identifying the four men flogged alongside Ahmadi as Soheil Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri, Amirali Pirnia and Mohsen Lashkari.

"Parastoo Ahmadi's flogging for singing and dressing as she chooses is a flagrant violation of her fundamental rights and a chilling demonstration of the Iranian authorities' determination to suppress women's freedoms and to violently punish anyone who dares to challenge their discriminatory laws and policies," said Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI).

Under Iranian law, which is based on the country's interpretation of Sharia, women and girls above the age of puberty must cover their hair with a hijab and wear long, loose-fitting clothing to disguise their figures.

In 2022, protests swept across the Islamic Republic following the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman who was detained by morality police in Tehran in September that year for allegedly wearing her hijab "improperly".

Women burnt their headscarves or waved them in the air at the nationwide demonstrations against the clerical establishment, during which hundreds of people were killed in a crackdown by security forces.

Since then, many women and girls have stopped covering their hair in public altogether in open defiance of the dress code. Authorities have responded with periodic waves of arrests, warnings, business closures and other measures.

In January this year, thousands of people were killed and tens of thousands were arrested when security forces crushed another wave of mass anti-establishment protests, this time sparked by the country's economic crisis.
Since the start of Iran's war with the US and Israel in late February, authorities have intensified their use of the death penalty against protesters.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqdr: Dowden has been open about her own cancer journey, including her experience with chemotherapy, surgery and egg retrieval
Strictly Come Dancing's Amy Dowden says the upcoming documentary from Catherine, the Princess of Wales, about her cancer journey will help many people, including herself, "not feel so alone".
Dowden praised the documentary and said it confirmed how "anyone can be dealt the devastating blow of a cancer diagnosis".
Dowden, Strictly's first Welsh professional dancer, was diagnosed with stage 3 breast cancer at 32 and has undergone chemotherapy and two mastectomies .
Catherine's BBC documentary, Heal, will reveal how cancer has impacted her outlook on life, as well as the people, places and experiences that have helped her.
Dowden told ITV's Lorraine she believed the documentary would be "quite raw" and emotional, but "so important" in showing the "truth and effects of cancer".
The dancer said she had a lot of admiration for the princess, adding: "Thank you Princess Catherine for doing this."
Prince William and Catherine had an official visit to India this month, their first overseas trip together since her cancer treatment
In the trailer for her documentary, Catherine is candid about the life-altering effect of the disease, saying: "Cancer does change you.
"It changes your body, it changes you physically... but there is a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you."
Dowden has previously echoed this feeling, saying that after a diagnosis, "in a click of the fingers, your life changes".
Heal will follow Catherine as she does the National Three Peaks challenge, which involves climbing the highest mountains in England, Scotland and Wales within 24 hours.
Catherine completed the challenge in June to raise funds for the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity - the hospital where she underwent treatment - and to "explore life beyond diagnosis".
When the princess revealed she had cancer, Dowden shared her sympathy on Instagram .
Since her own diagnosis aged 32 in 2023, the dancer has shared her experience of breast cancer online and in the BBC documentary Strictly Amy: Cancer and Me.
She said her decision to let a camera crew film her cancer journey was scary but she felt a duty to raise awareness.
"I felt straight away, well maybe I could make a difference."
Like Catherine , Dowden's cancer is in remission, and she has been performing in the current series of Strictly.
"It is often through pain that we realise there is a greater beauty that lies beyond that," Catherine says in her new documentary
In Heal, Catherine will discuss how the diagnosis made her "confront her own vulnerabilities".
"When you're faced with your own mortality, you have to accept that life is not infinite," she shared in a clip from the documentary .
The princess first revealed her diagnosis of cancer in March 2024 and announced she was in remission in January 2025, after chemotherapy.
However, she has said she wants to dispel the idea that people can immediately return to how they felt before illness.
Heal will be shown on BBC iPlayer from 12:00 GMT and BBC One at 18:40 GMT on 29 November.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq8e: Miley Cyrus has married her partner of four years Maxx Morando during a ceremony in Palm Springs, California.
A string of black and white photos shared by the Flowers singer on Instagram showed the pair kissing while surrounded by white roses.

Her mother, Trisha Cyrus, and sister, Noah Cyrus, could be seen in the background of one image. Her father Billy Ray Cyrus was not in the picture but was at the ceremony with his partner, actress Liz Hurley.
Grammy-winning Cyrus, 33, wore a white silk dress designed by Anthony Vaccarello for Saint Laurent, while 28-year-old drummer Morando said "I do" in a black suit from the same fashion house.
In one of the photographs, which was the first in a series of images shared by the singer in an Instagram post, the newly weds posed next to a golden retriever.
The post was captioned with "M+M" followed by a white heart and the ceremony date, 21 November.
Miley's sister Brandi Cyrus, singer Doechii and fashion designer Donatella Versace were among those to congratulate the couple in the comments.
The ceremony reportedly took place at a resort formerly owned by Fly Me To The Moon singer Frank Sinatra.
Guests stuck to an all-black dress code, according to reports.
'Angel by my side' - Miley Cyrus pays tribute to godmother Dolly Parton
The American singer confirmed her engagement to the 28-year-old drummer during an interview with US TV show Good Morning America last year.
She said Morando had got down on one knee for the proposal during a trip to Asia.
"I am not easy to surprise because I love to control every situation and I had completely surrendered and I'm telling you, I was so, so, so surprised," she said.
During an interview with Wonderland, Morando said he "had to be really sneaky" to keep his proposal plans a secret.

"We went to Tokyo first for a couple days, and then on to Kyoto. I think she had a sense that it was coming, so I was waiting until the very last moment of the very last day to throw her off the scent as much as I could," he said.

Speaking to British Vogue in 2023, Cyrus said she and 28-year-old Morando met after being "put on a blind date".

Morando is a drummer with LA-based band Liily. The band participated in NBC's Miley's New Year's Eve Party - hosted by Cyrus - in 2022, alongside musicians including Cyrus's late godmother Dolly Parton and David Byrne.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw07: British people, particularly teens and young adults, are having less or no sex compared to past generations, but lots are watching porn and sexting, a major study reveals.
It is the first time The National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles' ( Natsal , external ) research into general public sex lives has asked about online behaviours.
Half of people aged 16 to 24 have sent or received sexual images on their phone in the last year, while one in two young women and almost nine in 10 young men say they have viewed pornography.
But a third of this age group have never had sex, up from a fifth in the last study 12 years ago.
Adults under 45 are having less sex too, doing it twice a month, on average, down from once a week in 1990.
More than one in three (37%) women said they had watched porn in the past year.
Among the 16-24 year-olds, half of women and most young men (86%) said they watched it.

Porn use and masturbation were less common among people who had never had sex, which the authors say suggests solo and online activity is not simply replacing in-person sex, although they cannot be sure.
They didn't ask about AI or virtual relationships with romantic chatbots, but say they probably should next time.
Soazig Clifton, one of the Natsal team and from University College London, said: "When we did our fieldwork in 2022-24 that seemed a little bit sci-fi.
"In the future we might be looking at the impact of AI on people's sexual behaviour and on their relationships, thinking about things like AI companions."

Co-researcher Prof Wendy Macdowall, from the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine (LSHTM), says while it may be tempting to blame screen time for less sex, it's likely many other factors are involved, "especially for young people."
Young people are drinking less alcohol than past generations and more live at home with their parents, for example.
Rising rates of mental health conditions might also be involved, along with the Covid pandemic that stopped people going out.
She says more open discussion of consent could also mean young people feel better able to decide whether and when to have sex.
One in seven women (14%) reported ongoing upset with others about things done to them in their sexual past.
The same proportion of men reported feeling shame about some of their sexual thoughts and desires.
This fourth Natsal survey reveals trends, but cannot fully explain them.
The previous one, in 2010, suggested having sex too soon was the biggest regret of young people losing their virginity.
Almost two in five young women (38%) and more than one in four young men (28%) now report never having had sex. That is up from around one in five in the earlier surveys of 1990, 2000 and 2010.
And among all adults who are having sex, most are doing it less often. The average used to be once a week. Now, it's fortnightly.
The latest results, published in The Lancet and based on a survey of 6,700 people aged 16-59 selected at random across Britain, reveal:
women have sex once a month and men twice a month, on average
reports of sex with a same-sex partner have increased among both men and women, but by how much is less clear
Many Brits, young people in particular, are having unprotected sex that can lead to pregnancies and sexually transmitted infections (STIs), the figures suggest.
And use of the oral contraceptive pill has declined among young women.
But more women now say they do not want children - a doubling in the past decade, from 8% to 17% among those aged 16–44.

"Understanding what's driving this – whether economic insecurity, climate anxiety or changing life priorities – should now be a priority for future research and policy, as it has real implications for planning health, care and family services," says researcher Dr Laura Oakley from the LSHTM.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6rm: Ayana Bailey says she relies on her mum to go through the job application process with her
Nineteen-year-old Ayana Bailey doesn't always disclose her dyslexia in job applications, in case it counts against her.
"It's not like there's going to be a target on my back, but I'm just like, 'maybe they won't select me'," says Bailey, a part-time florist.
A British Dyslexia Association (BDA) survey of more than 1,200 working dyslexic adults found Bailey isn't alone - with 46% hiding their dyslexia at work.
Some 81% believe the condition adds to their work-related stress.
Bailey was diagnosed aged 11 and says she received good support at school, including mentoring, which helped her to understand her strengths and manage low self-esteem.
For Bailey, the application process is "daunting". She says she relies on her mum to go through it with her.
In interviews, Bailey says: "I just shut down. I completely forget who I am."
One way of coping, she says, is to have a little script, but she admits it doesn't always work.
Bailey, who studied film and wants to go into the creative arts, says that while dyslexia has sometimes made her feel anxious, it's also given her opportunities.
"I would definitely say my creativity and thinking outside the box [is my biggest strength]."
She says her dyslexia makes her a visual learner - able to imagine characters before seeing any written descriptions and helping her dream of becoming a casting director.
For nurse Lisa Daniels, her dyslexia meant leaving work more than an hour late most days just to finish the paperwork.
"I suppressed it. I was like 'Oh no, everything is fine. It's not affecting me.'" In reality, she says "it was majorly affecting me".
Daniels, 37, says a previous manager was dismissive of her request for adjustments.
"When I first started, they said, 'Oh they are babying some of these nurses' and I didn't have the confidence to challenge it."
She says her suggestions of having more accessible fonts and colours on documents were not listened to.
Five years into her career, Daniels' colleague told her about a staff network on neurodiversity and her confidence grew, along with adjustments such as noise-cancelling headphones.
"I have that resilience that, despite the sometimes lack of support, I'm still gonna show up. I'm still gonna try."
Lisa Daniels says she has built up her resilience despite previous bad experiences at work
Over half of people surveyed by the BDA say dyslexia makes them feel bad about themselves, while 39% have experienced bad mental health related to it.
The BDA is calling for workplaces to make reasonable adjustments for employees who need them, even without a diagnosis, and wants managers to be trained to understand and support dyslexic employees.
Its report finds dyslexic employees often have to put extra effort into work, finding their own ways to cope if systems, processes and communication are not accessible.
There are 3.3 million dyslexic adults currently in employment, estimates the BDA. Some told the report:
"I have to cope with little comments that are seen as banter about my spelling."
"My line manager is actually dyslexic and we happily talk about it. We share best practice and war stories."
"It would be nice to be seen as intellectual. Just because I cannot always write as well as others, doesn't mean I don't have the knowledge."
"I revealed my dyslexia quite early on in my employment… I do believe it was used as a stick to beat me with."
"I feel like I have got to do more, be more, show more... because I've got this deficit of being dyslexic".
Employment law solicitor Jenna Ide helped a client win a high-profile dyslexia discrimination case against Starbucks in 2016.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmpd: Prof Fiona Gilbert, who is co-leading the trial, will assess if AI can improve breast cancer diagnosis
Nearly 700,000 women across the UK are to be invited to join the world's largest trial of how artificial intelligence can help in breast cancer screening.
AI will be used to review mammograms to see if it can improve early cancer detection and ease the workload of clinical staff, while not over-diagnosing women unnecessarily.
Recruitment to the EDITH trial , external has already begun at Cambridge University Hospitals, the first of 30 sites across the UK.
Women aged 50 to 71 are invited for routine breast screening every three years in the UK, and more than two million attend annually.
At present two NHS experts look at each breast X-ray, known as a mammogram, but in the trial, one of the human readers will be replaced by AI.

Several smaller studies have already shown that AI can improve breast cancer detection rates, but researchers running this trial say they need to be sure it won't cause harm by leading to women being recalled unnecessarily for further tests.

Sian Taylor-Phillips, professor of population health at the University of Warwick, and co-chief investigator said: "AI-assisted technology could help improve early cancer detection but we want to avoid the overdiagnosis of milder disease that would never have caused symptoms."
Breast cancer is the most common cancer among women in the UK, with around 59,000 cases diagnosed each year.
About a third of these are picked up by routine mammograms, usually at an early stage when they can be more easily treated.
It's estimated the screening programme helps prevent around 1,300 deaths a year.

Prof Fiona Gilbert, department of radiology, University of Cambridge, honorary consultant at Addenbrooke's Hospital, and co-chief investigator said: "Millions of women have a mammogram each year and only a small number, less than 1%, will have cancer.

"Technology can make reviewing these images more efficient, freeing up specialist breast radiologists to spend more time caring for patients with cancer, supporting faster diagnosis and earlier treatment."
Gilbert told the BBC there was a "huge shortfall" in radiologists and that the number of imaging examinations was increasing by 8% a year.
Shirley Essex, 70, from Cambridgeshire, was diagnosed with early-stage breast cancer a year ago after a routine screening appointment.
She had surgery and radiotherapy, but did not require chemotherapy.
She told the BBC that her mammogram had saved her life: "I was astonished to be told I had cancer because I did not have any symptoms."
Shirley is not part of the study but is passionate about the importance of screening.
"I feel so lucky my cancer was detected early. It was my last routine mammogram, so if I had not attended, my cancer would have kept growing," she said.
Women will be informed about the study when they receive a routine screening invitation, but will not be obliged to take part.
The trial will not change what happens during a breast screening appointment.
Instead, it will test whether AI-assisted tools could replace one of the two human specialists reviewing mammograms.

Researchers say machine-learning software can be trained on millions of previous images in order to detect patterns, and so potentially find subtle changes in breast tissue that might be missed by the human eye.
In one arm of the trial, an AI programme will grade images before they are sent to NHS experts. In another, it will review images afterwards.
The £10m trial is funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR).
It is being led by the University of Warwick, the University of Cambridge and Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, working with NHS England.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw98: Sales of a baby sleeping bag have been halted in the UK by fashion retail chain Next, after a new mum raised the alarm over its safety.

Emma Hunter, 29 from Norwich, contacted BBC Your Voice to say she realised the neck hole was far too big - meaning her daughter Rosie could potentially wriggle down, burying her face and risking suffocation.
Emma recalls: "I woke up my husband and we both agreed there was no way we could put Rosie in it."
Next says its own-brand, 2.5 tog pink floral sleep bag with removable sleeves that comes in three sizes, has been removed from the website and stores and a product recall is under way.
Next will contact and advise customers who purchased the item from them.
The sleeping bag is now unavailable on Next's website after safety fears were raised

A spokesperson for Next said: "We can confirm the item has been removed from our website and all stores. A product recall is in place, and we are contacting all customers who purchased the item directly to advise them of the appropriate next steps."
Emma says she started doing her own research that same night she realised the sleeping bag was unsuitable for Rosie.

Although the product had a label stating that it met British standards, Emma discovered that the maximum neck circumference for that size of bag should be 32cm. When she measured the bag, the neck hole was 36cm.
According to the British Retail Consortium (BRC), a significant hazard arises if a child slips through the neck opening of a sleep bag and the material covers the child's nose and mouth.
They state that "suffocation can occur and may lead to the brain becoming starved of oxygen, which may result in asphyxia and potential brain damage or fatality."
To limit this hazard, the EN 16781 standard specifies a maximum and minimum size for the neck opening circumference in relation to the child's height.
For example, a sleep bag designed for a child 50 cm to 65 cm tall should have a minimum neck circumference of 28 cm and a maximum of 32 cm.
Rosie, who is now three and a half months old, measured 59cm at the time the bag was bought.
After flagging these issues to the company, Emma says she was surprised by their initial reaction.
"They seemed quite laissez faire about it and just offered me a refund, but I said 'it's dangerous, surely you shouldn't be selling it any more and there should be a product recall?'"
Emma was told by Next that they were looking into it and that their product team was examining the bag and would feed back.
Emma's older brother died of Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS) as a baby so the risk to babies from suffocation is something close to her heart.
She told the BBC: "I am more aware of this because of what happened to my brother and my family, but it shouldn't take an infant mortality to see change.
"They didn't have any sense of urgency about it at all and I expected a big high street store like that to have a certain standard. You put your trust into these retailers.
"How can a product have a label on it saying it met the British standard, when it clearly didn't?"
Ruth Watts, who is a qualified health visitor in England, says that babies will differ in terms of size and height, despite their age.
But if a sleeping bag covers the chin or face in any way it should not be used.

"The best thing to do is check the gap around the neck. If you can fit one to two fingers around the neck then that's safe. If it's any tighter or looser than that, then you shouldn't use it," she recommends.
Emma's baby Rosie is now 3 and a half months old and uses a different sleeping bag
The Lullaby Trust is a UK charity that works to prevent sudden, unexpected infant deaths, including SIDS.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqrm: CT scans before (left) and after treatment with daraxonrasib plus chemotherapy (gemcitabine and nabpaclitaxel) showing multiple tumours that are no longer visible. Yellow arrows indicate the tumours visible before treatment

Experts are calling it the biggest breakthrough in pancreatic cancer treatment for decades - a daily pill that appears to shrink and possibly even eliminate tumours in some patients with one of the deadliest and hardest-to-treat cancers.
Cancer became undetectable on scans in one in 12 of the patients given daraxonrasib along with chemotherapy in early medical trials.
Tumours stopped growing in almost all of the 61 participants who had recently been diagnosed with advanced pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body.
But doctors stress it is unclear how long it might keep the disease at bay and should not be seen as a cure.
Cancer Research UK called it "the biggest leap forward in decades" for pancreatic cancer patients.
The charity's Dr Sam Godfrey told BBC News that the results were incredibly exciting. "What this new drug has done is it's found a way of drugging the undruggable.
"We are finally seeing progress in pancreatic cancer which is so long overdue."
Pancreatic cancer is notoriously hard to treat and has the lowest survival rate of all common cancers in the UK.
Although chemotherapy can shrink tumours a bit, the cancer often grows again.
Most patients with advanced disease survive months, not years.
Doctors hope the new treatment might offer patients more time, even if it cannot stop cancers for good.
The trial followed patients for a year and a half, on average, and some did not see their cancer return during this time.
Longer studies are needed to understand if any of these cancers can be put into remission and for how long.
just over 60% of patients saw their tumours shrink or disappear
for around 8% of patients, or one in 12, tumours became undetectable on CT scans
Dr Wungki Park, from Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in the US and who is involved in the trial, said the results were extremely encouraging so far.

"We are beginning to see not only a higher percentage of tumour response rates, but also deeper responses and a near doubling in the duration of disease control, which may eventually translate into longer survival," he said.

Daraxonrasib is a targeted inhibitor treatment that has already been approved in the US . It works by locking on to and shutting off certain mutations, called RAS , external , found in most pancreatic cancers that drive tumour growth.
Dozens of other cancers, including lung and ovarian, can have similar mutations, meaning the drug might help lots of other patients too.
Dr Godfrey said: "I would hope that the early success that we are beginning to see in pancreatic cancer can also be rolled out to other cancers."
He said longer trials and results were vital. "Cancer can come back and even if scans show there is no sign of it, you don't necessarily know you are cancer-free until more time has passed."

Prof Elena Garralda, chair of a European cancer conference called EORTC–NCI–AACR Symposium 2026 , external where the work is being presented to other doctors, said: "These results are exciting because they show the combined treatment could potentially significantly improve patients' overall survival, as well as the time before tumours start to grow again."
Pancreatic cancer accounts for about 3% of all cancers in the United States and about 8% of all cancer deaths, killing around 53,000 people a year , external .
In Britain, there are 11,500 diagnoses of the disease each year and around 10,200 deaths, according to Cancer Research UK.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crx2: Early efforts to contain coronavirus "were doomed to fail" because the test, trace and isolate system in the UK could only handle a relatively small number of cases, the seventh report of the Covid inquiry says in a damning assessment.
Across 245 pages the inquiry looks at everything from border controls to how well contact tracing worked.
The report said the virus was allowed to spread virtually unchecked in the first few months after community testing and contact tracing was abandoned in mid-March 2020, costing lives.
Ministers said this was because testing capacity was being overwhelmed.
NHS Test and Trace was launched two months later and eventually became one of the biggest testing services in the world per head of population.
In the end, more than £30bn was spent across the UK during the pandemic on testing, tracing and isolating.
But in those early months the four UK nations were "effectively blind" to how quickly Covid was spreading, the inquiry said.

It criticises the government for not having a robust test, trace and isolate system in place to start with, saying this, alongside other failures, meant harsher measures, including lockdown and school closures, were needed.

Inquiry chair Baroness Hallett said the UK should have been better prepared and learnt lessons from other countries that had experience of dealing with outbreaks of other infectious diseases, such as Sars.
Unlike the UK, places such as Hong Kong, South Korea, Singapore and Taiwan had established systems ready to go.
This was despite the fact the UK had run a series of simulation exercises in the years leading up to Covid.
They included Exercise Cygnus into a flu pandemic and Exercise Alice into Mers. Both identified problems relating to test, trace or isolation, which appear not to have been fully acted on.

The report also raises the question of whether the government could have made use of non-government testing facilities in hospitals, universities and the private sector from the start, instead of just relying on 12 government labs.
When people in the UK were told to isolate, "many felt forgotten and let down by the lack of practical or financial support when trying to follow the rules", says the report.
In the early months of the pandemic, estimates suggested less than half of people were complying with the rules around isolating if infected.
Ministers and their advisers discussed this and fines of up to £10,000 were introduced for those who did not comply, which some experts have said was counter-productive.
Changes were made to allow people to claim statutory sick pay.
But it was not until September in England – and later in Scotland and Wales – that £500 financial payments were introduced to help those on low incomes comply.
More also needed to be done to provide practical support for things such as collecting medicines and shopping for food for those who did not have people to call on.

Suspending all flights from China to the UK in February 2020 could "have provided valuable additional time to prepare healthcare systems for the impact of the pandemic", said inquiry chair Baroness Hallett. That didn't happen.
The report says the UK lacked a clear strategy for implementing border control measures early in the pandemic, which left the country in an "extremely vulnerable position".

Although the closure and restriction of borders was noted as "immensely complex", the inquiry said that border control measures could serve as an important tool "to reassure the public and increase confidence."
By April 2020, 93% of countries had put measures in place, such as flight suspensions, border closures and travel restrictions, to control their international borders.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8wy: More than 200 doctors have had their details sent in error to the Times newspaper
The doctors' regulator the General Medical Council (GMC) has apologised after it mistakenly sent information about more than 220 doctors to a national newspaper.
The information included summaries of complaints alleging antisemitism or Islamophobia against the doctors.
For some of the medics involved, it was only when the GMC alerted them to the data breach that they discovered a complaint had been made about them.
The GMC says it is "very sorry" for the incident and has reported itself to the Information Commissioner's Office.

The GMC - an independent body that regulates doctors, physician associates and anaesthesia associates to protect patient safety - sent the information about 223 doctors to a journalist at the Times newspaper.
While no names were revealed, GMC identification numbers were included, which would easily allow doctors to be found on the regulator's register.
Some doctors have also raised concerns that their ethnicity was included in the data breach.
All the medics involved have been the subject of a complaint involving either antisemitism or Islamophobia, dating from the Hamas attack on Israel in October 2023 to September 2026.
The GMC says it has a legal and statutory responsibility to investigate such claims.
Meanwhile, the Times is understood to have promised not to make any of the details public, but has said it will not delete the information.
A spokesman for the doctor's trade union, the British Medical Association (BMA), condemned the release of personal information.

"The BMA is aware that a number of doctors have received communication from the GMC to say that it erroneously sent personal identifiable data about them to the Times newspaper when responding to a media request," it said.
"The GMC must take action to ensure such a breach never occurs again."
The BMA said it would look at ways to support members affected and urged them to make contact via their website.
A doctors' campaign group, The Doctors' Association UK (DAUK), called for an independent investigation into the error.
"If a doctor sent identifiable patient information to a newspaper, they could expect to be referred to the GMC," said Dr Matt Kneale, DAUK co-chairman.

"The GMC should hold itself to the same standard of confidentiality it expects from doctors. It owes every affected doctor a clear account of what it sent, how that happened and what it is doing to get the information deleted."

The doctors' regulator says around a fifth (20%) of the complaints made have already resulted in some sanction related to antisemitism, including two doctors who have been struck off the medical register.
Just over a quarter of complaints over Islamophobia - 26% - have led to disciplinary action.
But other complaints were closed, having failed to reach the threshold for investigation.
The GMC said it had contacted the doctors affected to explain what had happened, to apologise and provide information and support.
A spokesperson added: "We recognise the concern this will cause to both those impacted personally and other registrants and we are very sorry this happened.
"Our priority continues to be supporting those affected and taking steps to reduce the impact of this incident."

Clarification 20 November: This article was amended on 19 November to remove references to the information being 'leaked'. The information was mistakenly disclosed by the GMC in response to a media request.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6pw: Adverts for tests and services relating to low testosterone are allowed but must be rooted in evidence, the regulator said
Five adverts by online healthcare provider Voy have been banned by the watchdog for making misleading claims linked to low testosterone in men.
The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) said the adverts promoted Voy's at-home testosterone blood tests in three posters and two paid-for Facebook ads.
It said they were misleading as they linked common symptoms such as irritability and fatigue to low testosterone.
Voy said it had withdrawn the adverts while the investigation was under way and would not run them again.
The NHS says that while testosterone levels in men fall as they age, this is "unlikely" to cause any problems in itself.

It adds , external that while a testosterone deficiency in later life can sometimes be responsible for symptoms such as depression, loss of sex drive, erectile dysfunction, and other physical and emotional symptoms, they are often not linked.
Voy is a company that sells products such as testosterone, menopause and weight loss treatments.
Some of its testosterone test kit adverts drew a backlash online earlier this year when they appeared on the London Underground.
Some described them as "ragebait" for using phrases such as "It's not him, it's his hormones" and "Men get hormonal too".
At the time Voy said it was trying to destigmatise conversations about men's health.
Some of the adverts sparked discussion online after appearing at Tube stations
The ASA's ruling, however, took issue with how some of the adverts "exaggerated the connection between several common symptoms, which can have many possible causes, and low testosterone".
The ASA gave examples such as low sex drive, low energy, loss of motivation and changes in mood.

"While some symptoms may be more closely associated with the condition, others were much less specific and shouldn't have been presented as strong indicators of low testosterone in isolation," the watchdog said.
It added that one of the Facebook adverts also included the claim that "low testosterone sneaks up on 1 in 4 men over 30".
The ASA said this was misleading and not supported by the evidence provided by Voy.

Dr Earim Chaudry, chief medical officer for Voy, said: "Every patient decision at Voy is clinician-led and these campaigns were developed to align with UK advertising standards. We keep all our advertising under continual review to ensure it meets any updated guidance."

Wednesday's ruling followed two others in August by the watchdog, which found misleading claims in adverts for testosterone testing services from online providers BioID Health and Numan Digital Healthcare.
The rulings form part of a wider ASA investigation into adverts aimed at men concerned about their health.
This has identified a "recurring theme of advertisers playing on insecurities around libido, erectile problems, testosterone and ageing", the regulator said.
The watchdog said adverts for tests and services relating to low testosterone were allowed, but businesses needed to make sure the claims they made were accurate and supported by evidence.

Dr Richard Quinton, who is an expert in testosterone deficiency, said: "It's very easy to get a low testosterone level in any healthy man, simply by doing a blood test in the afternoon, after a meal, when unwell from any cause, or after an all-night sit up."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm0e: From Spring 2027, under 16s will no longer be able to access several social media applications
More than 300,000 young people in Britain will work with researchers to help understand how the UK's forthcoming social media ban for under-16s could affect mental health.
The studies will examine the habits of the children and teenagers, including whether they spend less time on their phones and what they are replacing scrolling with.
Ten different projects have been commissioned, taking place across England, Wales and Scotland, to help reflect a diverse range of teenagers.
The social media ban, beginning in spring 2027, will follow a similar model to that already introduced in Australia to stop children accessing platforms such as Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat.
Apps such as Instagram, TikTok, Facebook, Snapchat and YouTube will be banned under new rules
The work, funded by health charity The Wellcome Trust, will help inform future online safety policies in the UK and internationally, with some early results available before the ban happens.
Researchers will use wearable technology, smartphones, digital diaries and surveys to collect data to see how young people respond to the ban, both physically and mentally.
And they will check whether young people find ways to circumvent restrictions.
Dr Camilla Iannone, research lead at Wellcome, said it was a once-in-a-generation opportunity to study at scale how social media and its restrictions affected youth mental health.
"We really don't think that this is a simple binary question of whether social media is good or bad, or whether restrictions work or don't work.
"Instead, the teams will study whether changing young people's digital environment leads to meaningful changes in their mental health and wellbeing."
Participants are being recruited to reflect a diverse range of young people, including different genders and sexual orientations.
People with existing mental health conditions, such as anxiety and depression, will also be included, as well as young people who are neurodivergent.

Groups have been set up at Cardiff University, the University of Oxford, the University of Birmingham, King's College London, the University of Edinburgh, the University of Manchester, the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, and University College London.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6m2: Baroness Cass said the current wording of the bill risked "serious unintended consequences"
The author of the independent review into gender identity services for young people says she does not support the current draft bill banning conversion practices - having previously welcomed it.
Baroness Cass told BBC Radio 4's Today programme while it is "desirable" to ban the practices, "the challenge is that we have not yet as far as I can see got a workable bill".

At a parliamentary committee scrutinising the bill, she also said it risked "serious unintended consequences" for parents of children suffering gender distress, or medical professionals working in that area.
They added they would take all evidence put forward by the committee seriously as they "want to get this ban right". The government has said the bill would protect LGBT people in England and Wales.
Conversion practices are generally described as interventions, treatments or activities designed to change or suppress someone's sexual orientation or gender identity.
This can sometimes happen in religious or family settings and can be very distressing for the person at the centre of it.
There have been long-running campaigns in the UK to outlaw such practices, and in its 2024 manifesto, the Labour party promised to introduce a bill banning them.
When the government introduced its draft legislation , external in June this year, Baroness Cass was quoted in the publicity for it , external .

In it, she said: "I am pleased to see that the government is bringing forward legislation which not only gives a clearer definition of what conversion practices are, compared to previous drafts, but also what they are not."
She went on to say she looked forward to the bill receiving further scrutiny before it became law.
But asked at the Draft Conversion Practices Bill committee if she supported the bill's current form, she said simply "no".
Baroness Cass said the increased "polarisation" used in the debate around gender meant people may use the new law in a way that wasn't intended.

The current wording of the bill requires the victim to suffer "serious harm to the individual's physical or mental health, or serious alarm or distress to the individual which has a substantial adverse effect on their usual day-to-day activities".
But Baroness Cass said she worried this wording left open the possibility of "vexatious" complaints that could put therapists working with young gender-distressed people at risk of prosecution.
"Therapeutic interactions can be distressing and often are because you're discussing quite sensitive issues," she told the Today programme.
"So If a young person comes away feeling upset, distressed, angry, that might be the result of a quite appropriate therapeutic intervention but still could be judged as poor professional practice."
She told the committee that professionals working at the new NHS Gender Dysphoria Clinics were concerned that even complaints processes that didn't result in a prosecution could be damaging.
"The problem is the chilling effect of professionals knowing that they may be open to complaint, and indeed prosecution," she told the Today programme.
Baroness Cass also raised concerns about the possible impact the new law could have on families.

She said that, for instance, if a parent stopped a child's money if they thought they might buy a "breast binder or hormones" that this may also fall within the scope of the bill and result in prosecution.

Asked about her apparent support for the bill when it was first published, Baroness Cass said that she was in favour of the idea but had not had the time to read the details before the press release was to be published, but went ahead and gave the quote anyway.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqjd: Nicola Packer was acquitted of "unlawfully administering to herself a poison or other noxious thing" with the "intent to procure a miscarriage"
Women arrested or convicted for having illegal abortions will have their criminal records wiped as new automatic pardons come into force in England and Wales , external .

Ending the Victorian-era law should avoid traumatic experiences such as that of Nicola Packer, who was recently cleared by a jury after taking medication at home during a Covid lockdown. She had ended a pregnancy without realising she was around 26 weeks pregnant, far beyond the legal 10 week limit.
Her friend Helle Tumbridge told the BBC's Today Programme she had been "treated appallingly" until justice was served.

Labour MP Tonia Antoniazzi, who brought forward the decriminalisation amendment last year, says the change will clear the names of more than 100 women who have been "unnecessarily harmed" by an "outdated" law.
Ms Packer, who was 41 at the time, took pills called mifepristone and misoprostol, which were prescribed over the phone due to Covid restrictions, to end a pregnancy in 2020.
Prosecutors alleged that she knew she had been pregnant for more than 10 weeks, which she denied.
Jurors deliberated for more than six hours to reach their unanimous verdict, clearing her name.
Speaking with the BBC and Nicola's consent, her friend Ms Tumbridge said the whole incident was "incredibly traumatic".
"Nicky had what's known as a cryptic pregnancy - that's when you don't have any sign of a pregnancy, no baby bump, no other symptoms.
"She thought she was just a few weeks pregnant and she sought an abortion and was prescribed that by the NHS. Unfortunately, she was a lot more far gone."
Nicola experienced a stillbirth and went to hospital. The staff there called the police.

"She was arrested. She spent a time in her hospital room recovering with two police officers present, one was a man. She was treated appallingly. She was made to use the toilet with the door open in front of the police officers."
It took five years of investigations for a trial to eventually find her not guilty.
"Of course, by that point the damage had been done," says Tumbridge, "and she'll live with that trauma for the rest of her life."
At the time, The Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists said Nicola's trial demonstrated "just how outdated and harmful" that law was.
It is now no longer a criminal offence for a pregnant woman to terminate her own pregnancy at any stage.
Minister for Victims and Tackling Violence Against Women and Girls, Alex Davies-Jones, said pardoning women for abortion offences related to their own pregnancy had been a priority.
"I'm pleased to be able to commence the change that Parliament voted for.

"For those affected, I know that clear and accessible information about what happens next is vital. Women do not have to take any direct action themselves, but can find out more information online and contact our dedicated casework team."

Heidi Stewart, from the abortion care provider BPAS, said: "While no pardon can undo the distress and trauma these women have experienced, this historic change in the law recognises the profound harm caused by their criminalisation and represents a meaningful step towards justice."

Abortion in England and Wales is legal with an authorised provider up to 24 weeks, with very limited circumstances allowing one after this time, such as when the mother's life is at risk or the child would be born with a severe disability.
It is also legal to take prescribed medication at home if a woman is less than 10 weeks pregnant.
