https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm5y: The capsule dissolves in the stomach and releases a small sponge which collects cells from the lining of the oesophagus as it's removed
Some people with bad and persistent indigestion should be offered quick "sponge in the gullet" tests to check for oesophageal cancer, new draft guidelines for the NHS in England recommend.
The sponge tests can be carried out in GP surgeries in minutes, and are less invasive than hospital endoscopy checks that instead use a small camera to look inside the body.
The tests are already available in some places but could now be offered across England.
Heartburn or acid reflux can occur with a condition called Barrett's oesophagus that increases the risk of cancer in the long term.

It is thought between one and two adults in every 100 has Barrett's oesophagus, where cells have started to change. Most won't go on to develop cancer, but demand for NHS endoscopy is high, meaning some with the condition aren't checked as often as recommended.
The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) says the sponge tests, already offered in some places, could help give more patients peace of mind.

For the test, patients swallow a small dissolving capsule attached to a thread. Once in the stomach, it releases a tiny sponge. The sponge collect cells from the lining of the gullet as it is gently pulled back out of the patient's mouth by the doctor.

Prof Jonathan Benger, chief executive of NICE, says sponge tests offer a "quick and less invasive" way to detect concerning changes, helping to identify people who should go on to have further tests and treatment.

Prof Peter Johnson, national clinical director for cancer at NHS England, said: "The NHS is always looking for better ways to get to the bottom of people's symptoms, and thousands have already benefited from this incredibly efficient test through pilots we have been running, so it's fantastic it is now being considered for roll out across the country.

"Many people have acid reflux, and having an easier way to check for changes in the lining of the oesophagus can make a big difference for patients, reducing the need for more complicated endoscopy tests and helping the NHS free up resources to find cancers at an earlier stage."
However, no diagnostic test, including endoscopy, identifies every case and people who receive an all-clear sponge test result should still be monitored in the long term, NICE adds.
The sponge tests can help detect oesophageal cancer and Barrett's oesophagus in people with reflux disease.
The oesophagus leads to the stomach. Both are highlighed in red/orange
Reflux can cause heartburn, which is a burning sensation in the middle of your chest, as well as an unpleasant sour taste in your mouth, caused by stomach acid.
A lax or weakened sphincter at the bottom of the oesophagus or food pipe, where it meets the stomach, can be part of the issue, allowing digestive juices to seep up the wrong way.
Being overweight, smoking and drinking alcohol can increase a person's risk of reflux.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c65y: John Swinney has asked the government's top civil servant to review how correspondence is handled
Trust in doctors and other health professionals at NHS Grampian to provide the highest standards of treatment and care.
Trust in their managers to effectively deal with problems when they arise.
And trust in the Scottish government to step in if that does not happen.
What we have learned about the operation of NHS Grampian in the last two weeks raises huge questions in all of these areas.
First we had a scathing report by the watchdog Healthcare Improvement Scotland, which found serious shortcomings with NHS Grampian's leadership and oversight of clinical governance.
There was particular concern about patterns of repeated and avoidable harm, and the board's ability to learn from serious adverse events.

Man who nearly died during liver surgery at Aberdeen hospital says mistakes were made
The Scottish government has sent in a support team to help the current management at NHS Grampian make improvements.
Questions have been raised about the suitability of some of those appointed to carry out this work given problems they have faced in their own areas of responsibility .
The watchdog's report was followed by a powerful intervention from a surgeon-turned-whistleblower who works at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary.
Dr Mohammed Habib said he had been raising serious concerns about liver and pancreatic services at the hospital for 10 years.
He released a previously unpublished review from 2022 that looked at 45 patients in the care of this specialist unit over the previous seven years.
It said that 31 had died, and 19 of them were considered to have died of avoidable consequences of surgery or intervention.
Nineteen people died and their deaths were potentially avoidable.
This finding was not made public by NHS Grampian or those in the Scottish government who knew about it.
This is where this story becomes political - because Dr Habib tried to get the attention of ministers.
He raised his concerns with the Scottish government including, he said, writing to the first minister on three occasions.
At Holyrood question time, John Swinney acknowledged that the issues raised were of the "gravest concern".
He said Dr Habib's messages had received "appropriate responses" from officials.
It seems they directed him to a national whistleblowing service and to the police.
Dr Habib said he wrote to the first minister on three occasions
This is what, in my view, makes this potentially the most dangerous political moment for John Swinney since he took over as first minister in 2024.
A surgeon writes to him because 19 people may have died unnecessarily as a result of how they were treated by the NHS and nothing seems to happen.
We have since been told that Swinney's office did not make him personally aware of this correspondence.
That in turn raises questions about the operation of the highest political office in devolved Scotland.
After two decades in power would the SNP administration not have an established system for deciding what should and should not be seen by the first minister?
And if a pattern of seemingly avoidable deaths in the NHS is not serious enough to be escalated to the top then what is?
Swinney seemed to recognise the inadequacy of his parliamentary answers fairly quickly.
Soon after question time his team said he had asked the Scottish government's top civil servant to review how correspondence is handled.
This too was only the beginning of a realisation within government that this had the potential to develop into a political disaster.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm3e: A review into the health board found, in some areas, targets and money "have a greater priority... than the quality and safety of care"
Wales' largest health board is still failing, with "fundamental weaknesses" in governance and management, a new report says.
Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board (BCUHB) has been in special measures for nine years in total, with the latest period starting in 2023.
A review of its leadership published on Tuesday found, in some parts, targets and money "have a greater priority for senior management than the quality and safety of care".
Committed staff and ability to deliver some strong local services were highlighted.
The health board apologised and said it now needed to concentrate on improving its leadership and allowing its staff to "flourish".
The review was commissioned by the Welsh government in the summer , after it gave BCUHB a "final chance" to improve.
It concluded that senior leadership was "immature and ineffective", with weak senior management putting the quality of patient care at risk.
The review did not suggest splitting up the health board, but Wales' health minister said the findings were "unacceptable" and BCUHB "does not function as a single coherent organisation".
The report said: "Many areas reported a culture where targets and financial matters have a greater priority for senior management than the quality and safety of care.
"Fear of speaking up was described often... staff did not believe that raising a concern would result in corrective action.
"Despite this, the panel witnessed many teams striving to deliver the very best care they could for patients."
The reviewers also found a "toxic" culture at the health board where staff were afraid to speak out, and worried that no-one would listen if they did.
The chair of BCUHB, Dyfed Edwards apologised for the health board's failings.
"We have got things wrong. We need to take a step back from all the firefighting that has been going on and address key things.
"We need to allow staff to show leadership and to flourish, and for us all to get systems in place which will allow us to address key performance issues like waiting times."
The health board's chief executive, Carol Shillabeer, previously announced she would be leaving in the new year to take up an NHS role in England.
Her departure follows a string of other senior leaders who have left the organisation in recent months, including the chief operating officer and executive director of finance.
The report also said that bureaucracy and slow decision-making led to a "loss of local ownership" and staff feeling frustrated.

The reviewers wrote: "Staff and leaders described decisions moving through multiple layers of approval, authority becoming concentrated at senior levels and operational leaders lacking sufficient autonomy to act.
"A phrase used in a focus group characterised the resulting complexity as 'Betsi spaghetti'."
However, the review concluded the health board could still be improved without being broken up into smaller organisations - an option previously discussed by ministers.
It said staff were "loyal and committed", and there were "strong local services" and "significant clinical expertise across north Wales".
Health Minister Mabon ap Gwynfor commissioned the review in June, and warned the health board that this was its "last chance" to improve
Health Minister Mabon ap Gwynfor said: "these failings are utterly unacceptable".
"I also share the understandable frustrations of staff and patients alike in north Wales at the lack of progress in delivering and embedding improvements to services and standards of care," he said.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6x2: Historic space mission lifts off with first Pakistani astronaut aboard Chinese rocket

China launched its Shenzhou-24 space mission on Wednesday carrying three astronauts to its Tiangong space station, including Pakistan's Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, the first foreigner to join a Chinese crewed space mission.
Beijing said it hopes the flight will strengthen ties with Islamabad, as the two countries mark 75 years of co-operation in space.
Speaking to reporters at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, Ali said he was "carrying the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis".
The mission, which also comprises of commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer Wu Yi, took off at 08:18 (00:18 GMT) from the Gobi desert. Minutes later, it was declared a "complete success".
While in space, the Shenzhou-24 crew will carry out experiments and test technology in fields like aerospace medicine, combustion and study the effects of space on living organisms.
The mission comprises of payload specialist Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, flight engineer Wu Yi and commander Tang Hongbo
They will also study how the space environment affects aging, with the hope of developing new ways to prevent and treat age-related vascular diseases.
Ali will conduct studies on photosynthesis in bacteria and the effects of radiation and microgravity - a very weak gravity in space - on seeds.
The former fighter pilot will return to Earth after a short stay, with two other Chinese crew members who have been at the space station since May.

Tang and Wu will spend six months at Tiangong space station along with Zhu Yangzhu, a member of the Shenzhou-23 crew, which lifted off in May this year. Zhu has been studying how the human body adapts to long periods in space.
China has poured billions of dollars into its space programme and its prized Tiangong space station is stewarded by teams of three astronauts that are typically rotated every six months.
It is now keen to show the world that the station has the potential to become an international research platform rather than an exclusive Chinese facility.
Hundreds of people gathered at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center before dawn waving Chinese and Pakistani flags.

This also comes at a time when Beijing is trying to establish itself as a major alternative to the US-led space programme, with a bold goal to land Chinese astronauts on the moon for the first time by 2030.
For Pakistan, which does not have its own spacecraft to send astronauts to space, being invited to be a part of this mission is significant.

Ali and Khurram Dawood, the other candidate to reach the final stage in the Shenzhou-24 crew selection, were trained in China and had worked in Chinese space stations under the supervision of Chinese experts.
Mastering the Chinese language was one of his "biggest challenges", Ali said, according to Pakistani media.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/weather/articles/c: Christmas Day is a month away and as the festive season approaches you may start to wonder - could 2026 be a 'white Christmas'?
Over the past 65 years, there have been 41 white Christmases, meaning we are more likely than not to see one somewhere in the UK.
Forecasting the chances of a month ahead of the big day is a bit like staring into a crystal ball - but are there any early omens of snow on the festive horizon?

For a Christmas to be officially declared as 'white', a single snowflake needs to be recorded falling at any point during 25 December, at any of the Met Office's network of around 300 weather stations.
It means there doesn't have to be a thick covering of snow on the ground to qualify.
Indeed, the landscape could be beautifully festive and white with lying snow, but if no new snow falls on Christmas Day it cannot technically be called a white Christmas.
The last widespread white Christmas was in 2010, when snow fell at 19% of measuring stations and a significant 83% of stations reported snow lying on the ground.
Every year from 2020 to 2023 was officially a white Christmas, however very few places actually reported settling snow.
In December 2010 the UK experienced low temperatures and significant snowfalls. Lying snow was reported in many places on Christmas Day
A number of factors will influence the UK's weather in the run-up to the festive season.
A major one is the record-breaking El Niño which is, scientists predict, approaching its peak in the Pacific.

El Niño's strongest impacts tend to be felt close to where the phenomenon occurs, in the tropical Pacific, but the energy it releases into the atmosphere can send ripples through weather patterns across the globe.

Strong El Niño events can increase the odds of wet and stormy weather during the late autumn and early winter, and some studies suggest they can raise the chances of colder weather later in the season - but the evidence from past El Niños is decidedly mixed.
Will El Niño and the polar vortex bring snow to the UK this winter?
Stormy autumn, cold winter - how might El Niño affect the UK weather?
Earlier in November the winds of the stratospheric polar vortex weakened and reversed, marking the earliest sudden stratospheric warming event on record.
This phenomenon tends to occur much later in winter and can - but doesn't always - weaken the jet stream, increasing the chance of cold northerly or easterly winds.
Occurring so early in the season, the effects this time are harder to quantify. It is not known what - if any - impact it will have on the weather over the weeks ahead.

The latest predictions from scientists at the Met Office , external , taking these and other factors into account, suggest there could be an increased likelihood of colder and drier-than-average conditions during the winter months of December, January and February.

However this only represents an increased probability of these conditions and - even if this occurs across the season as a whole - there are still very likely to be shorter-term periods of milder, wetter weather.
It is often tricky to accurately forecast snow in the UK, even a day or two in advance.
Snow requires just the right combination of cold air and moisture, and small changes in either of these elements can mean predicted snow actually falls as rain or vice versa.
It goes without saying that longer range snow forecasts are even more challenging and with Christmas still a month away it is impossible to offer precise predictions.
You can keep up to date with the latest forecast by checking BBC Weather online and the app .

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm93: Between 2013 and 2026, almost 250,000 badgers were killed in England as part of widespread culling to tackle bovine tuberculosis (TB)
Plaid Cymru ministers have ruled out a mass badger cull as part of updated plans to tackle bovine tuberculosis (TB).
It follows months of speculation over the Welsh government's intentions, after an expert group warned "a step change" was needed in efforts to eradicate the disease.
While farming leaders have long called for tougher badger controls, a petition against culling has attracted more than 28,000 signatures on the Senedd website in recent weeks.
The Welsh government said it would take "a new and pragmatic approach to TB eradication that is evidence-based and science-led".
Latest figures show nearly 96% of cattle herds in Wales are now TB free.
But the problem - which can be devastating for affected farms - is concentrated, with higher incidence levels in west Wales and along the border with England.
There were 10,090 cows slaughtered following TB testing in the 12 months to June 2026.
Under the previous Labour-run Welsh government, a target was set for Wales to completely eradicate bovine TB by 2041.
But before May's Senedd election an expert group set up to advise ministers , external warned that goal would "not be met", and called for urgent action and more funding.
Cattle are slaughtered if they are found to be carriers of bovine TB
The Bovine TB Eradication Programme Board's latest recommendations were published on Tuesday, alongside the government's response.
On badgers, ministers said they were "not pursuing a mass, non-selective cull".
However further research is proposed of the role played by badgers and deer in spreading the disease via new population surveys and fieldwork.

This would then lead to developing "targeted and proportionate" interventions which could include trapping and testing badgers before vaccinating or euthanising them, "where the evidence supports this".

Localised trapping and culling was trialled in Wales on nine farms between 2017 and 2024, but the cost involved drew criticism after hundreds of thousands of pounds was spent on killing a small number of badgers.
Officials told a briefing for journalists that "selective removal" of badgers was a possibility in future, but "[we] cannot give you a timeline".
In July, the Senedd backed a Reform UK motion calling on the Welsh Government to consider targeted wildlife control, including badger culling
Changes to cattle testing were also being proposed by the government, to help spot infection earlier.
They will work with the farming industry to explore "safe ways" of moving cattle out of TB restricted herds, to help businesses continue to operate.
Farms experiencing persistent issues and under so-called enhanced management will be offered more choice in how their situation is handled.
There is talk of a new advisory service for farmers and vets - and moves to provide better, more up-to-date data on the latest disease risk.
For farming families "a TB breakdown can mean months or years of restrictions, uncertainty and difficult choices", said agriculture minister Llyr Gruffydd
Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability, Llyr Gruffydd MS, said bovine TB remained "one of the most serious animal health challenges facing Wales".
"We will not stand by while farmers face uncertainty and anxiety, nor will we pursue a mass non-selective cull," he added.
"Instead, we will be taking evidence-based and science-led action, incorporating the three pillars of cattle, people and wildlife.
"Farmers and the public will rightly judge us on whether we prevent disease and reduce its impact, even when the decisions are difficult."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq2e: An estimated 5,258 deaths in England were associated with this summer's hot weather
More than 5,000 people suffered heat-associated deaths in England this summer, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has estimated - the highest number since records began in 2016.
The UK experienced its hottest summer on record in 2026, and the estimated 5,258 heat-linked deaths were twice the previous high of 2,985 in 2022.
The most deadly period of the year for heat-related deaths was between 21 and 28 June, when there were an estimated 2,401 heat-associated deaths. Temperatures peaked at 38C in that period.
Climate change is expected to increase the length, frequency and intensity of extreme heat, the UKHSA has warned.

The UKHSA said summer 2026 was "exceptional", and that it recorded the highest annual number of heat episodes, which it defines as days when the average Central England Temperature (CET) is at least 20C.
There were seven heat episodes between May and August, adding up to a total of 41 days.
The UK experienced widespread heatwaves as 2026 became the hottest summer on record, according to provisional data from the Met Office.
A heatwave in May smashed the temperature record for that month by more than 2C, with a high of 35.1C recorded at Kew Gardens.
A month later, June's heatwave set another monthly temperature record - 38.0C in Lingwood, Norfolk. The previous high was 35.6C set in 1957 and equalled during the infamous 1976 heatwave.
Both were caused by heat domes - stalled areas of high pressure that trap hot air over the region.
Another heatwave in mid-August saw temperatures climb as high as 38.2C at Hartpury College in Gloucestershire, making it the hottest day of the year.
The UK's hottest day on record was 19 July 2022, when temperatures hit 40.3C in Coningsby, Lincolnshire.
A lack of rainfall this year also saw droughts declared in all of Wales and more than two-thirds of England, while wildfires caused devastation in some parts of the country.
UKHSA said the findings "underline the need for longer-term adaptation" to a warming climate, and that adapting homes, neighbourhoods and health and care settings would be "increasingly important".

Dr Ross Thompson, principal environmental health scientist at UKHSA, said this summer's hot weather had a substantial impact on public health, "particularly during the early heat episodes in May and June".
He added that periods of extreme heat are expected to become "longer, more frequent and more intense" as the climate continues to warm.
Speaking in the Commons, Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said she wanted "to offer the deepest condolences to all those who lost a loved one this summer".
"The numbers are a stark reminder of the human impact of climate change, and that is why I have asked the NHS to now prepare for summer as seriously as we do for winter," she said.
During a speech at the COP31 summit earlier this month, Prime Minister Andy Burnham spoke about the extreme weather experienced in the UK this summer, describing it as "not normal".

https://www.bbc.co.uk/weather/articles/c: BBC Weather's Elizabeth Rizzini looks at the weather that will impact travel over US Thanksgiving.
Stormy weather on both US coasts could disrupt travel for millions over the Thanksgiving period.
The American Automobile Association (AAA) predicts 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles from home for Thanksgiving between Tuesday 24 November and Monday 30 November.

The US National Weather Service says a series of Pacific storm systems will bring widespread rain, mountain snow, gusty winds and high surf to the West Coast this week, with coastal flood watches widely in place.

Meanwhile, Wednesday will see a storm off the south-east coast intensify and run north along the eastern seaboard. This will develop into a powerful Nor'easter storm over Thanksgiving, bringing floods, strong winds and heavy rain.
The West Coast will be badly affected in the run up to Thanksgiving, with a strong Pacific storm expected to move into the north-west on Tuesday night and affect the area throughout Wednesday.
The storm will bring particularly heavy rain because it will tap into an atmospheric river , a huge, invisible ribbon of water vapour.
Impacts will include strong winds, heavy rain at lower elevations and snow in the mountains from western Washington to Northern California.
The AAA predicts the vast majority of holiday travellers, 72.9 million, will travel by car.
Drivers could see significant delays along I-5 between Seattle and Sacramento as a result of the storm. Mountain travel could also be affected on the I-80 and I-90.
The heaviest rain is expected to miss Los Angeles and much of Southern California.
Moderate to major coastal flooding is forecast for the California coast

With the full Beaver moon on Tuesday , the West Coast is also expecting the highest tides of the year, coupled with the incoming storm. A coastal flood advisory is in place for the Pacific Northwest and parts of California.
The worst rain is expected to come late Wednesday into Thursday, with another storm forecast for Friday evening.
The San Francisco mayor has warned that the city is bracing for significant weather impacts in the coming days.
Daniel Lurie urged Bay Area residents to check the weather forecast before travelling and avoid unnecessary journeys.
A developing storm will impact the Northeast of the US on Thanksgiving Day
On the East Coast, a developing Nor'easter storm is expected to bring heavy rain, strong winds, and coastal flooding to the south-east.
It will hit Florida and the Carolinas on Wednesday, before moving northwards into the mid-Atlantic and Northeast on Thanksgiving Day.
The National Weather Service is predicting wind gusts of more than 40mph (64km/h) inland along the I-95 corridor, which connects 15 states and Washington DC.
Heavy rain is expected in New York City on Thanksgiving Day, with the city's emergency management authorities warning of "fowl weather" and a chance of coastal flooding.
The forecast has also raised questions about whether large balloons will be allowed to fly during the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade.
Under city regulations , external , full-size balloons are not allowed if sustained wind speeds are higher than 23mph (37km/h) or gusts surpass 35mph (56km/h).
Much of the US east coast will experience heavy rain over the holiday
A major worry for the 5.96 million travellers who will take domestic flights for Thanksgiving is whether the weather will cause flight disruption.
Flights across the US have recently returned to normal after the national air-traffic control system recovered from a technical failure that prompted a rare national ground stop .
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cky9: Some have hailed the lack of consensus as a sign of a positive shift, despite the Turkey summit failure
Some may have found it ironic that the world's biggest conference on climate change should collapse over the very mention of fossil fuels - the main cause of global warming.
The failure tells us something about the state of climate diplomacy. But it may tell us even more about the increasingly divided world in which the negotiations take place.

Chris Bowen, the Australian minister who led the negotiations, spoke of a backdrop constituting "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". The competing demands, he said, had become "unbridgeable red lines".

Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister and the summit's president, was blunter. Governments should not disappoint people desperate for climate action, he suggested, by getting "hung up on one word or phrase".
And Kurum had a point. Three years ago, at COP28 in Dubai, there was agreement to transition away from fossil fuels. The proposed Antalya Pact failed to mention them at all.
Was it really worth sacrificing the agreement over two words, then?

The countries that rejected it said the distinction was fundamental. They argued that there was a world of difference between promising to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and committing to move away from the fuels responsible for most of them. Without that explicit commitment, they feared the new agreement would weaken the one made in Dubai.
Co-leader of the negotiations Chris Bowen blamed the failure to reach an agreement on "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory"

Normally, it is difficult to establish exactly who has said what at these conferences. Much of the bargaining takes place behind closed doors, and governments are often reluctant to admit which proposals they have opposed.
This time, some of the opposition was public - mostly from oil-producing nations.

Mohammad Ayoub, a Saudi negotiator speaking on behalf of the 22 Arab League countries, argued that Arab nations had contributed less than 2% of historical greenhouse gas emissions. It was wealthy industrialised nations, he said, that bore the overwhelming responsibility for the problem.
He defended the Arab countries' right to choose how to tackle climate change according to their national circumstances.
Russia's delegate Sergei Kononuchenko went further. Cutting oil and gas supplies before demand fell, he warned, would cause shortages, higher prices and energy poverty.
"For that reason, we cannot agree to any formulation on fossil fuel," he said.

The US, which in previous rounds of talks had helped broker compromises - sometimes working alongside China - had no official delegation in Antalya. President Donald Trump has rejected the entire international climate process.

And while delegates argued over fossil fuels in Turkey, Trump, China's President Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin issued a joint declaration in Shenzhen that included a pledge to increase production and supply of refined petroleum products.
The priorities of some of the world's most powerful governments appeared very different from those being discussed in the negotiating rooms.
The EU's representative, Irish Minister Darragh O'Brien, said a deal that did not mention fossil fuels was "unconscionable"

Yet, perhaps, the picture is more optimistic than it first appears. About 130 governments backed a demand for explicit language on moving away from fossil fuels - roughly two-thirds of the countries represented in Antalya.

Christiana Figueres, who led the UN negotiations that delivered the Paris Agreement, argued that countries were right to walk away rather than endorse a weaker political commitment that might undermine the progress already made.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm75: The COP31 summit in Turkey came as evidence of climate change could not have been clearer - 2026 brought glacier collapses, record European heat, and wildfires across Asia - but also when geopolitical divisions could not have been deeper.
The result was the longest-running climate talks in UN history failed to deliver on its central political agreement – the Antalya Pacts - to further climate action.
Despite two countries, Australia and Turkey, leading the charge in their joint hosting of the negotiations, they could not bring the nations together.

After a dramatic and fractious final day where countries walked out over the absence of mention of fossil fuels in the text and money issues, questions are being asked more loudly than ever before about whether the COP process can still deliver.
Here are five, key takeaways from the talks which the hosts hoped would become known as the "implementation COP".

This was the first COP since the UN warned that global temperatures are expected to exceed 1.5C degrees above pre-industrial levels. That is the threshold which countries agreed not to breach as part of the Paris Climate Agreement signed in 2015.
The draft agreement had acknowledged the uncomfortable reality that climate action to date has failed on its most crucial of targets.
Almost exactly a decade ago a group of the world's climate scientists - the official UN body the IPCC - warned what would happen if temperatures rose 1.5C vs 2C:
Sea level rise would be 10cm higher - that would expose 10 million more people to flooding , external
The ocean would become more acidic risking irreversible damage to some marine life
Extreme heat - that's hot days and nights - in every inhabited part of the world
In a 2C world extreme heat is expected to be experienced in every inhabitated area on Earth
Throughout the talks and during the final day, many countries still acknowledged that the target remained their north star of climate action.

"This COP sought to confront hard truths – that global warming is set to overshoot 1.5C and that we must act with even more urgency to reduce emissions," said UK Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh at the close of the talks.
The draft had called for that overshoot to be kept as small and short-lived as possible – it also suggested something called carbon dioxide removal (CDR).
This is a process which takes greenhouse gases out of the atmosphere and has not been explicitly mentioned in a COP final agreement before.
Carbon dioxide can be removed naturally by planting trees - although there are limits to the scale and permanence of that.
There are other technological solutions, but these are controversial , external and are not well advanced.
This year's negotiations have exposed a troubling problem - consensus does not last forever.
On the central political agreement – the Antalya Pacts – countries could not bridge the divide on including language on fossil fuels.
And yet the very same pledge had been made just three years ago at COP28 in Dubai.
Rich nations also failed to put a figure to how much more money could be given to developing countries to adapt to climate change.
This is despite there already being a commitment from last year to triple the figure by 2035 from $40bn (£30bn) - but the interpretation of that pledge remains contested.
If governments cannot even agree to reaffirm commitments they've already made, it raises troubling questions about their ability to work together as the climate crisis intensifies.
Longest-ever UN climate talks end with no deal as deep divisions exposed

Minister Chris Bowen from Australia, who was co-leading the negotiations, pointed out at the end of the talks that the world is a very different place from when these commitments were struck just a few years ago.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqwy: Australia's Chris Bowen sits at the top table at the summit surrounded by other delegates
Countries have failed to reach a major new deal to tackle climate change after deep divisions over fossil fuels and money emerged at the UN COP31 talks in Turkey.
Negotiations were due to finish on Friday but ran late into Sunday in search of common ground, becoming the longest UN climate conference in history.
But the final deal proved unacceptable to the EU, Pacific island nations and others because it failed to directly mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.
Meanwhile, many poorer countries objected to the absence of any clear financial commitments from richer nations to help them adapt to the impacts of rising temperatures.
The last time a COP's main political agreement collapsed like this was in 2009 in Copenhagen.
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres, in his last COP before he steps down, said he was "deeply disappointed".

He took aim at what he called "powerful fossil fuel interests" who he said were taking "a page from Big Tobacco's playbook: distorting the science, delaying policy, blocking action, and piling up huge profits while people everywhere pay the price".
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, whose country co-hosted the talks, attributed the failure to "difficult geopolitical times".
After two weeks of negotiations, exhausted delegates were presented with a new, draft deal in the early hours of Sunday to try to break the deadlock.

But the words "fossil fuels" did not appear anywhere in the text. The only indirect reference to coal, oil and gas was a nod to a deal agreed at COP28 in 2023 , when countries agreed to "transition away" from fossil fuels in energy systems.

The EU's representative, Irish Minister Darragh O'Brien, made it clear that the EU "strongly" objected, saying that the "decisions go nowhere near the level of ambition needed to tackle climate change".
"It is unconscionable that we would have a climate pact that makes no mention of fossil fuels," he said.
Other countries, such as Panama and the Marshall Islands, also criticised the deal for doing nowhere near enough to tackle the pace of climate change.
A first draft of the deal on Monday mentioned "fossil fuel" or "fossil fuels" six times, but that was unacceptable to oil-producing nations.
Saudi Arabia's delegate Mohammad Ayoub said that Arab countries "continued to engage in good faith" but argued that they only accounted for a small proportion of historical greenhouse gas emissions.
Russia warned not to "turn to slogans" over coal, oil and gas, claiming that if countries moved away from fossil fuels too quickly it would lead to "fuel poverty".
Climate advocates reacted with dismay at the failure of the talks.
Former US vice-president and climate advocate Al Gore said it was "outrageous that a handful of petro-states have veto power over any mention of fossil fuels".
The COP process was "in need of significant reform", Gore wrote on X, as most countries sought "to move forward in good faith."
"It's time that we empower those leaders with a reinvigorated multilateral process that reflects the latest science and represents the will of the majority of the world," he added.
Another major sticking point has been money for poorer countries to adapt to the impacts of climate change, such as more intense heatwaves and more severe droughts.
Last year at COP30 in Brazil , nations agreed to triple the finance for that purpose.
But this year's deal contained no reference to concrete figures, nor the baseline against which that pledge would be measured. This raised fears it would give richer nations too much wriggle room.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c39w: After an eight-year journey travelling almost six billion miles (10bn km), a spacecraft called BepiColombo has arrived at its final destination and is now in orbit around Mercury.

It‘s operating in an extremely hostile environment: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun and temperatures can reach a fierce 430C and then plunge to -180C, and it is constantly blasted with intense solar radiation.
Until now, the planet has been little explored but the hope is this mission will solve some of Mercury's major mysteries.
These include uncovering why there is ice in its craters despite its proximity to the Sun, and understanding the mysterious hollows that are dotted all over its surface.

"I think it's a little bit of an under-loved planet in the inner Solar System, but I think that's one of the reasons why it is so compelling," said Prof Emma Bunce, from Leicester University, who is a principal investigator on the mission.

"There are lots of reasons, scientifically, why we really want to understand Mercury, how it formed, how it evolved, what it looks like today, but also how it interacts with the Sun and the extreme space weather that it experiences."
The spacecraft - just seen here - has taken selfies as it has closed in on Mercury
The BepiColombo mission, which is a collaboration between the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japanese Space Agency (JAXA), blasted off in 2018 , launching from French Guiana.
With the spacecraft heading deep into the inner Solar System, it has had to battle the Sun's immense gravitational pull.

So it has had its brakes on for the entire journey, and has also taken a very convoluted path - looping once around the Earth, twice around Venus and six times around Mercury - to slow it down enough to get into orbit.
This journey should have taken seven years, but a problem with BepiColombo's propulsion system meant the already epic voyage was extended by a year.
The final manoeuvre to get into orbit was a perilous one: a 37-minute handbrake turn that allowed it to be grabbed by the planet's gravity.

The European Space Agency said on X that the probe had made contact and its telemetry data confirmed that it was now flying around the planet, though it's thrusters had fired for a shorter time than planned following a software issue.
Only two spacecraft have visited Mercury until now - both Nasa missions.
Mariner-10 flew past the planet three times in the 1970s, and then the Messenger spacecraft arrived at Mercury in 2011 and spent four years in orbit.
Mercury is only a bit bigger than our Moon, and is covered in ancient volcanoes, towering cliffs and colossal craters.
The planet zips around the Sun so quickly, a year on Mercury lasts just 88 Earth days. But it turns incredibly slowly on its own axis, so a single day there lasts 59 Earth days.
These strange hollows have not been seen anywhere else in the Universe
As well as investigating why Mercury has ice in its craters in the polar regions, the mission will also spend time studying strange dents in the planet's surface.
There are thousands of hollows all over it. They are shallow but with steep sides and often clustered together, and in planetary terms, they are young: about 100,000 years old.
Scientists know they are not impact craters - larger pockmarks on the surface caused by colliding space rocks - but they are not really sure what the hollows are or how they formed.
BepiColombo will also help to study another aspect of Mercury that has been puzzling researchers. Despite the planet's tiny size, it has a huge metal core.
Prof Emma Bunce said that the planet could once have been much bigger, but was potentially the victim of a "hit and run" early in its history.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq78: Efforts to avert the collapse of talks at the UN COP31 summit have faced further delays on the second day of overtime, as countries struggle to reach a new global climate deal.
A new draft agreement was published in the early hours of Sunday which the Turkey and Australia co-hosts hoped would bridge the divide between nations.

Although it still includes no specific reference to "transitioning away from fossil fuels" - an omission in the previous draft that sparked threats of walkouts - it does acknowledge a previous commitment made by countries to do just that three years ago.
Countries were expected to reconvene to decide whether to approve a new deal, but that meeting was delayed on Sunday morning.
The president of the talks, Turkey's Environment Minister Murat Kurum, told the BBC he was "hopeful" of a breakthrough as he entered the summit on Sunday.
But that outlook was not shared by the EU, which the BBC understands considers the new text to be a backward step.
The EU and Pacific states had been arguing against the removal of fossil fuels from the draft text. The EU has not yet reacted to this latest draft.
The Africa Group is likely to be disappointed at this latest iteration as it includes no specific figure on money for adaptation and instead kicks that decision to future meetings.
The new draft also includes for the first time a recognition that the world is on track to miss the crucial goal of keeping temperatures below 1.5C of warming.
These talks are approaching the longest-running in the COP history.

If countries cannot reach consensus - as required by the UN's climate talks process - the negotiations could be suspended until next year. This has only happened once before since countries started holding COP climate meetings in 1995.
Just hours before the new text was published, EU Commissioner for Climate Wopke Hoekstra said if the bloc could not get "what is needed in terms of climate action... then there's no deal."
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, the UK's chief negotiator, struck a more hopeful tone, saying her team was still working to get an agreement.

A draft deal unveiled earlier this week called for a faster phase-out of fossil fuels, but a second, pared-down version released on Thursday stripped away all mentions of coal, oil and gas - sparking threats of a walk out.

The fallout led to the summit in Antalya blowing past the original deadline of Friday . On Saturday negotiating teams who had Sunday morning flights were rescheduling them - a sign a deal was still not in sight, and raising the risk that as teams eventually had to leave, the meeting could lose the critical numbers needed to pass an agreement.

As part of a last ditch effort to produce an acceptable text, the European Union and Saudi Arabia - who were deeply divided over the future of fossil fuels - were brought together on Saturday to seek a compromise.
COP31 President Murat Kurum says he believes the third version of the text sent to delegates addresses outlying concerns.
COP31 President and Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum told delegates in the early hours of Sunday he believed concerns had been addressed.
"We ask you to look at this decision carefully," Kurum said. "We are closer than ever to agreement on the remaining issues."

Ministers from Panama, Solomon Islands, Cote d'Ivoire and the EU were fighting to have a commitment to move away from fossil fuels put back into the final agreement, after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi Arabia pushed for its removal.

"It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it," said Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister for the environment.

According to the council, residents have a duty of care for their waste until it is disposed of correctly and should ensure it is given to a licensed waste operator.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c678: Television cook Delia Smith has joined opponents of a £1.2bn data centre, arguing it would threaten a nature reserve.
Campaigners fear the proposed centre at Keswick, on the edge of Norwich, will create noise pollution and have a negative impact on nearby Marston Marsh.

Smith, honorary life president and former majority shareholder of Norwich City FC, said: "I love Norfolk. You can't be involved in a football club for 55 years without being attached to the people and the beauty of Norfolk. I feel very strongly about it."
But developer Norwich Apex said an ecological impact assessment concluded no effect on the reserve was expected.
Delia Smith, pictured with fellow campaigner Jake Humphrey, says she feels very strongly about protecting Norfolk
Data centres are facilities that store and process vast amounts of data and run the software and online services used by millions of people.
This centre, off the A140 Ipswich Road, would need 150 MW of power to run and would feature 72 chiller units on its roof.
According to planning documents, the building would be about 20m (65ft) high.
A planning application for the centre has been lodged with South Norfolk Council.
If approved, construction could begin at the end of 2027 and it would be operational by 2028.

The plans have emerged at the same time as a much bigger proposal for a data centre and solar farm elsewhere in Norfolk, south of King's Lynn, which would require more than five times as much electricity.
The developer has said the Keswick facility would use " air-cooling technology " and not require water for cooling.
But Smith, who lives in Suffolk, said: "We haven't got enough water, and data centres use an awful lot of water.

""It's one of the biggest [data centres] and It doesn't do anything for the Norfolk community. Where is the £1.2bn coming from? And who are the people who are going to presumably make money out of it?
"It's not going to do anything for the local community, it's the opposite. It's going to be bad."
Campaigners have raised concerns about the proposed centre's effect on the nearby Marston Marsh nature reserve
It is hoped the centre will harness wind energy by connecting to the Hornsea 3 substation nearby.
Smith said: "Renewable energy is going into the grid but it doesn't supply everything now.
"What are you going to do when you have this huge data centre absolutely sucking up energy?"
Other opponents of the plan include broadcaster and entrepreneur Jake Humphrey .
Matt Tomlinson is worried that nocturnal wildlife including owls and bats will be driven away from the area
Other campaigners include Matt Tomlinson of Yare Valley Meadow Makers, who believes the development will have a "disastrous effect" on nocturnal wildlife.
"On this Marston Marsh site we have nine protected bat species, we have three different owl species and these will all need the quiet conditions to effectively hunt," he said.
"I think this is an awful idea; awful for the wildlife and awful for the people."

In recent days, Labour MP for South Norfolk, Ben Goldsborough, who believes the development would be in the wrong place , has been appointed to a new data centre committee that will scrutinise the government's national policies.

Matt Bartram, chief executive of Norwich Apex, said: "Our ambition is to deliver one of the UK's greenest data centres, using low-carbon power supplied via Norwich Main substation. Protecting nearby ecological sites, including Marston Marshes has shaped the design from the outset.
"Detailed environment assessments have informed our plans to reduce noise and screen the development from view.
"We propose planting more than 15,700 trees and over 1.7km of new hedgerow, with the plans delivering a 13% biodiversity net gain."

An Auckland University legal expert says behind the scenes pressure from the Ministry of Health altered toxicology & law experts' recommendations on the response to asbestos contaminated play sand.
This week a Consumer NZ investigation revealed conflicting claims and confusion among government agencies as concerns arose.
It said eight tonnes of the sand was sold over the last decade but Health NZ had baulked at proposals to monitor children exposed to the product.
Law Professor, Alex Sims told Checkpoint she worked alongside toxicologist, Professor Ian Shaw, in formulating recommendations for active monitoring of exposed children.
"The Ministry of Health were putting behind the scenes pressure for the briefing to be changed and, ultimately, it was changed. It's extremely disappointing.
"There were so many different government departments - they were all pointing fingers at other people. People don't seem to be doing what they're meant to do so it's all a bit of a mess," Sims said.
Sims said - despite initial claims the products were low risk - an Auckland University of Technology study would later find asbestos in the products could be inhaled when used .
"People didn't know the risks. It was thought that the asbestos wouldn't be freed unless [the sand] was mechanically compressed.
"When we changed the report we said 'you need more information' but then when the information came out later it showed that there really should be monitoring of those children," Sims said.

She said there were concerns that the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment's advisories about voluntary recalls were authored by suppliers such as Kmart and the company was told by WorkSafe that wording about the products was incorrect.

"If a recall notice has to go through, at a government department, it may take quite a while. So you might want an initial one but then there should be a thing then to look at and revise it as soon as you've got proper information and not just leave it there for, in this case, months," Sims said.
She said the country's systems for dealing with importing of potentially dangerous goods needed more teeth.

"There's no testing at the border. Since this has occurred there is a new notice that's not going to come in effect until the first of February, that's going to require suppliers of goods with sand in them, especially toys, that they have to get them tested.
"It's on the supplier to do that but the suppliers weren't following the existing law so what is there to make them follow that law?," Sims said.

In a statement, MBIE said the Consumer report raised important questions about how effectively agencies worked together and whether the country's product safety system had kept pace with global supply chains.
The Ministry of Health maintained its position that monitoring of people exposed to asbestos in sand was not recommended.
It advised people to discuss concerns with Healthline and avoid further exposure by removing the product safely.
The Ministry said concerns about an article authored by professors Sims and Shaw, recommending a public register, had been raised with Consumer NZ.

An Auckland heritage building developer says he is interested in taking on fixing up the former Fitzroy Hotel on Wakefield Street, one of the region's oldest building.
Built in the mid-1850s, the building has cracks in its facade and is the subject of a dangerous building notice.
Earlier this month, owner The Fitzroy Hotel Limited and company director Terry Huang were fined $135,000 for failing to make it safe .
The developer of St James Theatre on Queen Street, Steve Bielby of Auckland Notable Properties Trust, said the former hotel has suffered after years of no maintenance.
"That comes home to roost at some point, and unfortunately the wheel's stopped, and the current owner is holding the prize."
Auckland Council field operations manager for compliance, David Pawson said safety is the immediate priority and the dangerous building notice is still in place.
"While it's in its current state, we still need to keep Wakefield Street and Lyndock Street cordoned off to make sure that the public are safe."
The building is surrounded by high hoardings that have blocked the streets around it for years .
Huang told RNZ he could not get on with plans to prop the building until the council fixed the footpath next to the hotel, which he said was undermined.

Pawson said there had been numerous engineering reports, some potential issues were identified and investigated, and the council's investigations had shown there was no contributing cause from council assets that would be undermining the building.
A heritage assessment from 2010 showed there were cracks already present in the building before Huang's company bought it in 2015, Pawson said.
Auckland Council cannot compel the owner of a heritage building to carry out maintenance, he said.

"We can't force him to fix the roof, we can't force him to stop the water ingress which is making the problem worse. We can deal with the symptom through the building being dangerous and taking the action under The Building Act, with the dangerous building notices."
Auckland Council's spent $457,064 mitigating the risk to passersby from potential falling masonry.

Former Waitematā local board member Allan Matson pushed for heritage listing more than 20 years ago and has been watching closely. He said, with bills stacking up for Huang, one avenue could be he could sell the building.
Restoring the building is something Bielby would prepared to do.
"I have had discussions with the owner and the agent and I have put proposals forward to look at it.
"I think it is a significant place and I think it is worth saving and is capable of being saved, so I'd love to give it that opportunity if I can.
He estimated the work needed would cost between $1.5m and $2m.
A registered valuation Auckland Council presented as evidence at court earlier this month valued the property at $1.45m,
Huang's company paid $1.795m for it in March 2015. He told RNZ he would be prepared to sell "at a reasonable price".

Health officials are seeking assurances about staffing and care for patients at a Dannevirke health clinic, where the last onsite GP is leaving and telehealth services are relied on.
The doctor was working at the Barraud Street Health Centre in the Tararua town, but is moving to another practice.

RNZ understands this has left a small team of registered nurses, healthcare assistants and administrators at the centre, run by the troubled Tararua Health Group, whose operations in the district are under review by Health NZ.

Tony Wai, the chief executive of the The Primary Health Organisation (the PHO) - which contracts the Barraud Street Health Centre for its services - says a formal notice has been issued to the Tararua Health Group and talks were held on Wednesday morning about care options.
Tararua Health Group, owned by nationwide primary care provider Omnihealth, until October also ran the Dannevirke Community Hospital, which is next to the Barraud Street Health Centre.
Health NZ has since taken over operations at the community hospital after there was a temporary freeze on it taking new patients in September due to concerns about patient safety.
Tararua Health Group also previously ran the Pahīatua Medical Centre, which had seven staff resignations, due to overwork and safety concerns .
Earlier in November the medical centre was bought by Ngāti Kahungunu ki Tāmaki-nui-a-Rua Trust .

In Dannevirke, which has a population of just over 5500 people, Rangitāne o Tamaki nui-ā-Rua recently took over the Tini Whetū Health and Wellbeing Centre - this clinic wasn't run by Tararua Health Group.
Health officials are watching the Barraud Street Health Centre, where the last onsite GP is leaving.
RNZ understands remaining onsite staff at the Barraud Street Health Centre are supplemented by GPs and a nurse practitioner offering telehealth services.
It Is understood that this week the telehealth GP was sick for a day, placing extra pressure on staff.

A source told RNZ the small team of staff at the clinic were responsible for daily primary healthcare tasks, including clinical assessments, follow-up care, administration and co-ordinating consultations with clinicians working remotely.

"The absence of onsite GPs and nurse practitioners creates additional challenges for patients requiring physical examinations, urgent assessments and ongoing management of complex medical conditions," the source said.

"While telehealth can be a valuable component of healthcare delivery, it cannot fully replace accessible, face-to-face medical services, particularly in rural communities where alternative options may already be limited."

The source said it was concerning to hear patients from the Barraud Street Health Centre turning to other clinics because they were unable to access care, and that raised concerns about whether the clinic could provide appropriate primary healthcare and whether staff were under too much pressure.

"Patients should not have to reach a point of crisis before they can access appropriate healthcare, nor should neighbouring healthcare providers be expected to absorb the consequences of an under-resourced medical centre."
The source said they would like to see the Barraud Street Health Centre transferred to a new or existing entity.
Tararua Health Group director Mark Wills was approached for comment, but did not respond.
Wai said the PHO was aware of "workforce and service delivery challenges" at the Barraud Street Health Centre, including the impending departure of the onsite GP.

An independent workplace culture review of the country's lead agency supporting victims of crime and trauma says some staff believed speaking up about workplace concerns carried a "personal cost" including "isolation, being assigned extra work or changes in their relationship with their manager".

The review did not find evidence of an "organisation-wide" culture of bullying or toxicity at Victim Support but it also said that staff concerns could not be treated as "solely historical or as coming from a small number of dissatisfied individuals".

Although there was a "generally positive, values-led culture overall", the review found "uneven employee experience, with concerns particularly concentrated in certain local leadership relationships, psychological safety, and confidence in the outcomes of workplace concerns raised".
Eight of those spoken to as part of the review described "repeated conduct of undermining comments, aggressive behaviour, isolation, and informal consequences for speaking up".
The review made 12 recommendations and outlined five principal opportunities for improvement.
The external review came after reporting by RNZ in July over claims of a "toxic" and "bullying" workplace culture, four years after an investigation into similar allegations.
RNZ spoke to several current and former workers who raised concerns about the culture at Victim Support. One person described it as a "very unsafe environment".
The agency's chief executive James McCulloch earlier said the agency "does not accept that these claims reflect Victim Support today".
Then, in August, the agency announced it had agreed to commission a review of the organisation's workplace culture, confidence in people leadership and the processes for resolving workplace concerns.

The review, by Charlotte Stevens, heard from 57 current Victim Support employees between August and October. This represented about 36 percent of the workforce. The review did not include speaking to former staff .
Four people outside Victim Support, including representatives of the Ministry of Justice and Police, were also interviewed.
The overall assessment was that the agency had made "substantial organisational progress" since an earlier review.
"There are identifiable strengths in organisational culture, and considerable pride in Victim Support's purpose."
Employee experience was "not uniform and appears to be materially influenced by immediate leadership and local team dynamics".
"Employees generally understand how to raise concerns, but confidence in what happens after concerns are raised is less consistent, particularly among frontline employees."
It also said the evidence did not establish a "toxic and bullying workplace culture".
"The recurring concerns appear to reflect a mix of historical experiences, organisational change, differing expectations and understanding, and some current, localised issues."

Among the key findings of the review was that there was a "generally positive, values-led culture overall, with genuine pride in the organisation's purpose, but experience varies considerably depending on a person's specific team and immediate leader".

In relation to senior leadership, most participants who addressed the question had confidence in the Senior Leadership Team (SLT). Confidence was strongest among SLT and national office participants and some managers.
"Frontline views are more divided, partly because the SLT is less visible to frontline staff day-to-day, and some frontline staff do not know who is on the SLT."
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/science-and-t: Crucial digital infrastructure systems have been under pressure over the past few weeks, with a number of high-profile hacks and network outages reported both globally and locally.
RNZ has not proven immune to this, with an apparent cyber breach of its own systems reported today , but it is far from the only organisation struggling to deal with such digital dilemmas.

While a new major breach seems to be revealed every day, they appear to have no direct connection, as hackers use AI technology to break into systems, while networks struggle and sometimes collapse after upgrades. The National Cyber Security Centre says frontier AI is accelerating cyber threats , with vulnerabilities able to be identified and exploited faster.
Here are some of the major technological breakdowns that have been reported in New Zealand and around the world in just the past month:
Frontier AI is reported to be accelerating cyber threats, with vulnerabilities able to be identified and exploited faster
GORODENKOFF PRODUCTIONS/SCIENCE / GPR / Science Photo Library via AFP

The CIA and Office of the Director of National Intelligence in the United States have been subjected to an apparent hack affecting unclassified information, it was reported today , with the intrusion hit a system the agencies draw on​ for open-source intelligence analysis.
Officials emphasised that no classified information was affected.

While it was not immediately clear when the hack occurred, who was responsible for it, or if it has been resolved, the incident does not appear to be related to an apparent hack of the FBI's nation-wide criminal information database reported on Friday .

The FBI breach - which targeted its nation-wide criminal information database that serves as a lifeline between federal, state and local law enforcement - was the second attack on the federal agency in recent months.
The government agency hacks have followed a series of unrelated high-profile tech outages affecting banks and the FAA's air traffic control system.

All US flights were grounded for hours in mid-November after a massive systems failure , leading to thousands of flights being delayed or cancelled. The Federal Aviation Administration traced the problem to a single router in Arkansas. At about the same time, Chase Bank said thousands of its customers had trouble using online accounts , and several other banks reported issues.
Stranded travellers queue for rental cars at Salt Lake City International Airport during the nationwide ground stop.

The biggest tech outage of the month saw several key Microsoft services become unavailable for almost a day . Offices around the world were disrupted when services such as Outlook and Teams were out of action for more than 20 hours.
Meanwhile, some of the world's most visited websites, including those of Zoom, HSBC, Equifax , CNN, Salesforce and Ikea, were compromised in an effort to steal cryptocurrency and infect iPhones.

Travel booking companies Bookit, Booking.com and Expedia have each recently confirmed data breaches , while in late October, Sony confirmed a data breach had compromised 2.5 million records containing current and former customers' personal information.

In Europe, grocery stores from Sweden to Portugal were hit by a suspected cyberattack on their freezer systems with food retailers forced to throw out produce that had spoiled or was at risk of spoiling after refrigerator temperatures soared overnight.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/regional/2772: Dunedin's Port Chalmers Pool will remain open for now, with the council agreeing to investigate ways to make it more cost effective and involve the community in decisions about its longer-term future.
The Dunedin City Council was considering closing the pool after staff were asked to come up with operational savings costs as part of its long term plan.
A staff report said the pool received an average of 4735 visits per year, with the net operating cost amounting to $102.73 per visit.

At a meeting today, councillors agreed to keep the pool operating under its current seasonal lifeguarded model, with staff to report back to council by the end of January on ways to improve its financial sustainability.
A number of Port Chalmers residents and pool users showed up to the meeting in support of keeping the pool open. An online petition calling to halt its closure had received almost 2000 signatures.

Residents were unable to speak about the pool during the meeting's public forum because the council said it did not pre-consult on Long Term Plan proposals and the West Harbour Community Board had expressed disappointment that there was not a lack of meaningful engagement before the matter was brought forward to council.

A major point of debate was whether the reported pool attendance figures accurately reflected its use, and staff said they stood by the revenue and operating figures, but accepted there could be some variation in attendance numbers.

Councillors discussed to how reduce costs or increase use, including sponsorships and partnerships, volunteer lifeguards, longer opening hours, solar power and potentially a targeted rate for the Port Chalmers community.
The options before council were to close the pool after the summer season, create a new pool key access-only system or keep the pool open under the existing arrangements with lifeguards.

The staff report said the council had earmarked $577,000 for maintenance and upgrades in the invested in 2025-34 plan. Based on projected costs over the next decade, the unstaffed key access option would save about $72,000 per year, while closing the pool would save about $264,000 per year.
Councillor Steve Walker put through a motion that the council continue to operate the pool under its current seasonal lifeguarding model, pending further consideration by the council.

Staff were directed to investigate further options to improve the financial sustainability of the pool, including pricing, utilisation and attendance data, sponsorship and partnership opportunities and alternative operating arrangements, with a report to come back to council before the end of January.
"Port Chalmers Pool is far more than a swimming facility and its value to our community cannot be measured by its operating cost alone," Walker said.

"In a country surrounded by water, swimming is not simply a recreational activity, it is an essential life skill. The pool provides local children with opportunities to learn to swim, develop confidence and acquire the water safety skills that could one day save their lives."
He said the pool was also an important rehabilitation facility for older people, post-surgical patients, people living with chronic pain and those with disabilities.

When it came to the finances, Walker said a staff report estimated that closing the pool would save approximately $264,000 annually, but also identifies ongoing costs of around $109,000 even if it was to close.

A complaint over an alleged slap at an Auckland school has raised questions about when teachers are legally allowed to make physical contact with students.
Corporal punishment is banned in New Zealand schools under the Education and Training Act 2020.
However, teachers and other authorised school staff may use physical restraint in limited circumstances to prevent imminent harm to a student or another person.
So where does the law draw the line, and what can parents do if they believe a teacher has gone too far?
A mother is calling for the immediate suspension of a teacher who allegedly slapped her 7-year-old daughter's hand during a school rehearsal.
The alleged incident occurred on 5 November at Tōtara Point School, a state-funded charter school in Epsom, Auckland.
The mother, Amanda Chang, claimed a teacher slapped her daughter's hand while she was holding another student's hand during the rehearsal.
Chang said her daughter had been afraid to attend the teacher's classes since the alleged incident. She contacted the school immediately and requested an investigation.
According to the school's findings shared with RNZ by Chang, the school concluded the teacher had made physical contact with the two students to separate them while they were holding hands.
However, it described the contact as brief and said it was not intended as discipline or punishment.
The teacher would receive a verbal warning, a record of the incident would be kept on the teacher's file, and the school board had been informed, according to the findings.
The school's leadership team would also work closely with the teacher, who had been asked to complete refresher training on classroom management and physical restraint policies, it said.
Chang disputed the school's findings and had since lodged complaints with the school board, the Teaching Council, New Zealand Police, the Ministry of Education and the Charter School Agency.
"There is a significant difference between gently separating two children's hands and slapping a child's hand with an open palm while visibly angry," Chang said.
The school declined to comment publicly to RNZ, citing the interests of the children involved.
The dispute highlights a broader question about the boundaries of physical contact between teachers and students, and when such contact may cross the line.
Section 98 of the Education and Training Act 2020 explicitly prohibits corporal punishment and seclusion in registered schools.

Helen Hurst, group general manager of operational standards and support at the Ministry of Education, said all teachers were expected to maintain professional boundaries and follow the Teaching Council's Code of Professional Responsibility and Standards for the Teaching Profession.

Hurst said teachers and other school staff sometimes needed to make physical contact with students as part of ordinary school life, such as careful contact to guide a younger child, helping with an activity, providing comfort to a distressed student or administering first aid.

The ministry considered physical contact appropriate when it was for the student's benefit, the student was willing to be touched and the contact was limited to appropriate areas of the body, generally the shoulders, arms, hands and upper back.
The Education and Training Act 2020 sets strict conditions on the use of physical restraint .

Under Part 3, Subpart 3 of the Act, teachers and authorised staff members may use physical restraint only when necessary to prevent imminent harm to a student's or another person's health, safety or wellbeing, and when they reasonably believe there is no other option available.

A sharp rise in reported cyber security incidents has caused direct financial loss to climb to $5.9 million - more than double the $2.7m loss reported in the previous quarter.
The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) recorded its busiest quarter in two years, with about 1700 incidents reported between July and September - about 600 more than the previous quarter.
NCSC deputy director Catriona Robinson said frontier AI was accelerating cyber threats, with vulnerabilities able to be identified and exploited faster.
" Cyber threats are becoming more frequent , more sophisticated, and more costly."
The number of incidents that has potentially national significance almost doubled, with about 180 incidents needing specialist technical support.
Phishing and credential harvesting remained the most commonly reported incident category, with scams and fraud coming next.

"Individuals, businesses, and organisations should take this as a signal to review their cyber security settings, ensure basic protections are in place, and remain vigilant against increasingly sophisticated online threats," Robinson said.

There were 94 reports involving command and control server hosting - incidents when malicious actors establish a foothold within a target network and communicate with attacker-controlled infrastructure to issue commands, deploy additional malware, or extract data.
Incidents from the education and training sector rose from 13 to 43.

Robinson told Midday Report an attack described in the report as "highly significant" concerned the Zenith Technology (ZenTech) attack which involved the hacking of South Island patients' health data.
She said any business or organisation should not pay a ransomware demand.
"Don't trust cybercriminals for a start. There is no gentleman's agreement in cybercriminal land. Just because you pay a ransom doesn't guarantee you'll get what they say you will."
It only reinforced that the victim would pay a ransom and contribute to the criminals' business models.
She said recent international research suggested at least 20 percent of randomware victims were refusing to pay, which was forcing the criminals to change how they operated.
Robinson said China continued to be "a persistent and capable adversary active in New Zealand for sure".
While China was a major trading ally, New Zealand named it in reports such as the most recent one and also raised its objections via diplomatic efforts.

For the state-sponsored attacks, the hackers were after New Zealand's sensitive government secrets and /or intellectual property theft in contrast to overseas where there has been hacking of critical infrastructure.
"We haven't seen that in New Zealand yet but there's no reason to think that might not happen."
She didn't believe hackers were active during the recent general election.
